docs.title: Cortex Installation System Requirements
docs.text: Cortex requires a supported operating system, along with sufficient hardware resources, to ensure stable and efficient operation.

docs.title: Hardware requirements
docs.text:
Estimated resource recommendations are provided to offer guidance based on typical usage scenarios.

Hardware sizing guidance

The listed hardware values represent typical usage scenarios. However, hardware sizing for Cortex installation depends on several factors:

  • Usage intensity: Number of analyzers and responders running concurrently
  • Data volume: Number of observables submitted for analysis
  • Performance expectations: Expected job throughput under typical and peak loads
  • Deployment method: Installation via packages, Docker containers, or Kubernetes

Initial deployments can start with minimal configurations and be scaled based on observed performance.

Package installationDocker Compose deploymentKubernetes deployment with Helm

The following resources are recommended when Cortex and Elasticsearch are hosted on a single machine:

  • 8 vCPU
  • 16 GB of RAM

For Docker Compose deployments of Cortex with Elasticsearch, hardware requirements vary by setup profile. Each profile defines a specific performance level. The testing profile also deploys Cassandra and TheHive as part of a combined demo stack—see Deploy a Demo Docker Environment for details.

Profile Usage Recommended memory Recommended CPU Testing environment Functional testing of TheHive and Cortex 8 GB RAM 4 vCPUs Production environment #1 Standard production workload 16 GB RAM 4 vCPUs Production environment #2 High-performance production workload 32 GB RAM 8 vCPUs

For Kubernetes deployments, apply the same hardware recommendations as for the Docker Compose deployment in single-replica configurations. When deploying multiple replicas in a clustered setup, per-node hardware requirements can be reduced, as workload and resource utilization are distributed across replicas.

Heap size guidelines

Cortex and Elasticsearch each run on the JVM and require explicit heap size configuration in production environments. Especially when both services run on the same host, their combined heap allocation competes for available RAM. Undefined heap settings may cause memory contention or out-of-memory errors.

Deactivate memory swapping

Memory swapping on the host running Elasticsearch degrades performance: garbage collection and cluster communication then depend on disk speed instead of RAM. Deactivate swap entirely, or set bootstrap.memory_lock: true in elasticsearch.yml to lock the JVM heap in RAM. See Disable swapping in the official Elasticsearch documentation.

docs.title: Backup and Restore Data
docs.text:
All persistent data is stored in an Elasticsearch database. The backup and restore procedures are the ones that are detailed in Elasticsearch documentation.

Note: you may have to adapt your indices in the examples below. To find the right index, use the following command :

curl 'localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v'

To save all your data you only need to backup the last indice. For example, if the previous command gives you the following results, all your data belongs to cortex_1.

In the rest of this document, ensure to change to your own last index in order to backup or restore all your data.

docs.title: 1. Create a backup repository
docs.text:
First you must define a location in local filesystem (where Elasticsearch instance runs) where the backup will be written. This repository must be declared in the Elasticsearch configuration. Edit elasticsearch.yml file by adding:

path.repo: ["/absolute/path/to/backup/directory"]

Then, restart the Elasticsearch service.

Note: Be careful if you run Elasticsearch in Docker, the directory must be mapped in host filesystem using --volume parameter (cf. Docker documentation).

docs.title: 2. Register a snapshot repository
docs.text:
Create an Elasticsearch snapshot point named cortex_backup with the following command (set the same path in the location setting as the one set in the configuration file):

$ curl -XPUT 'http://localhost:9200/_snapshot/cortex_backup' -d '{
    "type": "fs",
    "settings": {
        "location": "/absolute/path/to/backup/directory",
        "compress": true
    }
}'

The result of the command should look like this :

{"acknowledged":true}

Since, everything is fine to backup and restore data.

docs.title: 3. Backup your data
docs.text:
Create a backup named snapshot_1 of all your data by executing the following command :

$ curl -XPUT 'http://localhost:9200/_snapshot/cortex_backup/snapshot_1?wait_for_completion=true&pretty' -d '{
  "indices": "<INDEX>"
}'
This command terminates only when the backup is complete and the result of the command should look like this:

{
  "snapshots": [{
    "snapshot": "snapshot_1",
    "uuid": "ZQ3kv5-FQoeN3NFIhfKgMg",
    "version_id": 5060099,
    "version": "5.6.0",
    "indices": ["cortex_1"],
    "state": "SUCCESS",
    "start_time": "2018-01-29T14:41:51.580Z",
    "start_time_in_millis": 1517236911580,
    "end_time": "2018-01-29T14:42:05.216Z",
    "end_time_in_millis": 1517236925216,
    "duration_in_millis": 13636,
    "failures": [],
    "shards": {
      "total": 41,
      "failed": 0,
      "successful": 41
    }
  }]
}

Note: You can backup the last index of Cortex (you can list indices in your Elasticsearch cluster with curl -s http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices | cut -d ' ' -f3 ) or all indices with _all value.

docs.title: 4. Restore data
docs.text:
Restore will do the reverse actions : it reads the backup in your snapshot directory and loads indices into the Elasticsearch cluster. This operation is done with the following command : 

$ curl -XPOST 'http://localhost:9200/_snapshot/cortex_backup/snapshot_1/_restore' -d '
{
  "indices": "<INDEX>"
}'

The result of the command should look like this :

{"accepted":true}

Note: be sure to restore data from the same version of Elasticsearch.

docs.title: 5. Moving data from one server to another
docs.text: If you want to move your data from one server from another: - Create your backup on the origin server (steps 1, 2, 3) - copy your backup directory from the origin server to the destination server - On the destination server : - Register your backup repository in the Elasticsearch configuration (step 1) - Register your snapshot repository with the same snapshot name (step 2) - Restore your data (step 4)

docs.title: Analyzers / Responders communication
docs.text:
From version 3, cortexutils 2.x is required because communication between Cortex and the analyzers/responders has changed. Analyzers and responders don't need to be rewritten if they use cortexutils. Cortex 2 send data using stdin and receive result from stdout.

Cortex 3 uses files: a job is stored in a folder with the following structure:

job_folder
  \_ input
   |    \_ input.json    <- input data, equivalent to stdin with Cortex 2.x
   |    |_ attachment    <- optional extra file when analysis concerns a file
   |_ output
        \_ output.json   <- report of the analysis (generated by analyzer or responder)
        |_ extra_file(s) <- optional extra files linked to report (generated by analyzer)

Job folder is provided to analyzer/responder as argument. Currently, only one job is acceptable but in future release, analyzer/responder will accept several job at a time (bulk mode) in order to increase performance.

docs.title: Switch to Manual Download and Installation
Switch to Manual Download and Installation for Cortex
docs.text:
Following the APT and YUM repositories deprecation notice, Cortex installations must switch from repository-based package management to a manual download and installation process.

For instructions on performing the same process for TheHive, see Switch to Manual Download and Installation for TheHive.

Are you concerned?

Use this procedure if you currently install or update Cortex with packages using apt-get install, apt-get upgrade, yum install, or yum update.

You aren't affected if you run Cortex through Docker deployments.

If you are a new user, follow the instructions in the step-by-step installation guide.

Dependencies

Before starting this procedure, run the following commands:

Procedure

docs.title: For DEB-based systems:
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install wget curl gnupg coreutils

docs.title: For RPM-based systems:
docs.text:
sudo yum update
sudo yum install wget curl gnupg coreutils

docs.title: Step 1: Manually install Cortex
docs.text:
DEBRPM

Destination path

The commands below use /tmp/ as the download path. Replace it with the full local directory path where you want to save the files.

  1. Download the installation package along with its SHA256 checksum and signature files.

    • Using wget:

      wget -O /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/deb/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb
wget -O /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/sha256/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.sha256
wget -O /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/asc/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.asc

      To download a specific version instead of the latest, use the following format:

      wget -O /tmp/<file_name>.deb https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/deb/<file_name>.deb
wget -O /tmp/<file_name>.deb.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/sha256/<file_name>.deb.sha256
wget -O /tmp/<file_name>.deb.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/asc/<file_name>.deb.asc
      • Replace <file_name> with the full name of the versioned file you want to install. For example, use cortex_3.2.1-2_all.
      • Replace <major.minor_version> with the corresponding version directory. For example, use 3.2.

      Package repository

      For details on package organization and naming conventions, see Cortex Package Repository.

    • Using curl:

      curl -o /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/deb/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb
curl -o /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/sha256/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.sha256
curl -o /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/asc/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.asc

curl -o /tmp/<file_name>.deb.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/sha256/<file_name>.deb.sha256
curl -o /tmp/<file_name>.deb.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/asc/<file_name>.deb.asc
      • Replace <file_name> with the full name of the versioned file you want to install. For example, use cortex_3.2.1-2_all.
      • Replace <major.minor_version> with the corresponding version directory. For example, use 3.2.

      Package repository

      For details on package organization and naming conventions, see Cortex Package Repository.

  2. Verify the integrity of the downloaded package.

    • Check the SHA256 checksum by comparing it with the provided value.

      a. Generate the SHA256 checksum of your downloaded package.

      sha256sum /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb

      b. Compare the output hash with the official SHA256 value listed in the .sha256 file.

      cat /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.sha256

      c. If both hashes match exactly, the file integrity is verified. If not, the file may be corrupted or tampered with—don't proceed with installation, and contact the StrangeBee Security team.

    • Verify the GPG signature using the public key.

      a. Download the public key at keys.download.strangebee.com using wget or curl.

      wget -O /tmp/strangebee.gpg https://keys.download.strangebee.com/latest/gpg/strangebee.gpg

      curl -o /tmp/strangebee.gpg https://keys.download.strangebee.com/latest/gpg/strangebee.gpg

      b. Import the key into your GPG keyring.

      gpg --import /tmp/strangebee.gpg

      c. Verify the downloaded package signature.

      gpg --verify /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb.asc /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb

      d. Expected result.

      You should see output similar to:

      gpg: Good signature from "TheHive Project (TheHive release key) <support@thehive-project.org>"

      The key fingerprint must match: 0CD5 AC59 DE5C 5A8E 0EE1 3849 3D99 BB18 562C BC1C

      Expected GPG warning

      gpg: WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature!
gpg:          There is no indication that the signature belongs to the owner.
      This warning is expected. It means the package is signed with the official TheHive release key, but you haven't marked this key as trusted in your local GPG setup. As long as you see Good signature and the fingerprint matches, the verification is successful. Don't mark our key as globally trusted—the warning is a normal safety reminder and should remain visible.

      If you don't see Good signature, if the fingerprint differs, or if the signature is reported as BAD, don't install the package. This indicates the integrity or authenticity of the file can't be confirmed. Report the issue to the StrangeBee Security team.

  3. Install the package.

    • Using apt-get to manage dependencies automatically:

      sudo apt-get install /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb

    • Using dpkg:

      sudo dpkg -i /tmp/cortex_4.1.0-1_all.deb

docs.title: Step 2: Remove the old repository
docs.text:
Then, remove or deactivate the old repository to avoid stale configurations.

Why you should remove or deactivate the old repository

Keeping the old repository configuration can cause your system to download outdated or conflicting packages during updates, potentially breaking your installation or causing unexpected behavior.

DEBRPM

Run the following commands:

sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/strangebee.list
sudo apt-get update

a. Deactivate the repository.

sudo yum-config-manager --disable strangebee

b. Optional: Remove the repository file.

sudo rm /etc/yum.repos.d/strangebee.repo
sudo yum clean all
Next steps
  • Switch to Manual Download and Installation for TheHive

docs.title: Upgrade Cortex to Version 4.1
docs.text:
In this tutorial, you'll upgrade Cortex from version 3.1.x+ to 4.1.x.

Because Cortex can't support multiple major versions of Elasticsearch simultaneously, this upgrade requires moving from Elasticsearch 7.x to 8.x.

By the end, you'll have successfully upgraded both Elasticsearch to 8.x and Cortex to 4.1.x, with all services running and connected.

Shared Elasticsearch instance

If you share the same Elasticsearch instance between Cortex and TheHive, ensure that your TheHive version also supports Elasticsearch 8.x. If you're running TheHive 5.2.16 or earlier, upgrade TheHive at the same time as Cortex.

Maintenance window required

This procedure involves restarting services. Schedule a maintenance window to prevent service disruption.

Back up before upgrading

Before upgrading Cortex, create a complete backup of your data and configurations. See Back Up and Restore Data for detailed guidance.

This tutorial applies to single-node Elasticsearch instances.

docs.title: Step 1: Stop Cortex service
docs.text:
Before upgrading Elasticsearch, stop the Cortex service to prevent index writes during the process.

Service commands

For stop/restart commands depending on your installation method, refer back to the relevant installation guide.

Stop TheHive if sharing Elasticsearch

If you share your Elasticsearch instance with TheHive, stop TheHive as well before upgrading Elasticsearch to prevent data inconsistencies.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the Elasticsearch version
docs.text:
You can't upgrade directly from Elasticsearch versions earlier than 7.17.x to 8.x. Before continuing, confirm that your deployment is running Elasticsearch 7.17.x.

  1. Check your current Elasticsearch version:

    curl -X GET "localhost:9200"

    Look for the version.number field in the response.

  2. If your Elasticsearch version is earlier than 7.17.x, continue to the next step. If you're already on 7.17.x, skip to Step 4.

docs.title: (Optional) Step 3: Upgrade Elasticsearch to 7.17.x
docs.text:
If your current version is below 7.17.x, upgrade to the latest 7.17.x release before moving forward.

Follow the official Elasticsearch 7.17 upgrade guide to complete this upgrade.

docs.title: Step 4: Prepare for Elasticsearch 8.x upgrade
docs.text:
Now that you're running Elasticsearch 7.17.x, verify that all features and indexes are ready for migration to 8.x.

  1. Check upgrade compatibility using the Elasticsearch feature upgrade API.

    curl -X GET "localhost:9200/_migration/system_features"

  2. Review the response to ensure all features and indexes report as ready for upgrade.

    If any elements require action, follow the recommendations in the API response before proceeding.

docs.title: Step 5: Upgrade Elasticsearch to 8.x
docs.text:
With compatibility verified, you're ready to upgrade Elasticsearch to version 8.x.

  1. Follow the official Elasticsearch upgrade documentation to complete the upgrade.

    Automatic restart

    If you're using package-based or containerized installations, Elasticsearch restarts are handled automatically during the upgrade.

  2. Verify that Elasticsearch 8.x is running successfully.

    curl -X GET "localhost:9200"

    You should see version 8.x in the response.

curl -o /tmp/<file_name>.noarch.rpm.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/sha256/<file_name>.noarch.rpm.sha256
curl -o /tmp/<file_name>.noarch.rpm.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/asc/<file_name>.noarch.rpm.asc
      • Replace <file_name> with the full name of the versioned file you want to install. For example, use cortex-3.2.1-1.
      • Replace <major.minor_version> with the corresponding version directory. For example, use 3.2.

      Package repository

      For details on package organization and naming conventions, see Cortex Package Repository.

  2. Verify the integrity of the downloaded package.

    • Check the SHA256 checksum by comparing it with the provided value.

      a. Generate the SHA256 checksum of your downloaded package.

      sha256sum /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm

      b. Compare the output hash with the official SHA256 value listed in the .sha256 file.

      cat /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm.sha256

      c. If both hashes match exactly, the file integrity is verified. If not, the file may be corrupted or tampered with—don't proceed with installation, and contact the StrangeBee Security team.

    • Verify the GPG signature using the public key.

      a. Download the public key at keys.download.strangebee.com using wget or curl.

      wget -O /tmp/strangebee.gpg https://keys.download.strangebee.com/latest/gpg/strangebee.gpg

      curl -o /tmp/strangebee.gpg https://keys.download.strangebee.com/latest/gpg/strangebee.gpg

      b. Import the key into your GPG keyring.

      gpg --import /tmp/strangebee.gpg

      c. Verify the downloaded package signature.

      gpg --verify /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm.asc /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm

      d. Expected result.

      You should see output similar to:

      gpg: Good signature from "TheHive Project (TheHive release key) <support@thehive-project.org>"

      The key fingerprint must match: 0CD5 AC59 DE5C 5A8E 0EE1 3849 3D99 BB18 562C BC1C

      Expected GPG warning

      gpg: WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature!
gpg:          There is no indication that the signature belongs to the owner.
      This warning is expected. It means the package is signed with the official TheHive release key, but you haven't marked this key as trusted in your local GPG setup. As long as you see Good signature and the fingerprint matches, the verification is successful. Don't mark our key as globally trusted—the warning is a normal safety reminder and should remain visible.

      If you don't see Good signature, if the fingerprint differs, or if the signature is reported as BAD, don't install the package. This indicates the integrity or authenticity of the file can't be confirmed. Report the issue to the StrangeBee Security team.

  3. Install the package.

    • Using yum to manage dependencies automatically:

      sudo yum install /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm

    • Using dnf to manage dependencies automatically:

      sudo dnf install /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm

    • Using rpm:

      sudo rpm -Uvh /tmp/cortex-4.1.0-1.noarch.rpm

If you prefer more control over where Cortex is installed, need to use it in environments without package managers, or want to avoid dependency issues, you can install Cortex by downloading a ZIP binary package.

Destination path

The commands below use /opt/ as the download path. Replace it with the full local directory path where you want to save the files.

  1. Download the binary package along with its SHA256 checksum and signature files. You can install Cortex anywhere on your filesystem.

    • Using wget

      wget -O /opt/cortex/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/zip/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip
wget -O /opt/cortex/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/sha256/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.sha256
wget -O /opt/cortex/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/asc/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.asc

      To download a specific version instead of the latest, use the following format:

      wget -O /opt/<file_name>.zip cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/zip/<file_name>.zip
wget -O /opt/<file_name>.zip.sha256 cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/sha256/<file_name>.zip.sha256
wget -O /opt/<file_name>.zip.asc cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/asc/<file_name>.zip.asc
      • Replace <file_name> with the full name of the versioned file you want to install. For example, use cortex-3.2.1-2.
      • Replace <major.minor_version> with the corresponding version directory. For example, use 3.2.

      Package repository

      For details on package organization and naming conventions, see Cortex Package Repository.

    • Using curl

      curl -o /opt/cortex/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/zip/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip
curl -o /opt/cortex/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.sha256 https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/sha256/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.sha256
curl -o /opt/cortex/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.asc https://cortex.download.strangebee.com/4.1/asc/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.asc

      To download a specific version instead of the latest, use the following format:

      curl -o /opt/<file_name>.zip cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/zip/<file_name>.zip
curl -o /opt/<file_name>.zip.sha256 cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/sha256/<file_name>.zip.sha256
curl -o /opt/<file_name>.zip.asc cortex.download.strangebee.com/<major.minor_version>/asc/<file_name>.zip.asc
      • Replace <file_name> with the full name of the versioned file you want to install. For example, use cortex-3.2.1-2.
      • Replace <major.minor_version> with the corresponding version directory. For example, use 3.2.

      Package repository

      For details on package organization and naming conventions, see Cortex Package Repository.

  2. Verify the integrity of the downloaded package.

    • Check the SHA256 checksum by comparing it with the provided value.

      a. Generate the SHA256 checksum of your downloaded package.

      sha256sum /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip

      b. Compare the output hash with the official SHA256 value listed in the .sha256 file.

      cat /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.sha256

      c. If both hashes match exactly, the file integrity is verified. If not, the file may be corrupted or tampered with—don't proceed with unzipping or installation, and contact the StrangeBee Security team.

    • Verify the GPG signature using the public key.

      a. Download the public key at keys.download.strangebee.com using wget or curl.

      wget -O /opt/strangebee.gpg https://keys.download.strangebee.com/latest/gpg/strangebee.gpg

      curl -o /opt/strangebee.gpg https://keys.download.strangebee.com/latest/gpg/strangebee.gpg

      b. Import the key into your GPG keyring.

      gpg --import /opt/strangebee.gpg

      c. Verify the downloaded package signature.

      gpg --verify /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip.asc /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip

      d. Expected result.

      You should see output similar to:

      gpg: Good signature from "TheHive Project (TheHive release key) <support@thehive-project.org>"

      The key fingerprint must match: 0CD5 AC59 DE5C 5A8E 0EE1 3849 3D99 BB18 562C BC1C

      Expected GPG warning

      gpg: WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature!
gpg:          There is no indication that the signature belongs to the owner.
      This warning is expected. It means the package is signed with the official TheHive release key, but you haven't marked this key as trusted in your local GPG setup. As long as you see Good signature and the fingerprint matches, the verification is successful. Don't mark our key as globally trusted—the warning is a normal safety reminder and should remain visible.

      If you don't see Good signature, if the fingerprint differs, or if the signature is reported as BAD, don't install the package. This indicates the integrity or authenticity of the file can't be confirmed. Report the issue to the StrangeBee Security team.

  3. Unzip the package.

    Unzip paths

    • Replace /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip with the full path to the ZIP file you downloaded.
    • Replace /opt/ after -d with the directory where you want to extract the contents of the archive.
    unzip /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1.zip -d /opt/
sudo ln -s /opt/cortex-4.1.0-1 /opt/cortex

  4. Make the Cortex binary executable.

    cd /opt/
chmod +x cortex

If you deployed using the StrangeBee Docker Compose profiles, pull the latest version of the repository before redeploying. The docker-compose.yml, configuration templates, and helper scripts may have changed between versions. The version is set in the versions.env file at the root of the repository, with the cortex_image_version variable.

If you used the public image directly, update the image tag to thehiveproject/cortex:4.1, or to a specific version if you don't want the latest.

docs.title: Step 7: Restart Cortex and verify connectivityNext steps
docs.text:
You're now ready to bring Cortex back online and ensure everything connects properly.

  1. Restart the Cortex service.

  2. Verify that Cortex connects successfully to the upgraded Elasticsearch instance.

    Check the Cortex logs for successful connection messages and confirm that the application is available.

  3. Optional: Restart TheHive if you share the Elasticsearch instance.

    This restores full connectivity between TheHive and the upgraded Elasticsearch instance.

  4. Verify that both Cortex (and TheHive, if applicable) are functioning normally.

You've successfully upgraded Cortex to version 4.1.x with Elasticsearch 8.x. Your system is now running the latest versions and ready for use.

  • Analyzers & Responders

docs.title: Migration from Elasticsearch 6.8.2 to ES 7.x
docs.text:
⚠️ IMPORTANT NOTE

  • This migration process is intended for single node of Elasticsearch database
  • The current version of this document is provided for testing purpose ONLY!
  • This guide has been written and tested to migrate data from ES 6.8.2 to ES 7.8.1, and Cortex 3.0.1 to Cortex 3.1.0 only!
  • This guide starts with Elasticsearch version 6.8.2 up and running, indexes and data. To test this guide, we recommend using a backup of your production server. (see Backup and Restore page for more information)
  • This guide is illustrated with Cortex index. The process is identical for Cortex, you just have to adjust index names.

docs.title: Prerequisite
docs.text: The software jq is required to manipulate JSON and create new indexes. More information at https://stedolan.github.io/jq/.

docs.title: Identify if your index should be reindexed
docs.text:
You can easily identify if indexes should be reindexed or not. On the index named cortex_4 run the following command: 

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9200/cortex_4?human | jq '.cortex_4.settings.index.version.created'

If the output is similar to "5xxxxxx" then reindexing is required, you should follow this guide.

If it is "6xxxxxx" then the index can be read by Elasticsearch 7.8.x. Upgrade Elasticsearch, and Cortex 3.1.0.

docs.title: Current status
docs.text:
Current context is: - Elasticsearch 6.8.2 - Cortex 3.0.1

All up and running.

Start by identifying indices on you Elasticsearch instance.

curl  http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices\?v

The output should look like this: 

health status index           uuid                   pri rep docs.count docs.deleted store.size pri.store.size
green  open   cortex_4    Y5rDTO23RBC_n6pjFP0-Qw   5   0       8531            8       13mb           13mb

The index name is cortex_4. Record this somewhere.

docs.title: Stop services
docs.text:
Before starting updating the database, let's stop applications:

sudo service cortex stop

docs.title: Create a new index
docs.text:
The first operation lies in creating a new index named new_cortex_4 with settings from current index cortex_4 (ensure to keep index version, needed for future upgrade).

curl -XPUT 'http://localhost:9200/new_cortex_4' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "$(curl http://localhost:9200/cortex_4 |\
   jq '.cortex_4 |
   del(.settings.index.provided_name,
    .settings.index.creation_date,
    .settings.index.uuid,
    .settings.index.version,
    .settings.index.mapping.single_type,
    .mappings.doc._all)'
    )"

Check the new index is well created:

curl -XGET "http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v"

The output should look like this:

health status index           uuid                   pri rep docs.count docs.deleted store.size pri.store.size
green  open   new_cortex_4    wRX6rhzXTuW_F2wLNxqVyg   5   0          0            0      1.1kb          1.1kb
green  open   cortex_4        Y5rDTO23RBC_n6pjFP0-Qw   5   0       8531            8       13mb           13mb

docs.title: Proceed to reindex
docs.text:
Next operation lies in running the reindex command in the newly created index:

curl -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:9200/_reindex -d '{
  "conflicts": "proceed",
  "source": {
    "index": "cortex_4"
  },
  "dest": {
    "index": "new_cortex_4"
  }
}'

After a moment, you should get a similar output: 

{
    "took": 5119,
    "timed_out": false,
    "total": 5889,
    "updated": 0,
    "created": 5889,
    "deleted": 0,
    "batches": 6,
    "version_conflicts": 0,
    "noops": 0,
    "retries": {
        "bulk": 0,
        "search": 0
    },
    "throttled_millis": 0,
    "requests_per_second": -1.0,
    "throttled_until_millis": 0,
    "failures": []
}

docs.title: Ensure new index has been created
docs.text:
Run the following command, and ensure the new index is like the current one (size can vary):

curl -XGET "http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v"

The output should look like this: 

health status index           uuid                   pri rep docs.count docs.deleted store.size pri.store.size
green  open   new_cortex_4    wRX6rhzXTuW_F2wLNxqVyg   5   0       8531            0     12.6mb         12.6mb
green  open   cortex_4        Y5rDTO23RBC_n6pjFP0-Qw   5   0       8531            8       13mb           13mb

docs.title: Delete old indices
docs.text:
This is the thrilling part. Now the new index new_cortex_4 is created and similar to cortex_4, older indexes should be completely deleted from the database. To delete index named cortex_4, run the following command: 

curl -XDELETE http://localhost:9200/cortex_4

Run the same command for older indexes if exist (cortex_3, cortex_2....). Elasticsearch 7.x cannot run with index created with Elasticsearch 5.x.

docs.title: Create an alias
docs.text:
Before stopping Elasticsearch service, let’s create an alias to keep index names in the future. 

curl -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json'  'http://localhost:9200/_aliases' -d '{
    "actions": [
        {
            "add": {
                "index": "new_cortex_4",
                "alias": "cortex_4"
            }
        }
    ]
}'

Doing so will allow Cortex 3.1.0 to find the index without updating the configuration file.

Check the alias has been well created by running the following command

curl -XGET http://localhost:9200/_alias?pretty

The output should look like:

{
  "new_cortex_4" : {
    "aliases" : {
      "cortex_4" : { }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Stop Elasticsearch version 6.8.2
docs.text: sudo service elasticsearch stop

docs.title: Update Elasticsearch
docs.text:
Update the configuration of Elasticsearch. Configuration file should look like this:

[..]
http.host: 127.0.0.1
discovery.type: single-node
cluster.name: hive
script.allowed_types: inline
thread_pool.search.queue_size: 100000
thread_pool.write.queue_size: 10000

Now, upgrade Elasticsearch to version 7.x following the documentation for your operating system, and ensure the service start successfully.

docs.title: Install or update to Cortex 3.1.0
docs.text:
DEBRPMDocker

Refer to the installation instructions and specify version 3.1.0.

Refer to the installation instructions and specify version 3.1.0.

Docker images are also provided on Docker Hub.

docker pull thehiveproject/cortex:3.1.0-1

⚠️ Starting from this version, Docker images don't contain analyzers anymore. Analyzers_/_Responders and Cortex have different life-cycles, their update including their dependencies should not be correlated to Cortex update.

It is recommended to use Docker version of analyzers : this can be done by binding Docker service docket inside Cortex container (run with -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock).

docs.title: Update database
docs.text:
Connect to TheHive (and Cortex), the maintenance page should ask to update.

Once updated, ensure a new index named cortex_5 has been created.

curl -XGET "http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v"

The output should look like this:

health status index           uuid                   pri rep docs.count docs.deleted store.size pri.store.size
green  open   new_cortex_4 GV-3Y8QjTjWw0F-p2sjW6Q   5   0      30977            0       26mb           26mb
yellow open   cortex_5     Nz0vCKqhRK2xkx1t_WF-0g   5   1      30977            0     26.1mb         26.1mb

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: This is the quick start guide for Cortex. It assumes that Cortex has been installed, and that the analyzers have been installed as well.

docs.title: Step 1: Connect to Cortex
docs.text: Once Cortex is installed and configured, open your web browser and connect to http://cortexaddress:9001.

docs.title: Step 2: Update the database
docs.text: Cortex uses ElasticSearch to store users, organizations and analyzers configuration. The first time you connect to the Web UI (http://<CORTEX_IP>:9001 by default), you have to create the database by clicking the Update Database button.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Cortex Super Administrator
docs.text:
You are then invited to create the first user. This is a Cortex global administration user or superAdmin. This user account will be able to create Cortex organizations and users.

You will then be able to log in using this user account. You will note that the default cortex organization has been created and that it includes your user account, a Cortex global administrator.

docs.title: Step 4: Create an organization
docs.text: The default cortex organization cannot be used for any other purpose than managing global administrators (users with the superAdmin role), organizations and their associated users. It cannot be used to enable/disable or configure analyzers. To do so, you need to create your own organization inside Cortex by clicking on the Add organization button.

docs.title: Step 5: Create an organization Administrator
docs.text:
Create the organization administrator account (user with an orgAdmin role).

Then, specify a password for this user. After doing so, log out and log in with that new user account.

docs.title: Step 6: Enable and configure Analyzers
docs.text: Enable the analyzers you need, configure them using the Organization > Configuration and Organization > Analyzers tabs. All analyzer configuration is done using the Web UI, including adding API keys and configuring rate limits.

docs.title: (Optional) Step 7: Create an account for TheHive integration
docs.text: If you are using TheHive, create a new account inside your organization with the read, analyze role and generate an API key that you will need to add to TheHive configuration.

docs.title: User Roles
docs.text:
Cortex defines four roles:

  • read: the user can access all the jobs that have been performed by the Cortex 2 instance, including their results. However, this role cannot submit jobs. Moreover, this role cannot be used in the default cortex organization. This organization can only contain super administrators.
  • analyze: the analyze role implies the read role, described above. A user who has a analyze role can submit a new job using one of the configured analyzers for their organization. This role cannot be used in the default cortex organization. This organization can only contain super administrators.
  • orgAdmin: the orgAdmin role implies the analyze role. A user who has an analyze role can manage users within their organization. They can add users and give them read, analyze and/or orgAdmin roles. This role also permits to configure analyzers for the organization. This role cannot be used in the default cortex organization. This organization can only contain super administrators.
  • superAdmin: this role is incompatible with all the other roles listed above (see chart below for examples). It can be used solely for managing organizations and their associated users. When you install Cortex, the first user that is created will have this role. Several users can have it as well but only in the default cortex organization, which is automatically created during installation.

The chart below lists the roles and what they can and cannot do:

Actions read analyze orgAdmin superAdmin Read reports X X X Run jobs X X Enable/Disable analyzer X Configure analyzer X Create org analyst X X Delete org analyst X X Create org admin X X Delete org admin X X Create Org X Delete Org X Create Cortex admin user X

docs.title: TheHive Flow Configuration Files
docs.text:
6.0 One

A TheHive Flow Docker Compose deployment is configured through a handful of files in the profile directory, prod1-thehive-flow or prod2-thehive-flow, of the StrangeBee Docker Compose repository. These files don't exist on a Kubernetes deployment, where the configuration is set through the Helm chart values, as described in Configuration and operations on Kubernetes.

The following table lists each file, what it holds, and the page that documents it.

File Purpose Editable after init .env Secrets, image versions, and runtime parameters, generated by init.sh Yes. Applied by recreating the affected service with docker compose up -d <service>. Running init.sh again rewrites the file and keeps the secrets thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml Application configuration Yes. Applied by recreating the thehive-flow service with docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow thehive-flow/secret/ TheHive API key file, thehive-api-key, read at startup Yes. Applied by restarting the thehive-flow service. See Rotate secrets certificates/ Custom TLS certificate, private key, and certificate authority (CA) certificate, copied to nginx/certs/ by init.sh Yes. A new run of init.sh copies the new files, and an nginx restart applies them. See TLS certificate renewal temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml.template Temporal cluster configuration template Yes, but rarely needed. The container reads temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml, which init.sh renders from this template with the database password filled in. An edit to the template takes effect after a new run of bash ./scripts/init.sh and a restart of the temporal service. The run also renews a self-signed certificate: see TLS certificate renewal temporal/config/dynamicconfig/production.yaml Temporal runtime knobs Yes. Most knobs reload live. Three history cache keys need a restart: see Runtime knobs nginx/templates/default.conf.template Nginx reverse proxy configuration Yes. Applied by restarting nginx nginx/docker-entrypoint.d/40-thehive-allow.sh Writes the list of addresses nginx accepts TheHive requests from, based on nginx_thehive_addresses at container start No. Editing nginx_thehive_addresses in .env and recreating nginx runs it again docker-compose.yml Service definitions: images, memory limits, published ports, and the variables passed to each container Yes, for the limits and ports, applied with docker compose up -d. StrangeBee maintains the rest: see Upgrade TheHive Flow with Docker Compose ../versions.env Image versions of every profile of the repository, maintained by StrangeBee Not for routine changes. Upgrades move the pins, and init.sh copies them into .env. The one exception is a temporary pin move to apply a security patch before the next release, as described in Respond to a CVE docker-compose.override.yml Optional file created next to docker-compose.yml, which Docker Compose reads automatically, for environment variable overrides, extra volumes, or published ports Yes. Applied by recreating the affected service Next steps
  • TheHive Flow Environment Variables
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration
  • Temporal Runtime Configuration

docs.title: TheHive Flow Environment Variables
docs.text:
6.0 One

The .env file at the root of the profile directory of TheHive Flow holds the secrets, image versions, and runtime parameters of the stack. The init.sh script generates it from dot.env.template, from versions.env at the root of the repository, and from the values it detects or prompts for.

The file is covered by .gitignore, so it isn't committed to git, and it's readable by its owner only. Edit it directly on the host after the initialization. To apply a change, recreate the service that reads the variable with docker compose up -d <service>. For most variables, that's the thehive-flow service. A plain docker compose restart reuses the existing container without re-reading .env.

Running init.sh again rewrites the file from the template. The script keeps the secrets and the values it prompted for, and refreshes the image versions from versions.env. Without a custom certificate, it also generates a new self-signed certificate, as described in TLS certificate renewal. A line added by hand outside the keys the template declares doesn't survive: set extra container variables in the environment: block of the service instead, as described in Optional container variables.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variable Set by Description thehive_flow_image_version versions.env Tag of the docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow image. Copied from versions.env by init.sh, with the other image versions below. See Upgrade TheHive Flow with Docker Compose. postgresql_image_version versions.env Tag of the postgres image. temporal_image_version versions.env Tag of the temporalio/server and temporalio/admin-tools images. seaweedfs_image_version versions.env Tag of the chrislusf/seaweedfs image, used by the s3-store and init-s3-store services. nginx_image_version versions.env Tag of the nginx image. postgres_password init.sh PostgreSQL superuser password, a random 256-bit hex value. PostgreSQL reads it at its first start only. flow_db_password init.sh Password of the thehive_flow database role. Each run of init.sh aligns the role with the value. temporal_db_password init.sh Password of the temporal database role. Each run of init.sh aligns the role with the value and renders it into temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml. s3_access_key_id Preset Access key ID of the shipped object storage. Not a secret. Default: thehive-flow. s3_secret_access_key init.sh Secret access key of the shipped object storage, a random 256-bit hex value. See S3 credentials. jwt_signing_key init.sh HS256 symmetric key shared with TheHive. At least 32 characters: TheHive Flow doesn't start with a shorter key. See Configure TheHive to reach TheHive Flow. flow_thehive_url init.sh Required. URL of TheHive host reachable from the thehive-flow container. The init.sh script prompts for it and refuses an empty or malformed value. thehive_api_key Operator TheHive API key for outbound requests. Optional: when empty, the thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key file is used instead. The variable wins when both are set. See Provision TheHive API key. flow_public_url init.sh Public URL at which callers reach TheHive Flow, used to build webhook URLs. Set to https://<nginx_server_name> at the first run and kept on later runs. See Public URL. UID, GID init.sh User and group identifiers of the user who ran init.sh. The postgresql, temporal, s3-store, and thehive-flow services run as that user, which must keep read and write access to the profile directory. The other services, such as nginx, keep the default user of their image. docker_gid init.sh Group identifier of the Docker socket, as seen from inside a container. Added to the groups of the thehive-flow container so that it can start code transformation containers. See Docker engine access. nginx_server_name init.sh Host name used in the TLS certificate and as the nginx server name. nginx_ssl_trusted_certificate init.sh Filled when a custom certificate authority (CA) is provided. nginx_thehive_addresses init.sh / Operator Needed for TheHive to reach TheHive Flow. IPv4 addresses TheHive calls from, comma-separated. A range in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation is also accepted. The init.sh script prompts for it and only warns when the answer is empty, without stopping. Nginx forwards TheHive requests only from these addresses, and refuses them from every address while the value is empty. Webhook calls aren't affected. Entries covering the Docker network gateway are skipped. A change is applied with docker compose up -d --no-deps nginx.

The file also carries the image versions of the profiles of TheHive and Cortex, copied from versions.env with the others. The stack doesn't use them.

The lowercase names are deliberate

docker-compose.yml reads the lowercase names to fill the variables of each container, such as SERVER_NAME, NGINX_SSL_TRUSTED_CERTIFICATE, and NGINX_THEHIVE_ADDRESSES for the nginx service. Don't rename them to upper case: the interpolation silently falls back to an empty value.

docs.title: Variables of the thehive-flow container
docs.text:
The docker-compose.yml file passes the values of .env to the thehive-flow container under the names TheHive Flow reads:

Container variable Value Role BEEFLOW_SECRET_JWT_SYMMETRIC_KEY jwt_signing_key JWT signing key, injected into the api.public.jwt.secret key of thehive-flow.yml BEEFLOW_SECRET_THEHIVE_API_KEY thehive_api_key TheHive API key, read from the secret file when empty FLOW_DB_PASSWORD flow_db_password Expanded into the PostgreSQL connection string of thehive-flow.yml FLOW_THEHIVE_URL flow_thehive_url Expanded into the modules.workers.activities.thehive.url key of thehive-flow.yml BEEFLOW_API__PUBLIC__URL flow_public_url Overrides the api.public.url key BEEFLOW_BLOBSTORE__S3__ACCESS_KEY_ID s3_access_key_id Overrides the blobstore.s3.access_key_id key BEEFLOW_SECRET_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY s3_secret_access_key Secret access key of the object storage GOMEMLIMIT Fixed in docker-compose.yml Go memory limit, sized for the memory limit of the profile. See System Requirements OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, USER Fixed in docker-compose.yml Service name of the telemetry, and user name required by the telemetry runtime

docs.title: Optional container variables
docs.text:
The following variables aren't declared in .env or in the shipped docker-compose.yml. To set one, add it to the environment: block of the thehive-flow service, in docker-compose.yml or in a docker-compose.override.yml file created next to it, as described in Environment variable overrides. Then apply it with docker compose up -d thehive-flow.

Variable Description BEEFLOW_LOG_LEVEL Log level threshold of the thehive-flow service. See Change the log level. BEEFLOW_CONFIG_FILES Comma-separated paths of configuration files inside the container, merged in order: a later file overrides the keys of an earlier one, and environment variables still override every file. The variable replaces the -config /thehive-flow.yml argument of the service, so list /thehive-flow.yml first. Mount each extra file in the volumes: block of the service. BEEFLOW_VERBOSE_ERRORS Set to true to return the full error details, cause chain and stack included, in 5xx responses instead of a generic message. Authentication still applies. Debug aid only: never set it in production, since the details can reveal internal information. See HTTP errors. OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT OTLP endpoint of an external observability back end, receiving the application traces, metrics, and logs. OTLP export is off when unset. OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL OTLP transport protocol, for example grpc. OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS Headers added to OTLP requests, such as an authorization token. OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER Trace sampling strategy, for example parentbased_traceidratio. OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG Argument of the sampling strategy, such as the ratio of traces to sample. OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES Extra resource attributes, such as a service namespace separating clients in a shared observability back end. SSL_CERT_FILE CA bundle replacing the system trust store of the container. See TLS toward TheHive. BEEFLOW_MODULES__WORKERS__ACTIVITIES__MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITY_TASK_POLLERS Number of Temporal pollers fetching activity tasks. When unset, the value of 32 from thehive-flow.yml applies. A value of 0 lets the Temporal SDK decide, server-side autoscaling included. A higher value is only justified after measuring under load. A negative value stops TheHive Flow from starting. BEEFLOW_MODULES__WORKERS__WORKFLOWS__MAX_CONCURRENT_WORKFLOW_TASK_POLLERS Number of Temporal pollers fetching workflow tasks. When unset, the value of 32 from thehive-flow.yml applies. A value of 0 lets the Temporal SDK decide, server-side autoscaling included. A higher value is only justified after measuring under load. A negative value or 1 stops TheHive Flow from starting.

docs.title: S3 credentials
docs.text:
The two object storage credentials travel together: the application rejects a configuration where exactly one of them is set. The init.sh script generates s3_secret_access_key and keeps s3_access_key_id at its preset value, thehive-flow.

The pair the thehive-flow service uses must match what the init-s3-store container provisioned. Because both read the same two variables, they can't disagree unless .env is edited between the two starts. For the full behavior, including what changing a credential after first start involves, see the blob store section of the application configuration.

docs.title: Public URL
docs.text:
flow_public_url is the public URL at which callers reach the root of TheHive Flow. TheHive Flow builds the URL of each Webhook trigger from it, as <flow_public_url>/webhook/<webhook_id>. Webhook callers use this address directly, not through TheHive, so it must be reachable from each of them.

The init.sh script sets it to https://<nginx_server_name> at the first run, which suits a standard installation, and keeps the value on later runs. Change it only when callers reach TheHive Flow through another reverse proxy, host name, path prefix, or port, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow. With a path prefix, the proxy in front must remove the prefix before forwarding requests to TheHive Flow.

The value is checked at startup. TheHive Flow doesn't start if it's malformed. It must be an absolute http or https URL with a host, and without credentials, a query, or a fragment.

docs.title: Docker engine accessNext steps
docs.text:
TheHive Flow launches containers on the host Docker daemon to run Python and JavaScript code transformations. The docker-compose.yml file mounts the Docker socket, /var/run/docker.sock, into the thehive-flow container, and adds the group owning the socket to the container process, so that the non-root process can use it. The init.sh script detects that group by reading the socket from inside a throwaway container and writes it to docker_gid. The detection therefore also works where the socket group differs between the host and the containers, such as Docker Desktop.

If the Docker setup changes after the initial install, run bash ./scripts/init.sh again to detect the group again, then apply it with docker compose up -d thehive-flow. A Docker daemon reachable over TCP only isn't supported by the shipped file.

Mounting the socket grants the thehive-flow container root-equivalent access to the host, as mounting it in Cortex does for analyzers. See Code transformation isolation.

  • TheHive Flow Configuration Files
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Deploy TheHive Flow with Docker Compose

docs.title: TheHive Flow Application Configuration
docs.text:
6.0 One

The thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml file holds the application configuration of TheHive Flow. It's mounted read-only at /thehive-flow.yml inside the thehive-flow container.

After any change, recreate the service:

docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow

The file is mounted into the container on its own, and some editors replace the file instead of writing into it. A plain docker compose restart thehive-flow can then leave the container reading the previous version, while recreating it always picks up the file on disk.

On a Kubernetes deployment, the Helm chart exposes only a subset of these keys, mostly through the config.* values. Settings it doesn't expose, such as the blob size limits, aren't available there. Apply a change with helm upgrade, as described in Configuration and operations on Kubernetes.

docs.title: Shipped configuration
docs.text:
Secrets aren't stored in the file. They're read from /secret, mounted from ./thehive-flow/secret/, and from the BEEFLOW_SECRET_* variables docker-compose.yml passes to the container from .env.

secret_path: /secret

temporal:
  addr: temporal:7233

database:
  postgres:
    connection_string: postgres://thehive_flow:${FLOW_DB_PASSWORD}@postgresql:5432/thehive_flow?sslmode=disable

blobstore:
  backend: s3
  s3:
    # Shipped SeaweedFS; the bucket is created by init-s3-store before TheHive Flow starts.
    # Credentials are injected from .env by docker-compose.yml.
    endpoint: http://s3-store:8333
    bucket: thehive-flow
    # Required by the S3 client for request signing, ignored by SeaweedFS
    region: us-east-1
    use_path_style: true

api:
  public:
    enable: true
    addr: "0.0.0.0:8081"
    jwt:
      # Shared with TheHive; set by BEEFLOW_SECRET_JWT_SYMMETRIC_KEY
      secret: ""

modules:
  observability:
    # /livez and /readyz
    listener:
      addr: "0.0.0.0:9090"
    metrics:
      prometheus:
        enabled: true
    pprof:
      enabled: false
  runs:
    # This stack owns its Temporal namespace: keep its retention aligned with runs retention
    sync_temporal_retention: true
  workers:
    workflows:
      max_concurrent_workflow_task_pollers: 32
    activities:
      max_concurrent_activity_task_pollers: 32
      # Outbound connections to non-public addresses (loopback, RFC 1918, link-local, ...)
      # are blocked. To reach TheHive, Cortex or another service on a private network,
      # allowlist its CIDR range. A bare IP without prefix fails startup.
      # egress:
      #   allowlist:
      #     - 192.168.1.0/24
      #     - 192.168.1.10/32
      thehive:
        # TheHive URL reachable from this stack (flow_thehive_url in .env)
        url: ${FLOW_THEHIVE_URL}
        # File name inside /secret, used when BEEFLOW_SECRET_THEHIVE_API_KEY is empty
        api_key: thehive-api-key

The ${FLOW_DB_PASSWORD} and ${FLOW_THEHIVE_URL} references are expanded from the container environment when the file loads. Any other value can be overridden the same way, as described in Environment variable overrides.

docs.title: Run retention
docs.text:
The run retention sets how long a run stays reachable. It drives the purge of the run list and the deletion of the files those runs reference in the blob store. Because sync_temporal_retention is enabled in the shipped file, it also drives the history retention of the Temporal namespace. It's set with the modules.runs.retention key.

The shipped file deliberately leaves the key out, which keeps the application default of 30 days. To use another value, add the key under modules.runs and recreate the thehive-flow service. To use the environment variable override instead, set BEEFLOW_MODULES__RUNS__RETENTION=168h in the environment: block of the service and apply it with docker compose up -d thehive-flow. The namespace follows shortly after.

Shortening the retention deletes history

The Temporal namespace retention is aligned downward too. Lowering modules.runs.retention deletes the history of runs older than the new value, and that history can't be recovered by raising the value again.

For the operational details, including the 24-hour floor, the non-retroactive behavior, and how to check what the namespace currently holds, see Temporal workflow history retention.

docs.title: Code transformation images
docs.text:
Python and JavaScript code transformations run in disposable containers, launched for each execution and removed as soon as the script exits. The two default images are pinned by immutable digest in the application itself and don't appear in the shipped file:

Language Default image Python 3.11 gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 JavaScript on Node.js 24 gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian12

Both are distroless images that ship the language runtime and its standard library only. To make additional libraries available to scripts, or to pull from an internal registry on an air-gapped host, build or mirror an image. Then override the image key under modules.codex.languages, using the built-in language names:

modules:
  codex:
    languages:
      python@v3_11:
        image: <registry>/<image>:<tag>
      javascript@v24:
        image: <registry>/<image>:<tag>

Omitted keys keep their built-in values, so overriding image alone is enough as long as the image keeps the interpreter at the same path: /usr/bin/python3 for Python and /nodejs/bin/node for JavaScript. For an image that places it elsewhere, override the entrypoint key too. For a registry that requires authentication, declare it under modules.codex.docker.docker_registries.

On Kubernetes deployments, transformations run as Kubernetes jobs and the images are set through the codex.languageImages chart values instead.

docs.title: Concurrent code transformations per language
docs.text:
TheHive Flow caps how many code transformations one language runs at once. The cap is set with the modules.codex.max_concurrent_activity_execution_size key. Each language runs its own worker, so the cap applies per language. With both built-in languages enabled, the stack runs up to the configured value for Python and, separately, up to the same value for JavaScript. A transformation submitted above the cap waits in the Temporal task queue. The wait doesn't count against the node's own timeout, but it does count against the workflow-level timeout.

The key is absent from the shipped file, which keeps the Temporal SDK default of 1000 per language. To override it, set BEEFLOW_MODULES__CODEX__MAX_CONCURRENT_ACTIVITY_EXECUTION_SIZE in the environment: block of the thehive-flow service, as described in Environment variable overrides. On Kubernetes deployments, set the codex.maxConcurrentActivityExecutionSize chart value instead. Each transformation runs as a Kubernetes job, so the value caps how many jobs one language runs at once. An empty value or 0 keeps the default.

docs.title: Egress allowlist
docs.text:
Workflow authors control the target URL of the nodes that open outbound connections: the HTTP request, integration, and AI nodes. To prevent server-side request forgery (SSRF), TheHive Flow blocks these connections when the target resolves to a non-public address: loopback, link-local, private, unique local, carrier-grade NAT, and reserved ranges. The check runs on the resolved IP address at connection time, after DNS resolution, so it also covers redirects and DNS rebinding.

A blocked connection fails the workflow step with the following error:

egress guard: outbound connection to non-public address blocked

Allowlist legitimate internal targets, such as TheHive or Cortex on a private network, or a locally hosted LLM provider. List their address ranges under modules.workers.activities.egress.allowlist in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation, an IP address followed by a prefix length: 192.168.1.0/24 covers a whole subnet, and 192.168.1.10/32 covers a single host. The shipped file carries the block as a comment: uncomment it and fill it in, then recreate the service with docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow:

modules:
  workers:
    activities:
      egress:
        allowlist:
          - <internal_cidr>

Five properties are worth knowing:

  • An allowlisted range is reachable even though it falls in an otherwise blocked range. Public addresses stay reachable either way, and the guard itself can't be turned off.
  • Requests sent through the Default proxy mode aren't checked at connection time. The proxy configured in TheHive is treated as the egress boundary: only its own address is validated against the allowlist, when TheHive pushes it. A proxy defined on the node itself, with the Enabled mode, stays checked.
  • The allowlist is validated at startup. A malformed CIDR, including a bare IP address without a prefix length, stops TheHive Flow from starting instead of silently dropping the exception.
  • The same allowlist also validates the proxy, email server, and LLM provider hosts pushed by TheHive. Widening it for workflow traffic widens it for them too. An email server override isn't checked.
  • Python code and JavaScript code nodes aren't covered: their scripts open connections from their own container, outside the guard. See Code transformation isolation.

On Kubernetes, the same list is set through the config.modules.workers.activities.egress.allowlist value, in the values file written at installation time, then applied with helm upgrade:

config:
  modules:
    workers:
      activities:
        egress:
          allowlist:
            - <internal_cidr>

docs.title: Email server override
docs.text:
By default, Send email nodes use the SMTP configuration defined in TheHive, which TheHive pushes to TheHive Flow. When that SMTP server isn't reachable from TheHive Flow, define another one in the modules.workers.activities.mailer section. TheHive Flow then ignores the configuration pushed by TheHive. Recreate the service with docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow to apply the change:

modules:
  workers:
    activities:
      mailer:
        host: <smtp_host>
        port: <smtp_port>
        tls: true
        user: <smtp_user>
        password: <password_file_name>   # Filename inside secret_path (/secret)
        from: <sender_address>
Key Description host SMTP server address. Setting it turns the override on. port SMTP port. Required. tls Upgrades the connection with STARTTLS. Required to send credentials to a server other than localhost. tls_required Same as tls. ssl Accepted only together with tls. TheHive Flow doesn't support implicit TLS, also called SMTPS, commonly served on port 465. user SMTP username. Must be set together with password: setting only one of them stops TheHive Flow from starting. password Name of the file holding the SMTP password, in ./thehive-flow/secret/, readable by its owner only like the API key file. The BEEFLOW_SECRET_MAILER_PASSWORD environment variable can hold the password instead. from Default sender address.

The egress allowlist doesn't apply to this server. To go back to the configuration pushed by TheHive, remove the section and recreate the service. On Kubernetes, the same settings are exposed through the config.modules.workers.activities.mailer.* values, with the password in the Secret named by secrets.mailerPassword.existingSecret.

docs.title: Trusted proxies
docs.text:
Each Webhook trigger accepts 120 requests per minute from a given client address. Requests reach TheHive Flow through the shipped nginx, so every webhook call carries the address of nginx, and all callers of a webhook share the same limit. See Rate limiting.

To apply the limit to each caller instead, list the range nginx connects from in the api.public.trusted_proxies key of thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml, then recreate the service:

api:
  public:
    trusted_proxies:
      - <thehive_flow_network_cidr>

For a request coming from one of these ranges, TheHive Flow reads the caller address from the X-Forwarded-For header, which nginx fills with the address of its own client. Each entry is a Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) range, such as 172.20.0.0/16. Docker Compose names the network of the stack after the profile directory, for example prod1-thehive-flow_thehive-flow-network. Find its range with the following commands:

docker network ls --filter name=thehive-flow-network
docker network inspect <network_name> --format '{{range .IPAM.Config}}{{.Subnet}}{{end}}'

A bare IP address, a /0 range, or an IPv4-mapped range prevents TheHive Flow from starting. The list is empty by default. When callers reach TheHive Flow through another reverse proxy placed in front of nginx, that proxy must append the address of its own client to X-Forwarded-For, and its range must be listed too.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
When the thehive-flow service stops, TheHive Flow finishes its in-flight work within the delay set by the shutdown.timeout key: 20 seconds by default. The key is absent from the shipped file.

Keep the value at or below 25 seconds. The stop_grace_period of the thehive-flow service in docker-compose.yml is 30 seconds, and TheHive Flow needs about 5 more seconds after the timeout to flush its telemetry. Above 25 seconds, Docker may kill the process before it finishes, and TheHive Flow logs a warning at startup. To raise the timeout anyway, raise stop_grace_period by the same amount.

docs.title: Environment variable overrides
docs.text:
Any value in thehive-flow.yml can be overridden with an environment variable using the pattern BEEFLOW_<SECTION>__<KEY>, where a double underscore separates each nesting level. For example:

BEEFLOW_TEMPORAL__ADDR=temporal:7233
BEEFLOW_MODULES__OBSERVABILITY__LISTENER__ADDR=0.0.0.0:9091

Set overrides in the environment: block of the thehive-flow service. To keep the shipped docker-compose.yml untouched, which makes upgrades simpler, put them in a docker-compose.override.yml file created next to it. Docker Compose reads that file automatically and merges it with docker-compose.yml. For example:

services:
  thehive-flow:
    environment:
      BEEFLOW_MODULES__OBSERVABILITY__LISTENER__ADDR: "0.0.0.0:9091"

Apply an override change by recreating the service with docker compose up -d thehive-flow. A plain restart doesn't re-read the file. Don't set overrides in .env: its values only reach the container through the variables docker-compose.yml declares, listed in TheHive Flow Environment Variables.

docs.title: Blob store
docs.text:
TheHive Flow requires durable blob storage for files ingested through webhooks or runs, and for activity outputs too large to keep in the database. The blobstore.backend key selects one of two back ends:

  • s3, the shipped and recommended back end, using an S3-compatible object store. The stack ships one, the s3-store service, so there's nothing to provision.
  • local, which writes blobs to a directory on the host. It's available on the Docker Compose deployment only, for a single-node installation that accepts the restrictions below.

The blobstore.backend key is required: TheHive Flow doesn't start when it's missing.

Whichever back end is selected, the storage behavior is identical: blobs are addressed by organization and SHA-256 hash, identical content is deduplicated within an organization, and files follow the run retention.

docs.title: Blob size limits
docs.text:
Three keys of the modules.variables section set the size limits described in Files. They're absent from the shipped file, which keeps the defaults. Values are in bytes.

Key Default Description max_blob_size 25 MiB (26214400) Largest file the blob store accepts. A node output above this size is rejected. min_size_promote_to_blobref 1 MiB (1048576) Node outputs of this size or more are stored as files instead of inline. Binary content is always stored as a file, whatever its size. max_blob_inline_size 1.5 MiB (1572864) Largest JSON file content that a variable reference returns transparently. Above this size, the reference returns the file metadata instead.

TheHive Flow doesn't start when max_blob_inline_size or min_size_promote_to_blobref is zero or negative, or when min_size_promote_to_blobref exceeds max_blob_size.

A fourth key, modules.workers.activities.integration.max_response_body_bytes, caps the response body that an integration node accepts. Its default is 10 MiB (10485760). A larger response fails the node without a retry. TheHive Flow doesn't start when the value is smaller than min_size_promote_to_blobref or larger than max_blob_size.

docs.title: S3 back end
docs.text:
The shipped configuration selects the s3 back end. It points at the shipped s3-store service over the internal Docker network, with the bucket provisioned by init-s3-store before startup. The shipped service is a single-process SeaweedFS instance, the supported default for a single-host deployment. It keeps its data in the ./s3-store/data directory.

The back end works with any S3-compatible object storage, whether managed by a cloud provider, such as Amazon S3, or self-hosted. To use an external store instead of the shipped one, point blobstore.s3.endpoint and blobstore.s3.bucket at it in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml, and set region to the one the store expects. Keep use_path_style: true for non-AWS gateways, and provide the credentials in .env. The stack still starts the s3-store and init-s3-store services, which then hold no data.

Endpoint and availability

TheHive Flow uses a single S3 endpoint. With self-hosted object storage, make sure the endpoint is highly available, for example through the storage platform itself or a correctly configured load balancer.

Three properties of the back end are worth knowing:

  • Both credentials travel together. The application rejects a configuration where exactly one of access_key_id and secret_access_key is set. With both empty, it doesn't fail. It falls back to the AWS SDK credential chain, which against the shipped store means unsigned or wrong requests rather than a clear error. That's why thehive-flow.yml leaves both out and docker-compose.yml injects the pair from .env.
  • Changing a credential after first start requires provisioning again. The store must learn the new value: run docker compose up -d init-s3-store. A new secret under the same access key ID replaces the previous one in place. A new access key ID is added beside the previous one, which stays valid. See Rotate secrets for the full procedure.
  • The identity needs delete rights. The application deletes the files of purged runs with DeleteObject, so on an external store the principal needs s3:ListBucket, s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, and s3:DeleteObject on the bucket. Without s3:DeleteObject, runs are still purged, but their files stay in the bucket, queued for deletion, and each deletion pass logs an error. On a versioned bucket, DeleteObject leaves a noncurrent version, so add a noncurrent-version expiration rule to reclaim that space. Don't add a lifecycle rule that expires current objects. A run that reuses stored content doesn't always rewrite the object, so such a rule can delete a file that a retained run still uses. The shipped store needs nothing more, because its Write action covers both uploads and deletions.

docs.title: Local filesystem back end
docs.text:
The local back end stores blobs as plain files in a directory, for a single-node Docker Compose installation that prefers a plain disk over an object store. Kubernetes deployments don't support it: the Helm chart refuses to render with any blobstore.backend other than s3, because the application and the code transformation jobs don't share a disk on a cluster. Selecting the back end is a manual configuration change: init.sh doesn't offer it, and the stack ships, provisions, and starts the shipped object storage either way.

blobstore:
  backend: local
  local:
    path: <blob_directory>

path is required and must be an absolute path. Both constraints are checked when the configuration loads, before anything starts. The directory must already exist and be writable by the application: nothing creates it, and startup performs a real write test and aborts on failure. In practice, mount a dedicated host directory at that path in the thehive-flow service, through the volumes: block of the service in docker-compose.yml or in a docker-compose.override.yml file. The directory ownership must match the user the stack runs as.

Blobs are stored as <path>/<organization>/<prefix>/<sha256>, where <prefix> is the first four characters of the hash, so that no single directory grows too large. Writes are atomic and durable. Each blob is written to a temporary file, flushed to disk, then renamed, so a visible file is always complete, even after a power loss. Temporary files orphaned by a crash are removed at a later startup, once they're old enough not to belong to a write in progress. Disk full and I/O errors are treated as transient and retried, like S3 errors.

Guardrails the object store provides fall on the operator here

  • A single shared directory is required. Every process of the stack must read and write the same directory on the same host. Nothing verifies it, and a mismatch surfaces as file-not-found errors at run time, never as a startup refusal.
  • A local filesystem is required. The atomicity guarantee relies on the rename operation, so network filesystems such as NFS, and overlay filesystems, aren't supported. This isn't verified at startup.
  • A case-sensitive filesystem is required. On a case-insensitive filesystem, two organizations whose names differ only by case end up sharing one directory, which breaks tenant isolation. This isn't verified at startup either.
  • No disk supervision exists. The application exposes no metric for the space left in the directory, and a full disk shows up as workflow steps failing and being retried, not as an operational alert. Add a host-level disk alert on the filesystem holding path, as described in Monitor TheHive Flow.
  • The backup scripts don't cover the directory. backup.sh and restore.sh copy the folders of the profile directory only: a blob directory located elsewhere must be captured together with the PostgreSQL data by other means. See Back Up and Restore TheHive Flow.

Switching back end doesn't migrate the blobs

The database references blobs by content hash without recording where they live. Pointing an existing installation at another back end, or at an empty directory, leaves every existing reference dangling: workflows reading files ingested before the switch fail at run time, not at startup.
