docs.title: Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration
docs.text:
6.0 One

In a TheHive Flow Docker Compose deployment, nginx is the HTTPS entry point. Its configuration comes from the nginx/templates/default.conf.template file. After changing the template, restart the service:

docker compose restart nginx

On a Kubernetes deployment, nginx isn't deployed. An Ingress applies the equivalent body size and timeout limits through annotations, as described in Expose TheHive Flow outside the cluster.

docs.title: Template variables
docs.text:
The nginx Docker image injects the following variables at container start, from the environment: block in docker-compose.yml.

Variable Value ${SERVER_NAME} The value of nginx_server_name from .env ${NGINX_SSL_TRUSTED_CERTIFICATE} ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/nginx/certs/ca.pem; when a custom certificate authority is provided, an empty string otherwise NGINX_THEHIVE_ADDRESSES The value of nginx_thehive_addresses from .env. It isn't a template variable. Before nginx starts, the nginx/docker-entrypoint.d/40-thehive-allow.sh script turns it into the allow lines of /etc/nginx/thehive-allow.conf. The script skips any entry that isn't an IPv4 address or a Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) range, or that covers the Docker network gateway

Apply a change to nginx_thehive_addresses with docker compose up -d --no-deps nginx. The entrypoint script runs again and logs the addresses it allows and skips.

docs.title: Service name and published port
docs.text:
TheHive in a container on the same host

Changing the name or port doesn't let a TheHive running in a container on the same host reach TheHive Flow.

The nginx service in docker-compose.yml runs as a container named nginx and publishes port 443 on the host. When another container or service on the host already uses that name or port, change them for TheHive Flow, using any unused container name and any free host port:

nginx:
  container_name: <container_name>
  ports:
    - '<host_port>:443'

Keep the container port set to 443, the port the template listens on.

Make the change in docker-compose.yml rather than in a docker-compose.override.yml file: Compose adds the ports of an override file to those of the base file instead of replacing them, so port 443 would stay published.

Publishing another host port changes the address TheHive Flow answers on, https://<flow_host>:<host_port>/. Use that address in TheHive configuration, and set flow_public_url to it so that webhook URLs include the port.

docs.title: ListenerNext steps
docs.text:
The template configures a single listener on port 443, with HTTP/2 enabled. It terminates TLS and routes requests by path to thehive-flow:8081 on the internal Docker network:

  • /webhook/ is proxied for any caller
  • /api/ is proxied only for the addresses listed in nginx_thehive_addresses, and answers 403 Forbidden to anyone else
  • Every other path answers 404 Not Found

Nginx resolves the thehive-flow service name through the Docker embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11, and resolves it again every 10 seconds. Recreating the thehive-flow service, for example with docker compose up -d thehive-flow after a configuration change, gives it a new IP address that nginx picks up without a restart. If nginx can't resolve the name, it still starts, returns 502 Bad Gateway, and logs thehive-flow could not be resolved.

The listener sets the Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, and X-Forwarded-Proto headers on proxied requests, adds a Strict-Transport-Security response header, and applies the following limits:

Setting Value client_max_body_size 2 GB Proxy timeouts 600 s

A request that exceeds the proxy timeout returns 504 Gateway Timeout. Before raising the limit, see Troubleshoot TheHive Flow.

The listener also turns response buffering off with proxy_buffering off: nginx streams each response to the client as the application produces it, instead of buffering it first. Request bodies remain buffered, a behavior described in Troubleshoot TheHive Flow.

To restrict which sources can reach the webhook paths, see Webhook exposure.

  • TheHive Flow Configuration Files
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Troubleshoot TheHive Flow

docs.title: Temporal Runtime Configuration
docs.text:
6.0 One

Temporal is the workflow engine of TheHive Flow. Its runtime knobs live in temporal/config/dynamicconfig/production.yaml. Temporal rereads most of this file automatically, so most changes apply without a restart.

The cluster configuration template, temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml.template, is rendered into temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml by init.sh, with the database password filled in. After editing the template, run bash ./scripts/init.sh again, then docker compose restart temporal. Without a custom certificate, the run also generates a new self-signed certificate: see TLS certificate renewal.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Runtime knobs
docs.text:
Knob Value Purpose limit.maxIDLength 255 Allows long unique identifiers and scoped names in workflow definitions system.forceSearchAttributesCacheRefreshOnRead true Refreshes the search attribute cache eagerly, avoiding a 60-second stale-read window when new attributes are registered limit.historyCount.suggestContinueAsNew 30 000 Accommodates long retry chains and fan-out patterns matching.numTaskqueueReadPartitions 1 Single-node deployment: colocation minimizes latency matching.numTaskqueueWritePartitions 1 Single-node deployment: colocation minimizes latency matching.rps 4000 Caps the rate of matching requests, sized from the sizing campaign's measured load history.transferProcessorMaxPollRPS 100 Per-shard limiter on loading history tasks history.hostLevelCacheMaxSize 33 000 Upper bound on the workflow-state cache, sized for the 1 GB Temporal memory limit of the Production environment #1 profile history.cacheTTL 480s How long an entry stays in the workflow-state cache before it's evicted history.cacheBackgroundEvict enabled, 15s interval, 1024 entries per call Evicts expired cache entries in the background instead of only on access

The three history cache keys need a restart

history.hostLevelCacheMaxSize, history.cacheTTL, and history.cacheBackgroundEvict are read once, when Temporal builds the workflow-state cache, and background eviction can't be turned on live. Changing any of them requires docker compose restart temporal. Every other knob applies without a restart.

docs.title: Payload size limitNext steps
docs.text:
The stack leaves the Temporal per-payload error limit, limit.blobSize.error, at its 2 MiB default. TheHive Flow enforces its own budget, slightly under that value, on the variable payloads it evaluates. Those are exit variables, loop variables such as the ones a For each flow produces, and the input variables passed to another workflow. An evaluation whose combined result would cross 2 MiB fails fast with a clear error instead of stalling the run on a payload the server keeps rejecting.

That budget is fixed. Raising limit.blobSize.error to accept larger payloads has no effect on TheHive Flow, which still refuses the runs the higher server limit was meant to allow. The effective ceiling stays about 2 MiB either way, so keep the two aligned and leave limit.blobSize.error at its default.

  • TheHive Flow Configuration Files
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Monitor TheHive Flow

docs.title: Deploy TheHive Flow with Docker Compose
docs.text:
6.0 One

Deploy and configure TheHive Flow using Docker Compose, on a single host connected to TheHive. TheHive and TheHive Flow should run on separate hosts.

Two deployment profiles for production environments are available on a dedicated GitHub repository, beside the profiles of TheHive and Cortex. TheHive Flow isn't distributed as Linux packages: Docker Compose and Kubernetes are its only deployment methods, whatever the method used to install TheHive itself.

If you want to use only TheHive Flow Docker image, get it from Docker Hub. You'll need to install the other required services separately.

Trying out TheHive Flow?

To test TheHive Flow with TheHive and Cortex on a single host, use the testing profile of the same repository, described in Test TheHive Flow on a single host.

Before you begin

To ensure a smooth deployment process, make sure you have:

  • A host that meets TheHive Flow system requirements and software requirements
  • At least sudo permissions on TheHive Flow host
  • A maintenance window for TheHive: upgrading it at Step 8 stops the service, and a later step requires editing TheHive configuration and restarting TheHive

TheHive and TheHive Flow on the same host

Keep TheHive and TheHive Flow on separate hosts. A TheHive running in a container on the same host as TheHive Flow can't reach the production profiles below. Docker replaces the address of its requests with the address of the Docker network gateway, which nginx never accepts. The testing profile of the repository is the exception. It runs TheHive, Cortex, and TheHive Flow on one host for functional testing, with TheHive calling TheHive Flow directly on the shared Docker network.

A single TheHive Flow instance

TheHive Flow can't run as a cluster: deploy one instance only. A TheHive cluster is supported in front of this single instance.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
The stack deploys the following services on the host:

Nginx is the only service published on the network. The health endpoints of thehive-flow are published on the loopback interface only. Blue arrows mark the services TheHive Flow needs to start: Temporal, PostgreSQL, and the blob store. The yellow arrows are used at run time only, when users work in the Flow view or when workflows run.

docs.title: Step 1: Install required dependencies
docs.text:
Start by installing the necessary dependencies for deploying TheHive Flow with Docker Compose.

  • Docker Engine: version v23.0.15 or later
  • Docker Compose plugin: version v2.20.2 or later
  • openssl, rsync, and jq, from the packages of your Linux distribution

docs.title: Verify dependencies installation
docs.text:
Run the following commands to ensure the dependencies are correctly installed:

  • Check the Docker engine version:
docker version
  • Confirm the current user can run Docker commands:
docker run hello-world

For details on post-installation steps and user permissions, see the Docker post-installation guide.

  • Check the Docker Compose plugin version:
docker compose version

docs.title: Step 2: Clone the GitHub repository
docs.text:
Next, clone the StrangeBee Docker repository on the target host:

git clone https://github.com/StrangeBeeCorp/docker.git

The repository holds the deployment profiles of TheHive Flow alongside those of TheHive and Cortex.

docs.title: Step 3: Choose your deployment profile
docs.text: Before proceeding with any commands, take a moment to choose the deployment profile that best fits your needs. Two prebuilt profiles are available for production environments. Both deploy the same services on a single host and differ only in the resources allocated to each service, listed in the system requirements.

docs.title: Profile n°1: Production environment #1 (TheHive Flow)
docs.text: Single server deployment of TheHive Flow for standard production workloads.

docs.title: Profile n°2: Production environment #2 (TheHive Flow)
docs.text: Single server deployment of TheHive Flow for high-performance or resource-intensive workloads.

docs.title: Step 4: Review the application stack
docs.text:
The Docker Compose file deploys the following components:

  • PostgreSQL: Database used by TheHive Flow and Temporal
  • Temporal: Workflow engine of TheHive Flow
  • SeaweedFS: S3-compatible object storage holding the files
  • TheHive Flow: Main application
  • Nginx: HTTPS reverse proxy

docs.title: Configuration and data files
docs.text:
Each container has a dedicated folder for configuration and data files.

├── certificates
├── docker-compose.yml
├── dot.env.template
├── nginx
├── postgresql
├── README.md
├── s3-store
├── scripts
├── temporal
└── thehive-flow

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
postgresql
└── data
  • ./postgresql/data: Database files, holding the thehive_flow, temporal, and temporal_visibility databases.

Don't modify

Don't manually modify these folders.

docs.title: Temporal
docs.text:
temporal
└── config
    ├── dynamicconfig
    │   └── production.yaml
    └── temporal-server.yaml.template
  • ./temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml.template: Template of the Temporal server configuration. temporal-server.yaml is generated from it, with the database password filled in, when you use the init.sh script.
  • ./temporal/config/dynamicconfig/production.yaml: Temporal runtime configuration.

docs.title: SeaweedFS
docs.text:
s3-store
└── data
  • ./s3-store/data: Files of the object storage.

Don't modify

Don't manually modify these folders.

docs.title: TheHive Flow
docs.text:
thehive-flow
├── config
│   └── thehive-flow.yml
└── secret
  • ./thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml: Application configuration.
  • ./thehive-flow/secret: TheHive API key file, provisioned at Step 9.

docs.title: Nginx
docs.text:
nginx
├── certs
├── docker-entrypoint.d
│   └── 40-thehive-allow.sh
└── templates
    └── default.conf.template
  • ./nginx/templates/default.conf.template: File used to initialize the nginx configuration when the container starts.
  • ./nginx/docker-entrypoint.d/40-thehive-allow.sh: Script run when the container starts, writing the list of addresses nginx accepts TheHive requests from.
  • ./nginx/certs: Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate and private key, placed there by the init.sh script.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
This folder is empty by default. The application stack initializes with self-signed certificates.

To use your own certificates, such as certificates signed by an internal authority, create the following files with these exact filenames, as described at Step 6:

certificates
├── server.crt         ## Server certificate
├── server.key         ## Server private key
└── ca.pem             ## Certificate Authority (CA)

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
scripts
├── check_permissions.sh
├── generate_certs.sh
├── init.sh
├── output.sh
├── reset.sh
├── backup.sh
└── restore.sh

The application stack includes several utility scripts:

  • check_permissions.sh: Ensures proper permissions are set on files and folders.
  • generate_certs.sh: Generates a self-signed certificate for nginx, or installs the custom one.
  • init.sh: Initializes the application stack. See Step 7.
  • output.sh: Displays output messages called by other scripts.
  • reset.sh: Resets the environment. Running this script deletes all data, the secrets, and the certificates.
  • backup.sh: Performs a cold backup of the current environment. See Back Up and Restore TheHive Flow for more details.
  • restore.sh: Restores the environment from a previously taken backup.

docs.title: Step 5: Go to the selected profile
docs.text:
Go to the directory of your chosen profile. For example, to select the Production environment #1 profile:

cd docker/prod1-thehive-flow

docs.title: (Optional) Step 6: Provide custom TLS certificates
docs.text:
If you have certificates signed by your own certificate authority (CA), place them in the certificates directory before running init.sh. The script matches on the exact file names server.crt, server.key, and ca.pem, so rename your files as you copy them:

cp /path/to/<certificate>    ./certificates/server.crt
cp /path/to/<private_key>    ./certificates/server.key
cp /path/to/<ca_certificate> ./certificates/ca.pem

Restrict the private key to its owner:

chmod 600 ./certificates/server.key

All three files are in PEM format:

  • server.crt: The certificate nginx sends to clients. It must hold the server certificate first, followed by the intermediate certificates of the chain, up to but not including the root.
  • server.key: The private key matching the server certificate, without a passphrase. Nginx can't prompt for one at container start.
  • ca.pem: The CA certificate. Nginx uses it for OCSP stapling and client certificate verification, and never sends it to clients, so it doesn't replace the intermediates in server.crt.

The three files work as a set. With all of them present, init.sh copies them to ./nginx/certs/ and turns on the ssl_trusted_certificate directive in the nginx configuration, which gives ca.pem to nginx. With any of them missing, the script prints a notice, ignores the files, and generates a self-signed certificate for the server name set at Step 7, valid for 365 days.

docs.title: Step 7: Initialize the stack
docs.text:
The init.sh script automates the following setup tasks:

1/ Checks the ownership and permissions of the files and folders, and offers to fix them.

2/ Prompts for the server name, used as the nginx host name, in the TLS certificate, and in the default public URL of TheHive Flow. The default is the system host name.

3/ Prompts for TheHive URL, as reachable from the thehive-flow container. The value is required: the script stops on an empty or malformed value.

4/ Prompts for the addresses TheHive calls from, and writes them to nginx_thehive_addresses.

5/ Installs the custom TLS certificate, or generates a self-signed one.

6/ Generates .env from dot.env.template, with random 256-bit secrets produced by openssl rand, the image versions pinned in versions.env, your user and group identifiers, and the group identifier of the Docker socket. The socket group is read from inside a throwaway container, so the detection also works where the socket group differs between the host and the containers, such as Docker Desktop.

7/ Renders temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml from its template, with the Temporal database password filled in.

8/ Starts PostgreSQL, then creates the thehive_flow and temporal roles and the thehive_flow, temporal, and temporal_visibility databases.

9/ Creates the Temporal schema in the two Temporal databases, starts Temporal, and creates its default namespace.

10/ Prints the next steps.

Run the script:

bash ./scripts/init.sh

The script asks three questions:

  • Server name: press Enter to accept the default, the system host name. With a custom certificate provided at Step 6, enter a name the certificate carries, as its common name or one of its subject alternative names. TheHive calls that name in flow.url, and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) running TheHive rejects a mismatch. When webhook callers reach TheHive Flow through another reverse proxy, host name, path prefix, or port, set flow_public_url in .env to that address. See Public URL.
  • TheHive URL: the address of TheHive host as reachable from the thehive-flow container, for example http://<thehive_host>:9000. TheHive doesn't need to be running yet: set the address it will be reachable at. TheHive itself is deployed at Step 8. For an https:// address whose certificate is signed by an internal CA, see TLS toward TheHive. When TheHive sits on a private network, the TheHive integration node and the HTTP request node can't reach it until its address range is added to the egress allowlist.
  • TheHive addresses: the IPv4 addresses TheHive calls TheHive Flow from, comma-separated, for example 192.168.1.10,192.168.1.11. A range in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation, such as 192.168.1.0/28, is also accepted. With a TheHive cluster, list every node. These are the addresses TheHive requests come from. They can differ from the address in TheHive URL, for example with a TheHive cluster behind a virtual IP address, a Network Address Translation (NAT) device, or an outbound proxy. Nginx forwards TheHive requests only from these addresses, and refuses them from every address while the list is empty. See TheHive address filtering.

PostgreSQL and Temporal stay up once the script completes. The script ends with a warning that no TheHive API key is set yet: the key is provisioned at Step 9.

Safe to run again

Running init.sh again on an initialized stack is safe. It keeps the secrets already in .env, offers the values it holds as defaults for the three questions, and only creates the databases, the Temporal schema, and the namespace when they're missing. If it fails partway, fix the cause and run it again.

One side effect: without a custom certificate in ./certificates/, each run generates a new self-signed certificate. Restart nginx to serve it, and if TheHive trusts the specific certificate as described in Option B, copy the new nginx/certs/server.crt to TheHive host again. See TLS certificate renewal.

Expected output

The transcript below is trimmed: the Docker Compose progress lines, the certificate generation details, and the next-steps text vary.

[✔] All files and folders have expected permissions.
[*] Define the hostname used to connect to this server
Server Name (default: flow-host): flow.example.com
[*] Define the TheHive URL, as reachable from the TheHive Flow container
TheHive URL, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:9000 (required): http://192.168.1.10:9000
[*] Define the addresses TheHive calls this server from (IPv4 or CIDR, comma-separated)
TheHive addresses (default: none): 192.168.1.10
[*] No custom certificate found.
[*] If you want to provide your custom certificate for the Reverse Proxy, please copy the following files in the ./certificates directory:
    * ./certificates/server.crt
    * ./certificates/server.key
    * ./certificates/ca.pem
[✔] Generating self-signed certificate...
[✔] Self-signed certificate generated for flow.example.com.
[✔] ./.env written.
[✔] ./temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml written.
[*] Starting PostgreSQL...
[✔] Databases ready.
[*] Creating the Temporal schema...
[✔] Temporal schema created.
[*] Starting Temporal...
[✔] Temporal namespace 'default' created.
[!] No TheHive API key: TheHive Flow does not start without one. Write it to ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key or set thehive_api_key in .env.
[✔] Initialisation completed.
...
  • The [!] warning about TheHive API key is expected at this point: the key is provisioned at Step 9.
  • With the prompt for TheHive addresses left empty, a [!] warning follows it. The script still completes, but nginx refuses every TheHive request until nginx_thehive_addresses is set in .env and nginx is recreated with docker compose up -d --no-deps nginx.
  • With custom certificates provided at Step 6, a single Using custom certicates found in ./certificates. line replaces the certificate lines.
  • On a second run, Temporal schema already exists. and Temporal namespace 'default' already exists. replace the two creation lines, and the three prompts offer the current values as defaults. The certificate lines appear again: a new self-signed certificate is generated at each run.
  • A line starting with /!\ is an error: the script stops, and running it again after fixing the cause is safe.

docs.title: Step 8: Deploy or upgrade TheHive
docs.text:
The following steps require TheHive 6.x running and reachable from TheHive Flow stack. TheHive 6.x installs with the standard methods: Linux packages, Docker Compose, or the Kubernetes Helm chart.

Package installations: TheHive 6.x requires Java 17, Cassandra 4.0.x to 4.1.x requires Java 11

On a package installation, TheHive 6.x runs on Java 17, while Cassandra 4.0.x to 4.1.x, the database it relies on, still requires Java 11 and doesn't support Java 17. When both share a host, install the two Java versions side by side and pin each service to its own: see Run TheHive 6 and Cassandra on the Same Host. Docker and Kubernetes deployments aren't affected: the images ship their own runtime.

  • For a new deployment, see TheHive Installation Methods.
  • To upgrade an existing TheHive 5.x instance installed with packages or Docker Compose, see Upgrade from TheHive 5.x. For a Kubernetes Helm deployment, upgrade the release as described in Deploy TheHive on Kubernetes.

docs.title: Step 9: Provision TheHive API key
docs.text:
1. Sign in to TheHive with an account that has the predefined Org-Admin profile.

  2. Generate a dedicated API key for a user account whose profile includes the Manage analysis and Manage actions permissions. TheHive Flow uses the key to run Cortex analyzers and responders through TheHive, from the Analyzer and Responder action nodes. Each call runs in the organization of the workflow, so the account must belong to every organization whose workflows use these nodes. The key is required even when no workflow uses these nodes: TheHive Flow doesn't start without it.

    Any account type works, but a service account is recommended: it can't sign in to the UI and isn't tied to a person. See Create a User Account and Manage a User Account API Key.

  3. On TheHive Flow host, store the key in the secret file, readable by its owner only:

    printf '%s' '<thehive_api_key>' > ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key
chmod 600 ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key

    Alternatively, set it in .env, which is at mode 600 already:

    thehive_api_key=<thehive_api_key>

    When both are set, thehive_api_key in .env takes precedence over the secret file. See the secrets inventory.

docs.title: Step 10: Configure TheHive to reach TheHive Flow
docs.text:
TheHive must know the address at which it reaches TheHive Flow and the JWT signing key generated by init.sh. That address is the nginx entry point: it isn't necessarily the public URL webhook callers use. Where that configuration goes depends on how TheHive is deployed.

On a package installation, everything goes in /etc/thehive/application.conf. On a Docker deployment, it depends on how TheHive container starts: check the thehive service in TheHive docker-compose.yml file for --no-config in its command, or TH_NO_CONFIG=1 in its environment. The StrangeBee Docker Compose profiles, testing, prod1-thehive, and prod2-thehive, all ship command: '--no-config --no-config-secret'.

The same logic applies to TheHive image run without Docker Compose, with docker run or another container runtime. The image entrypoint reads the same variables and files, so follow the matching Docker Compose tab and recreate the container with the commands of your runtime.

  1. On TheHive Flow host, read the key from the .env file at the root of the profile directory:

    grep jwt_signing_key .env

  2. On TheHive host, declare the connection and activate the feature, using the key from the previous command.

    The lines play two roles. The flow.url and flow.jwt_signing_key keys declare the connection. The scalligraph.modules line loads the connector that talks to TheHive Flow, and the features.Orchestrator.enabled flag displays the Flow view and opens its routes.

    TheHive installed with packagesTheHive deployed with Docker Compose, started with --no-configTheHive deployed with Docker Compose, started without --no-config

    Add the following to the /etc/thehive/application.conf file, next to the connector lines it already holds:

    flow.url             = "https://<flow_host>/"
flow.jwt_signing_key = "<jwt_signing_key>"
features.Orchestrator.enabled = true
scalligraph.modules += "org.thp.thehive.connector.flow.FlowModule"

    With command: '--no-config' or TH_NO_CONFIG=1, TheHive ignores the TH_* environment variables that generate configuration. All configuration goes in the application.conf file TheHive reads at /etc/thehive/application.conf.

    The StrangeBee Docker Compose profiles ship that file as thehive/config/application.conf and mount the directory at /etc/thehive in TheHive container. The file already holds the scalligraph.modules line of TheHive Flow, commented out. Uncomment it, and add the other lines next to it:

    flow.url             = "https://<flow_host>/"
flow.jwt_signing_key = "<jwt_signing_key>"
features.Orchestrator.enabled = true
scalligraph.modules += "org.thp.thehive.connector.flow.FlowModule"

    On a deployment that provides no such file, create it and mount it in docker-compose.yml:

    volumes:
  - /path/to/application.conf:/etc/thehive/application.conf:ro

    TheHive Docker entrypoint reads TH_* environment variables. Declare the connection in TheHive docker-compose.yml file:

    environment:
  TH_FLOW_KEY: "<jwt_signing_key>"
  TH_FLOW_URL: "https://<flow_host>/"

    The two variables declare the connection but don't turn it on: add the feature flag and the connector module to an application.conf file mounted at /etc/thehive/application.conf in TheHive container. The entrypoint includes that file automatically in the configuration it generates.

    features.Orchestrator.enabled = true
scalligraph.modules += "org.thp.thehive.connector.flow.FlowModule"

    Mount the file in docker-compose.yml:

    volumes:
  - /path/to/application.conf:/etc/thehive/application.conf:ro

  3. Apply the change.

    TheHive installed with packagesTheHive deployed with Docker Compose

    Restart TheHive:

    sudo systemctl restart thehive

    Recreate TheHive container. A plain docker compose restart applies neither the environment variables nor the new volume mount:

    docker compose up -d thehive

docs.title: TLS with a self-signed certificate
docs.text: When init.sh generated a self-signed certificate because no custom certificate was provided at Step 6, TheHive JVM rejects the connection by default. Two options are available. Both go under flow.wsConfig, so they apply to the connection to TheHive Flow only. Cortex, Malware Information Sharing Platform & Threat Sharing (MISP), and the other connectors keep their own certificate verification.

docs.title: Option A: Turn off certificate verification
docs.text:
With this option, TheHive accepts any certificate from TheHive Flow without verifying it. It's the quickest to set up, but TheHive can no longer detect a server impersonating TheHive Flow host: reserve it for trusted internal networks.

Add the following line to TheHive application.conf file:

flow.wsConfig.ssl.loose.acceptAnyCertificate = true

docs.title: Option B: Trust the specific certificate
docs.text:
With this option, certificate verification stays on and TheHive trusts the specific TheHive Flow certificate. It's the more secure choice.

  1. Copy nginx/certs/server.crt from TheHive Flow host to TheHive host.

  2. Make it readable by TheHive at /etc/thehive/thehive-flow-nginx.crt.

    TheHive installed with packagesTheHive deployed with Docker Compose

    Place the file directly:

    sudo cp /path/to/server.crt /etc/thehive/thehive-flow-nginx.crt

    Mount it into TheHive container in docker-compose.yml:

    volumes:
  - /path/to/thehive-flow-nginx.crt:/etc/thehive/thehive-flow-nginx.crt:ro

  3. Declare it as trusted in TheHive application.conf file:

    flow.wsConfig.ssl {
  trustManager {
    stores = [
      { type: "PEM", path: "/etc/thehive/thehive-flow-nginx.crt" }
    ]
  }
}

  4. Apply the change.

    TheHive installed with packagesTheHive deployed with Docker Compose

    Restart TheHive:

    sudo systemctl restart thehive

    Recreate TheHive container. A plain docker compose restart doesn't apply the new volume mount:

    docker compose up -d thehive

docs.title: Step 11: Start the stack
docs.text:
Back on TheHive Flow host, start all services with Docker Compose:

docker compose up -d

The first start pulls the remaining images from Docker Hub.

docs.title: Step 12: Verify the deployment
docs.text:
On TheHive Flow host, check that all containers are running and that the health endpoints respond:

docker compose ps -a
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/livez
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

The -a flag also lists stopped containers, such as the one-shot init-s3-store. /livez confirms the HTTP server is up. /readyz confirms TheHive Flow can reach its database and the Temporal workflow engine, and returns 503 naming the failing check otherwise.

From a host that isn't listed in nginx_thehive_addresses, check that nginx refuses TheHive requests:

curl -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<nginx_server_name>/api/v1/version

The command prints 403.

Expected output

The docker compose ps -a listing, trimmed to the relevant columns:

NAME                         SERVICE         STATUS
nginx                        nginx           Up 2 minutes
thehive-flow                 thehive-flow    Up 2 minutes
thehive-flow-init-s3-store   init-s3-store   Exited (0)
thehive-flow-postgresql      postgresql      Up 2 minutes (healthy)
thehive-flow-s3-store        s3-store        Up 2 minutes (healthy)
thehive-flow-temporal        temporal        Up 2 minutes (healthy)

The thehive-flow and nginx containers define no Docker health check, so their status carries no (healthy) suffix: the two curl probes cover TheHive Flow health instead.

A healthy /livez returns 200 with an empty body. A healthy /readyz reports each check:

{"status":"ok","checks":{"db":"ok","modules":"ok","temporal":"ok"}}

In docker compose ps -a, init-s3-store shows Exited (0) and that's the expected steady state: it's a one-shot container that provisions the object storage identity and bucket, verifies both, then exits. Everything else should show a running or healthy status. Only a non-zero exit code on init-s3-store indicates a problem: see Troubleshoot TheHive Flow.

docs.title: Step 13: Check the connection in TheHive
docs.text:
Sign in to TheHive with an account that has the predefined Org-Admin profile, which includes TheHive Flow permissions automatically.

The health indicator at the bottom of the sidebar menu reports the connection from any view. It covers every configured connector: TheHive Flow, Cortex, MISP, and Email Intake. Its color reflects all of them at once:

  • Green: every configured connector is healthy.
  • Red: at least one configured connector is in error.
  • Faded: no connector is configured.

Select the indicator to see the details. Its Flow section shows TheHive Flow URL and its own status, OK or ERROR. TheHive probes TheHive Flow every minute by default, so allow that long for the status to reflect a fix. Changing flow.url or flow.jwt_signing_key triggers an immediate check.

Then go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  • If the view displays the workflow list, empty on a fresh deployment but with the Import workflow button visible, TheHive and TheHive Flow are connected.
  • If the view is missing from the sidebar, review the configuration from Step 10 and restart TheHive.
  • If the view displays an error notification over an empty workflow list, TheHive can't reach TheHive Flow: run the check from TheHive host to tell a network or nginx problem from a JWT problem.

docs.title: Step 14: Grant users access to TheHive Flow
docs.text: Users who don't have one of the predefined Org-Admin and Analyst profiles need TheHive Flow permissions through a custom profile: see Perform TheHive Flow Initial Setup as an Admin.

docs.title: Test TheHive Flow on a single hostNext steps
docs.text:
Testing only

This profile must never be used in production.

One license required

TheHive Flow requires a One license. The 14-day Platinum trial that comes with the environment doesn't cover it: activate your One license in TheHive before connecting TheHive to TheHive Flow.

The testing profile of the repository deploys TheHive, Cortex, and TheHive Flow on one host, for functional testing only. The Docker demo environment describes its TheHive and Cortex side, including the sample data script and the default accounts. TheHive Flow services are the same as in the production profiles, with three differences:

  • TheHive calls TheHive Flow directly on the shared Docker network, at http://thehive-flow:8081. Nginx forwards only the /flow/webhook/ path to TheHive Flow, so webhook URLs take the form https://<server_name>/flow/webhook/<webhook_id>.
  • The init.sh script prompts for the server name only. It generates the secrets of TheHive Flow, keeps them on later runs, creates the databases, the Temporal schema, and the namespace, and writes a placeholder TheHive API key to ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key.

  • The profile doesn't declare the connection in TheHive configuration: add it yourself once the environment runs.

  • Deploy the environment as described in Deploy a Demo Docker Environment, from the docker/testing directory. TheHive Flow services start with the rest. Check that TheHive Flow is ready:

    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

  • Read the JWT signing key init.sh generated, and add the connection to ./thehive/config/application.conf, then restart TheHive:

    grep jwt_signing_key .env

    flow.url             = "http://thehive-flow:8081"
flow.jwt_signing_key = "<jwt_signing_key>"
features.Orchestrator.enabled = true
scalligraph.modules += "org.thp.thehive.connector.flow.FlowModule"

    docker compose restart thehive

  • In TheHive, generate an API key for an account whose profile includes the Manage analysis and Manage actions permissions, as described at Step 9. Replace the placeholder with it, then restart TheHive Flow:

    printf '%s' '<thehive_api_key>' > ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key
docker compose restart thehive-flow

  • Check the connection in TheHive, with the health indicator and the Flow view, as described at Step 13.

To apply a change to ./thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml, recreate the service with docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow, as on the production profiles. To start over, bash ./scripts/reset.sh deletes all the data of the environment, TheHive Flow included.

  • Build Your First Workflow
  • Upgrade TheHive Flow with Docker Compose
  • TheHive Flow Configuration Files
  • TheHive Flow Environment Variables
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Authentication Between TheHive Flow Components
  • Monitor TheHive Flow
  • Troubleshoot TheHive Flow

docs.title: Deploy TheHive Flow on Kubernetes
docs.text:
6.0 One

Deploy and configure TheHive Flow on a Kubernetes cluster using the Helm chart published in the StrangeBee Helm chart repository, and connect it to TheHive. TheHive Flow isn't distributed as Linux packages: Kubernetes and Docker Compose are its only deployment methods, whatever the method used to install TheHive itself.

Installing the chart deploys the application and its own Temporal workflow engine, as a subchart. It doesn't deploy the PostgreSQL database and the S3-compatible object storage TheHive Flow needs: they're provisioned first, at Step 3. For testing, the deployment scenarios shipped beside the chart provide both, and the steps below use them. For production, use a PostgreSQL database and S3-compatible object storage you operate.

The application runs as a single replica: the chart enforces replicaCount: 1.

Before you begin

To ensure a smooth deployment process, make sure you have:

  • A cluster that meets the software requirements and the chart sizing defaults
  • A maintenance window for TheHive: upgrading it at Step 4 stops the service, and a later step requires editing TheHive configuration and restarting TheHive

A single TheHive Flow instance

TheHive Flow can't run as a cluster: deploy one instance only. A TheHive cluster is supported in front of this single instance.

The examples below use the thehive-flow namespace and the thehive-flow release name, which are the names the deployment scenarios use. Adapt them to your cluster conventions.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
The chart and its deployment scenarios deploy the following on the cluster:

Inside the cluster, TheHive calls the thehive-flow-api Service. PostgreSQL and the S3-compatible object storage are provisioned before the chart, by the deployment scenarios for testing or by your own tooling for production. The code transformation Jobs use the assistant image to move files between the object storage and each Job. Blue arrows mark the services TheHive Flow needs to start: Temporal, PostgreSQL, and the object storage. The yellow arrows are used at run time only, when users work in the Flow view or when workflows run.

docs.title: Step 1: Install required dependencies
docs.text:
Start by installing the necessary tools on the machine that will run the following commands.

  • Helm: version v3.8.0 or later
  • kubectl: version matching the cluster, within one minor version
  • openssl: any version, to generate the JWT signing key

The cluster itself must run Kubernetes v1.29.0 or later. The deployment scenarios also need a default storage class for their persistent volumes.

docs.title: Verify dependencies installation
docs.text:
Run the following commands to ensure the tools are correctly installed and reach the cluster:

helm version
kubectl version
kubectl get nodes

docs.title: Step 2: Add the Helm repository and get the scenario files
docs.text:
The chart is published in the StrangeBee Helm chart repository on GitHub, under thehive-charts/thehive-flow, alongside the chart of TheHive itself.

  1. Add the StrangeBee Helm repository and update your local Helm repositories:

    helm repo add strangebee https://strangebeecorp.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

    The chart is then available as strangebee/thehive-flow. To list every value it accepts, run helm show values strangebee/thehive-flow.

  2. Optional: For testing, also clone the GitHub repository to get the deployment scenarios, which hold the manifests and values files that provision PostgreSQL and the S3-compatible object storage. A production deployment that uses its own PostgreSQL and object storage doesn't need them.

    git clone https://github.com/StrangeBeeCorp/helm-charts.git
cd helm-charts/thehive-charts/thehive-flow

    The scenarios live in the scenarios/ directory of the chart: cnpg provides PostgreSQL, seaweedfs provides the object storage, and combined layers both for a full installation.

docs.title: Step 3: Provision PostgreSQL and the object storage
docs.text:
The chart itself deploys only TheHive Flow and the Temporal subchart. The two stateful dependencies are provisioned before it, either with the deployment scenarios shipped beside the chart, or by your own tooling:

Component Provisioned by the scenarios External alternative PostgreSQL A CloudNativePG cluster named thehive-flow-postgresql, with one instance and 10 GiB of storage, the thehive_flow and temporal roles, and the thehive_flow, temporal, and temporal_visibility databases. The cnpg scenario Any PostgreSQL reachable from the cluster, with the roles and databases described in External PostgreSQL Object storage A single-pod SeaweedFS release in its own seaweedfs namespace, with a 10 GiB persistent volume and the thehive-flow bucket, installed from the upstream SeaweedFS Helm chart. The seaweedfs scenario Any S3-compatible storage, set through the blobstore.s3.* values as described in External object storage

Whichever way you provision them, first create the namespace TheHive Flow runs in:

kubectl create namespace thehive-flow

docs.title: Deployment scenarios
docs.text:
The scenarios run the services as single replicas, with placeholder credentials that start with ChangeThis. Change them in scenarios/cnpg/postgres-secrets.yaml for the database roles, and in both scenarios/seaweedfs/seaweedfs-s3-secret.yaml and scenarios/seaweedfs/thehive-flow-s3-secret.yaml for the object storage, which must hold the same key.

To provision the scenario defaults, run the following commands from the chart directory. The machine running them must be able to reach the CloudNativePG and SeaweedFS Helm chart repositories.

  1. Install the CloudNativePG operator, then create the PostgreSQL cluster and its databases. The role Secrets come first: the cluster creates the roles from them.

    helm upgrade --install cnpg cloudnative-pg \
  --repo https://cloudnative-pg.github.io/charts --version 0.29.1 \
  -n cnpg-system --create-namespace --wait

kubectl apply -n thehive-flow -f scenarios/cnpg/postgres-secrets.yaml
kubectl apply -n thehive-flow -f scenarios/cnpg/postgres-cluster.yaml
kubectl wait -n thehive-flow cluster/thehive-flow-postgresql \
  --for=condition=Ready --timeout=5m
kubectl apply -n thehive-flow -f scenarios/cnpg/databases.yaml

    Check the result with kubectl get -n thehive-flow cluster,database: the cluster reports Cluster in healthy state and the three databases APPLIED: true.

  2. Create the object storage credentials, in the seaweedfs namespace for the store and in the thehive-flow namespace for TheHive Flow, then install SeaweedFS. A post-install hook creates the thehive-flow bucket.

    kubectl create namespace seaweedfs
kubectl apply -f scenarios/seaweedfs/seaweedfs-s3-secret.yaml
kubectl apply -n thehive-flow -f scenarios/seaweedfs/thehive-flow-s3-secret.yaml

helm upgrade --install seaweedfs seaweedfs \
  --repo https://seaweedfs.github.io/seaweedfs/helm --version 4.48.0 \
  -n seaweedfs -f scenarios/seaweedfs/seaweedfs-values.yaml --wait

    Check that the bucket exists:

    kubectl exec -n seaweedfs deploy/seaweedfs-all-in-one -- \
  sh -c 'echo s3.bucket.list | weed shell'

The scenario values files, scenarios/cnpg/values.yaml and scenarios/seaweedfs/values.yaml, point the chart at these two services. They're passed to the chart at Step 6.

docs.title: External PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The chart creates no roles or databases. On a PostgreSQL server of your own, create them before the installation, with the same names the chart values use by default:

CREATE ROLE thehive_flow LOGIN PASSWORD '<thehive_flow_password>';
CREATE ROLE temporal LOGIN CREATEDB PASSWORD '<temporal_password>';
CREATE DATABASE thehive_flow OWNER thehive_flow;
CREATE DATABASE temporal OWNER temporal;
CREATE DATABASE temporal_visibility OWNER temporal;
  • The thehive_flow role owns the thehive_flow database. Ownership is all the pre-install migrations Job needs to create and alter the tables.
  • The temporal role owns the temporal and temporal_visibility databases and carries the CREATEDB attribute, which the Temporal schema setup requires.
  • The two passwords go into the thehive-flow-postgresql-thehive-flow-user and thehive-flow-postgresql-temporal-user Secrets created at Step 5. The thehive_flow password is expanded into a postgres:// URL, so it must be URL-safe.
  • The server address, port, and TLS mode are set at Step 6, where TheHive Flow and the Temporal subchart must point at the same server. To use other role or database names, set postgresql.username and postgresql.database for TheHive Flow, and the user and databaseName keys of both Temporal datastores.

docs.title: External object storage
docs.text:
S3-compatible object storage is the only blob store supported on Kubernetes, set through the blobstore.s3.* values:

  • A managed S3-compatible object storage service, such as Amazon S3 or the service of your cloud provider, for performance and resilience.
  • A self-hosted S3-compatible object storage system. For example, SeaweedFS has been tested and works well with TheHive Flow: it's the one the scenario deploys, as a single pod. Whichever store you self-host, make sure its endpoint is highly available, for example through the storage platform itself or a correctly configured load balancer.

Create the bucket first: TheHive Flow checks it at startup and doesn't start if it's missing. Then point the chart at the store in the values file written at Step 6:

blobstore:
  s3:
    bucket: <bucket_name>
    region: <region>
    endpoint: <endpoint_url>
    usePathStyle: true
    accessKeyId: <access_key_id>
  • The chart default for blobstore.s3.endpoint doesn't match the scenario: always set it. Keep the full domain name of an in-cluster endpoint, such as http://<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:8333: the code transformation jobs run in their own namespace and use the value as is.
  • For Amazon S3, leave blobstore.s3.endpoint empty and set blobstore.s3.usePathStyle to false.
  • The secret access key goes into the thehive-flow-s3 Secret created at Step 5, whose AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID key must hold the same value as blobstore.s3.accessKeyId.

To use the AWS SDK default credential chain instead of a static key, set blobstore.s3.accessKeyId to an empty value. Its default, thehive-flow, matches the scenario object store. A deployment on AWS can then bind an IAM role to the service accounts instead of storing a static secret. Bind the application service account through serviceAccount.annotations, and the codex-jobs one, which code transformation jobs run as, through codex.kubernetes.serviceAccountAnnotations. Whichever identity you use, grant it the permissions the S3 back end needs, including the delete right.

docs.title: Step 4: Deploy or upgrade TheHive
docs.text:
The following steps require TheHive 6.x running and reachable from the cluster. TheHive 6.x installs with the standard methods: Linux packages, Docker Compose, or the Kubernetes Helm chart.

Package installations: TheHive 6.x requires Java 17, Cassandra 4.0.x to 4.1.x requires Java 11

On a package installation, TheHive 6.x runs on Java 17, while Cassandra 4.0.x to 4.1.x, the database it relies on, still requires Java 11 and doesn't support Java 17. When both share a host, install the two Java versions side by side and pin each service to its own: see Run TheHive 6 and Cassandra on the Same Host. Docker and Kubernetes deployments aren't affected: the images ship their own runtime.

  • For TheHive in the cluster, see Deploy TheHive on Kubernetes, which also describes how to upgrade an existing release.
  • For TheHive outside the cluster, see TheHive Installation Methods for a new deployment, or Upgrade from TheHive 5.x for an existing instance installed with packages or Docker Compose.

docs.title: Step 5: Provision the secrets
docs.text:
The chart creates no Secrets in the release namespace: it reads every secret from existing Kubernetes Secrets there, named as follows by default. The names and keys are configurable through the secrets.* values. The only Secret the chart writes is a copy of the object storage credentials in the code transformation jobs namespace, where the jobs read them.

Secret Key Holds Created by thehive-flow-jwt jwt-symmetric-key JWT signing key shared with TheHive. Generate a strong random value of at least 32 bytes, such as openssl rand -base64 32: TheHive Flow refuses to start with a shorter key. Keep it stable across upgrades: changing it invalidates every token already issued You thehive-flow-thehive api-key TheHive API key used to run Cortex analyzers and responders through TheHive You thehive-flow-postgresql-thehive-flow-user password Password of the thehive_flow database role The cnpg scenario, or you thehive-flow-postgresql-temporal-user password Password of the temporal database role The cnpg scenario, or you thehive-flow-s3 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Object storage credentials, also copied to the code transformation jobs. AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID must match the blobstore.s3.accessKeyId value The seaweedfs scenario, or you

For the API key, sign in to TheHive with a user account that has the predefined Org-Admin profile. Then generate a dedicated key for an account whose profile includes the Manage analysis and Manage actions permissions, both in the Licensed category. TheHive Flow uses the key to run Cortex analyzers and responders through TheHive, from the Analyzer and Responder action nodes. Each call runs in the organization of the workflow, so the account must belong to every organization whose workflows use these nodes. The key is required even when no workflow uses these nodes: TheHive Flow doesn't start without it.

A service account is recommended: it can't sign in to the UI and isn't tied to a person. See Create a User Account and Manage a User Account API Key.

Create the two Secrets the scenarios don't provide:

kubectl create secret generic thehive-flow-jwt -n thehive-flow \
  --from-literal=jwt-symmetric-key="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"

kubectl create secret generic thehive-flow-thehive -n thehive-flow \
  --from-literal=api-key='<thehive_api_key>'

Scenario Secrets are placeholders

The manifests applied at Step 3 ship placeholder credentials for test clusters only. In production, manage these Secrets with your own tooling, such as sealed-secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

docs.title: Secrets for external PostgreSQL and object storage
docs.text:
With an external PostgreSQL and an external object storage, the scenarios create nothing. Create the three remaining Secrets too, with the passwords of the two database roles and the credentials of the object storage identity. The commands below create them directly, for a cluster where that's acceptable. With a secret management tool, give the Secrets it produces the same names and keys, or point the chart at other names through the secrets.* values.

kubectl create secret generic thehive-flow-postgresql-thehive-flow-user -n thehive-flow \
  --from-literal=password='<thehive_flow_password>'

kubectl create secret generic thehive-flow-postgresql-temporal-user -n thehive-flow \
  --from-literal=password='<temporal_password>'

kubectl create secret generic thehive-flow-s3 -n thehive-flow \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<access_key_id>' \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<secret_access_key>'

With the AWS SDK default credential chain, described in External object storage, the thehive-flow-s3 Secret isn't needed.

docs.title: Step 6: Install the chart
docs.text:
Installing the chart deploys two TheHive Flow images: the application image, docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow, and the code transformation assistant image, docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow-assistant. The assistant image runs as helper containers inside each code transformation job, moving the script inputs and outputs between the object storage and the job working directory. The chart defaults point at both released images, and the tag falls back to the chart appVersion, which is the released version. The cluster pulls them at install time, with no registry setup needed.

  1. Write a values file pointing the chart at TheHive and setting the public URL of TheHive Flow. With the scenarios, set the two values in scenarios/combined/values.yaml, which carries placeholders for both:

    config:
  api:
    public:
      url: <thehive_flow_public_url>
  modules:
    workers:
      activities:
        thehive:
          url: <thehive_url>

    The config.modules.workers.activities.thehive.url value is the address TheHive Flow calls TheHive at, as reachable from the cluster. The default, http://thehive:9000, assumes a Service named thehive in the release namespace: set it whenever TheHive runs elsewhere, for example http://thehive.<thehive_namespace>.svc.cluster.local:9000 for a TheHive release in another namespace. An in-cluster Service or a private network address is a non-public address. The TheHive integration node and the HTTP request node can't reach it until its range is listed in the egress allowlist, in the same values file.

    The config.api.public.url value is the public URL at which webhook callers reach the root of TheHive Flow, such as https://<flow_host> behind the Ingress described below. TheHive Flow builds the URL of each Webhook trigger from it. The value has no default, and the chart refuses to render without it, or when it isn't an absolute http or https URL free of credentials, a query, and a fragment.

    On a cluster that can't reach the public registries, mirror the two TheHive Flow images, and the other images listed in Images pulled at first start, to a registry of your own. Use a tool that preserves the architectures, such as skopeo copy --all or crane. Then point the chart at the registry, with a pull secret when the registry requires one:

    image:
  repository: <registry>/<flow_image_repository>
  tag: 6.0.0

imagePullSecrets:
  - name: <registry_pull_secret>

codex:
  kubernetes:
    assistantImage:
      repository: <registry>/<assistant_image_repository>
      tag: 6.0.0
    imagePullSecrets:
      - <registry_pull_secret>
    • An empty or omitted tag falls back to the chart appVersion, which is the released version.
    • The codex.kubernetes.imagePullSecrets entries are plain Secret names, without the name: key the top-level imagePullSecrets list uses.
    • Point the other images at the registry through their own values: temporal.server.image, temporal.admintools.image, temporalReadiness.image, waitContainers.image, tests.image, and codex.languageImages.

  2. With an external PostgreSQL, align the Temporal subchart with it. TheHive Flow and Temporal share one PostgreSQL server, and the chart refuses to render when their addresses diverge. If you change postgresql.host or postgresql.port, set both Temporal datastore addresses to the same <host>:<port> in the values file. The cnpg scenario values already do so for the scenario cluster.

    postgresql:
  host: <postgres_host>
  port: <postgres_port>

temporal:
  server:
    config:
      persistence:
        datastores:
          default:
            sql:
              connectAddr: "<postgres_host>:<postgres_port>"
          visibility:
            sql:
              connectAddr: "<postgres_host>:<postgres_port>"

    The chart connects to PostgreSQL with sslmode=require by default: the connection is encrypted, but the server certificate isn't checked. The postgresql.sslMode value sets that mode, and accepts the standard PostgreSQL values: disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca, and verify-full. For a PostgreSQL server without TLS, set it to disable. For the strongest guarantee, set it to verify-full. The chart provides no value for the server certificate authority (CA), so the certificate must be verifiable from the trust store of TheHive Flow image, which holds the public CAs only. The Temporal subchart carries its own TLS settings under temporal.server.config.persistence.datastores.<datastore>.sql.tls.

    postgresql:
  sslMode: disable

  3. Render the chart before installing. This catches the PostgreSQL mismatch above and any placeholder you missed, without touching the cluster. With the scenarios:

    helm template thehive-flow strangebee/thehive-flow \
  --namespace thehive-flow \
  -f scenarios/cnpg/values.yaml \
  -f scenarios/seaweedfs/values.yaml \
  -f scenarios/combined/values.yaml > /dev/null && echo OK

    With your own PostgreSQL and object storage, replace the three scenario files with --values <values_file>.

  4. Install the chart, with the same values files:

    helm install thehive-flow strangebee/thehive-flow \
  --namespace thehive-flow \
  -f scenarios/cnpg/values.yaml \
  -f scenarios/seaweedfs/values.yaml \
  -f scenarios/combined/values.yaml \
  --wait --timeout 10m

The installation runs a pre-install Job that applies the database migrations, then deploys the application and the Temporal Server subchart, so the first installation takes longer than later upgrades. The pre-install Job pulls TheHive Flow image, so the cluster must be able to pull the images before the installation starts. On a private mirror, the pull secret must already exist. TheHive Flow and the Temporal services may restart once while Temporal initializes its schema and namespace.

The code transformation Jobs pull the assistant image in their own namespace, thehive-flow-jobs by default. With a private mirror, image pull Secrets are namespace-scoped. Declare the Secret name through the codex.kubernetes.imagePullSecrets value at install time, then create the same Secret in the Job namespace once the chart has created that namespace.

To use an external Temporal cluster instead of the subchart, set temporal.enabled: false and fill the externalTemporal.* values. The external frontend must be reachable in-cluster or over a private network without TLS or API keys: Temporal Cloud isn't supported.

For the Temporal subchart, the temporal.server.config.persistence.numHistoryShards value is immutable once its databases exist: change it before the first installation or not at all.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify the deployment
docs.text:
Check that the pods are running and that the release passes its smoke test:

kubectl -n thehive-flow get pods
helm test thehive-flow -n thehive-flow --logs

The test runs a throwaway pod that calls the unauthenticated version endpoint of TheHive Flow, and passes on a 2xx response.

Expected output

The pod listing of a release installed with the scenarios, trimmed to the relevant columns. The hash suffixes vary:

NAME                                              READY   STATUS      RESTARTS
thehive-flow-7d9f6c5b8-x2k4q                      1/1     Running     0
thehive-flow-postgresql-1                         1/1     Running     0
thehive-flow-temporal-admintools-6b7c9d4f5-m8n2p  1/1     Running     0
thehive-flow-temporal-frontend-5f8d7b6c9-q4r7s    1/1     Running     0
thehive-flow-temporal-history-7c6b5d8f4-t9w3x     1/1     Running     0
thehive-flow-temporal-matching-8d7c6b5f9-v2y5z    1/1     Running     0
thehive-flow-temporal-namespace-1-7-0-1-k6j8h     0/1     Completed   0
thehive-flow-temporal-worker-9e8d7c6b5-b3c6d      1/1     Running     0
  • The thehive-flow pod and the five Temporal pods show Running with every container ready.
  • thehive-flow-postgresql-1 is the scenario PostgreSQL instance. It's absent with an external PostgreSQL, and the scenario object storage runs in the seaweedfs namespace.
  • The namespace creation Job of the Temporal subchart stays listed as Completed. Its name carries the subchart version and the release revision.
  • The database migrations Job and the Temporal schema Jobs don't appear: Helm deletes them once they succeed. A thehive-flow-migrations pod still listed means the migrations failed: read its logs with kubectl -n thehive-flow logs job/thehive-flow-migrations.
  • A RESTARTS count of 1 on the thehive-flow pod or a Temporal pod right after the installation is expected: they may restart once while Temporal initializes its schema and namespace.

The helm test command ends with the test suite result and the logs of the probe pod, which hold the response of the version endpoint:

TEST SUITE:     thehive-flow-test-api
Last Started:   ...
Last Completed: ...
Phase:          Succeeded
POD LOGS: thehive-flow-test-api
{"version":"6.0.0","dependencies":{"postgresql":"...","docker":"n/a (kubernetes backend)","temporal":"..."}}

The test pod stays listed as Completed after the run, and is replaced at the next helm test.

To check the health endpoints directly, forward the observability port and query it:

kubectl -n thehive-flow port-forward deploy/thehive-flow 9090:9090
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

A healthy /readyz returns {"status":"ok","checks":{"db":"ok","modules":"ok","temporal":"ok"}}.

docs.title: (Optional) Step 8: Expose TheHive Flow outside the cluster
docs.text:
TheHive Flow needs an entry point outside the cluster when TheHive runs outside it, or when external systems call Webhook triggers, even with TheHive inside the cluster. The chart ships no Ingress and no TLS termination: expose the thehive-flow-api Service through an Ingress or a load balancer of your own.

Whatever the entry point, follow the exposure rule of TheHive Flow. TheHive is the only client of the /api/ paths, and it enforces the security of these routes. A call that reaches them without going through TheHive bypasses it, so only TheHive may reach them. The /webhook/ paths may be exposed to any caller.

TheHive Flow serves plain HTTP on port 8081. It authenticates the /api/ requests at the application level with the JWT, and the /webhook/ requests with the method of each webhook, so terminate TLS at the Ingress.

The following manifests use the ingress-nginx controller. Replace <tls_secret> with the name of a TLS Secret in the thehive-flow namespace that holds the certificate and private key for <flow_host>. Create it with kubectl -n thehive-flow create secret tls <tls_secret> --cert=<certificate_file> --key=<key_file>, or have a certificate controller of your own issue it.

The first Ingress exposes the /webhook/ paths to any caller:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: thehive-flow-webhook
  namespace: thehive-flow
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 2g
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "600"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "600"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - <flow_host>
      secretName: <tls_secret>
  rules:
    - host: <flow_host>
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /webhook/
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: thehive-flow-api
                port:
                  number: 8081

When TheHive runs outside the cluster, the second Ingress exposes the /api/ paths on the same host to TheHive only. Replace <thehive_address_ranges> with the addresses TheHive calls from, as comma-separated ranges in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation, such as 192.168.1.10/32,192.168.1.11/32. A CIDR range is an IP address followed by a prefix length. With a TheHive cluster, list every node:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: thehive-flow-api
  namespace: thehive-flow
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range: "<thehive_address_ranges>"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 2g
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "600"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "600"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - <flow_host>
      secretName: <tls_secret>
  rules:
    - host: <flow_host>
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api/
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: thehive-flow-api
                port:
                  number: 8081

The restriction relies on the ingress controller seeing the real address of TheHive. A load balancer in front of the controller that replaces source addresses defeats it. So does an outbound proxy or a Network Address Translation (NAT) device on TheHive side, which opens the /api/ paths to every other client of that device.

The annotations mirror the limits the nginx reverse proxy applies on the Docker Compose deployment: a 2 GB request body cap, needed for file ingestion through Webhook triggers, and 600-second proxy timeouts. On another ingress controller, set the equivalent options, and restrict the /api/ paths to TheHive addresses with its own access control.

With these manifests, the public URL of TheHive Flow is https://<flow_host>: it's the value of config.api.public.url set at Step 6.

Inside the cluster, the chart provisions no NetworkPolicy, so any pod can reach the thehive-flow-api Service on every path. To apply the exposure rule there too, add a NetworkPolicy to the thehive-flow namespace that admits traffic to TheHive Flow on port 8081 only from TheHive pods and the ingress controller.

docs.title: Apply the webhook rate limit to each caller
docs.text:
Each webhook accepts 120 requests per minute from a given client address. Behind the Ingress, every webhook call reaches TheHive Flow from the address of the ingress controller, so all callers of a webhook share the same limit. To apply the limit to each caller instead, list the ranges the ingress controller connects from in the values file:

config:
  api:
    public:
      trusted_proxies:
        - <ingress_controller_cidr>

For a request coming from one of these ranges, TheHive Flow reads the caller address from the X-Forwarded-For header, which the ingress controller must fill with the address of its own client. IPv6 callers outside fc00::/7 are counted per /64 network. Each entry is a CIDR range, such as 10.244.0.0/16. A bare IP address, a /0 range, or an IPv4-mapped range prevents TheHive Flow from starting. The list is empty by default.

Trusted ranges and rate limit bypass

A caller inside a trusted range can set its own address in the X-Forwarded-For header and bypass the rate limit. Behind an in-cluster ingress controller, whose pods have no fixed address, the list usually holds the pod CIDR of the cluster: every pod in that range is then trusted.

docs.title: Step 9: Configure TheHive to reach TheHive Flow
docs.text:
TheHive must know the URL of TheHive Flow and the JWT signing key.

  1. Read the key from the thehive-flow-jwt Secret:

    kubectl -n thehive-flow get secret thehive-flow-jwt \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.jwt-symmetric-key}' | base64 -d

  2. Declare the connection and activate the feature in TheHive. The <flow_url> value depends on where TheHive runs:

    • TheHive in the same cluster: use the thehive-flow-api Service directly, http://thehive-flow-api.thehive-flow.svc.cluster.local:8081.
    • TheHive outside the cluster: use the address of the Ingress or load balancer set up at (Optional) Step 8, such as https://<flow_host>/. TheHive validates the certificate of the URL it calls: a certificate signed by a public certificate authority works as is. For a certificate signed by an internal certificate authority, or self-signed, configure TheHive to trust it, with the same options as on a Docker Compose deployment. See TLS with a self-signed certificate.

    The settings play two roles. The URL and the signing key declare the connection. The scalligraph.modules line loads the connector that talks to TheHive Flow, and the features.Orchestrator.enabled flag displays the Flow view and opens its routes.

    TheHive deployed with the StrangeBee Helm chartTheHive installed with packages

    Set the thehive.flow.* values of TheHive release, and add the feature flag and the connector module to the application.conf content the chart renders through thehive.configFile. The values declare the connection but don't load the module.

    thehive:
  flow:
    enabled: true
    url: "<flow_url>"
    signingKey: "<jwt_signing_key>"
  configFile: |
    features.Orchestrator.enabled = true
    scalligraph.modules += "org.thp.thehive.connector.flow.FlowModule"

    To read the key from an existing Secret instead of writing it in the values, set thehive.flow.k8sSecretName and thehive.flow.k8sSecretKey in place of thehive.flow.signingKey. Then apply the change with helm upgrade on TheHive release.

    Add the following to the /etc/thehive/application.conf file, next to the connector lines it already holds, then restart TheHive:

    flow.url             = "<flow_url>"
flow.jwt_signing_key = "<jwt_signing_key>"
features.Orchestrator.enabled = true
scalligraph.modules += "org.thp.thehive.connector.flow.FlowModule"

    sudo systemctl restart thehive

docs.title: Step 10: Check the connection in TheHive
docs.text:
Sign in to TheHive with an account that has the predefined Org-Admin profile, which includes TheHive Flow permissions automatically.

The health indicator at the bottom of the sidebar menu reports the connection from any view. It covers every configured connector: TheHive Flow, Cortex, Malware Information Sharing Platform & Threat Sharing (MISP), and Email Intake. Its color reflects all of them at once:

  • Green: every configured connector is healthy.
  • Red: at least one configured connector is in error.
  • Faded: no connector is configured.

Select the indicator to see the details. Its Flow section shows TheHive Flow URL and its own status, OK or ERROR. TheHive probes TheHive Flow every minute by default, so allow that long for the status to reflect a fix. Changing flow.url or flow.jwt_signing_key triggers an immediate check.

Then go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  • If the view displays the workflow list, empty on a fresh deployment but with the Import workflow button visible, TheHive and TheHive Flow are connected.
  • If the view is missing from the sidebar, review the configuration from Step 9 and restart TheHive.
  • If the view displays an error notification over an empty workflow list, TheHive can't reach TheHive Flow: check that the flow.url address is reachable from TheHive host, then read the application logs with kubectl -n thehive-flow logs deploy/thehive-flow.

docs.title: Step 11: Grant users access to TheHive Flow
docs.text: Users who don't have one of the predefined Org-Admin and Analyst profiles need TheHive Flow permissions through a custom profile: see Perform TheHive Flow Initial Setup as an Admin.

docs.title: Application configuration
docs.text:
The config.* Helm values set the application configuration, rendered into a ConfigMap mounted at /thehive-flow.yml. The chart exposes only a subset of the keys described in TheHive Flow Application Configuration, with the same meanings. It also exposes the SMTP settings of the email server override through config.modules.workers.activities.mailer.*, with the password in the Secret named by secrets.mailerPassword.existingSecret.

The chart sets the run retention to 168h instead of the application default of 30 days. With an external Temporal, the chart doesn't align the Temporal namespace retention, to avoid deleting histories another team owns. Set it yourself, or set config.modules.runs.syncTemporalRetention to true when the namespace belongs to TheHive Flow only.

The chart leaves the Temporal task poller counts unset, so the Temporal SDK decides them. To set them, use the config.modules.workers.workflows.max_concurrent_workflow_task_pollers and config.modules.workers.activities.max_concurrent_activity_task_pollers values, and raise them only after measuring under load. The chart refuses to render a value that isn't a whole number or is negative, and refuses 1 for the workflow task pollers.

docs.title: Code transformations
docs.text: Python and JavaScript code transformations run as short-lived Kubernetes Jobs in a dedicated namespace, thehive-flow-jobs by default, so no Docker socket is needed. The chart provisions the namespace and its role-based access control. The cluster must be able to pull the transformation images: on an air-gapped cluster, mirror them to an internal registry and set codex.languageImages.

docs.title: Code transformation isolation
docs.text: The script a code transformation runs is arbitrary code written by a workflow author, so every user holding the manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows permission can run code on the cluster. The Job pod runs it with all Linux capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile, and no service account token. Root isn't forbidden, because the default images run as root. The chart provisions no NetworkPolicy and no resource limits: the script has unrestricted egress, including to the cluster's internal services, and isn't covered by the egress allowlist. The only bounds are a 2 GiB cap on the working directory and a 24-hour cap on a job's run time. Add a NetworkPolicy on the jobs namespace to restrict egress, and set codex.kubernetes.resources, codex.kubernetes.ephemeralStorage, and codex.kubernetes.activeDeadlineSeconds as listed in System Requirements. To limit how many jobs run at once, set codex.maxConcurrentActivityExecutionSize, which applies per language. A secret variable the script references is handed to it in clear, and anything the script prints lands in the execution logs without redaction.

docs.title: Routine operations
docs.text:
The following table lists how to run each routine operation on Kubernetes.

Operation On Kubernetes Configuration change Edit the config.* keys, described in TheHive Flow Application Configuration, in the values file written at installation time, then run helm upgrade with the same command and chart version as for an upgrade. No manual restart is needed: the Deployment carries a checksum of the ConfigMap, so a changed value rolls out new pods Upgrade See Upgrade TheHive Flow on Kubernetes Backup and restore The state lives in PostgreSQL and the object storage. Back up the scenario PostgreSQL with the CloudNativePG backup tooling, or your own database tooling for an external instance. Back up the object storage with the tooling of your storage service, or snapshot its volume: the scenario SeaweedFS keeps its files in a persistent volume claim in the seaweedfs namespace. Capture both together: the database references blobs by content hash, and restoring one without the other leaves dangling references Logs Every container logs to its standard output: read them with kubectl logs and ship them with the cluster log stack Monitoring Scrape the /metrics endpoint on port 9090 with your own Prometheus, and alert on /readyz returning non-200 Troubleshooting Check the pod state with kubectl get pods, the application logs with kubectl logs, and the health endpoints through a port forward as in Step 7 Uninstall Run helm uninstall thehive-flow -n thehive-flow. The command removes TheHive Flow, the Temporal subchart, and the thehive-flow-jobs namespace, and leaves PostgreSQL, the object storage, and the Secrets in place. To remove the scenario services too, run helm uninstall seaweedfs -n seaweedfs, delete the cluster and databases with kubectl delete -n thehive-flow -f scenarios/cnpg/databases.yaml -f scenarios/cnpg/postgres-cluster.yaml, then helm uninstall cnpg -n cnpg-system. The persistent volume claims of PostgreSQL and SeaweedFS are kept: delete them to remove the data Next steps
  • Build Your First Workflow
  • Upgrade TheHive Flow on Kubernetes
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Authentication Between TheHive Flow Components

docs.title: Perform TheHive Flow Initial Setup as an Admin
docs.text:
6.0 [admin] manageProfile One

After deploying TheHive Flow, complete the setup in TheHive as an administrator by granting users access to the Flow view. Users with the predefined Org-Admin or Analyst profile have access automatically. For all other users, grant the permissions through a custom profile.

Requirement

This procedure assumes that TheHive Flow is deployed and running.

Six permissions, grouped under Manage Flow in the profile editor, control access to TheHive Flow.

Permission Grants Read Flow workflows Displaying the Flow view and the workflow pages Write Flow workflows Creating, editing, and running workflows Delete Flow workflows Deleting workflows Read Flow variables Displaying the global variables page Write Flow variables Creating and editing global variables Delete Flow variables Deleting global variables

The permissions are independent: a write or delete permission doesn't include the matching read permission. Grant the matching read permission alongside write or delete, because a user with Write Flow workflows alone can't display the workflow pages or run a workflow.

Predefined profiles

The predefined Org-Admin and Analyst profiles include all six permissions. The other predefined profiles include none of them. To grant access to users with another profile, create or edit a custom profile.

Procedure

  1. Go to the Entities management view from the sidebar menu.

  2. In the Profiles tab, select next to the profile you want to update.

  3. Select Edit.

  4. In the Editing a profile drawer, select the relevant permissions in the Manage Flow group.

  5. Select Confirm profile edition.

Next steps

  • Manage Workflows
  • Manage LLM Providers
