docs.title: TheHive Flow Software Requirements
docs.text:
6.0 One

Deploying TheHive Flow requires specific software components at specific versions, depending on the deployment method: Docker Compose or Kubernetes.

No package installation for TheHive Flow

Unlike TheHive, TheHive Flow isn't distributed as Linux packages and can't be installed with a package manager. The only supported deployment methods are Docker Compose and Kubernetes, whatever the method used to install TheHive itself.

docs.title: Software prerequisites
docs.text: Docker Compose deploymentKubernetes deployment with Helm Component Minimum version Notes Docker Engine v23.0.15 The docker daemon must be running, and the user deploying the stack must be able to run Docker commands Docker Compose v2.20.2 plugin The legacy Python docker-compose, end of life since 2023, isn't supported openssl 1.1.1 Used by init.sh to generate random secrets and the self-signed certificate rsync Any Used by backup.sh and restore.sh jq Any Used by several log and maintenance commands Component Minimum version Notes Kubernetes 1.29 Any conformant distribution, with a default storage class for the deployment scenarios Helm 3.8.0 Installs the chart from the StrangeBee Helm repository kubectl Any Matching the cluster version openssl Any Used to generate the JWT signing key CloudNativePG 0.29.1 chart, installed by the cnpg deployment scenario Runs the PostgreSQL cluster of the scenario, from its own cnpg-system namespace. Not needed when the chart points at an external PostgreSQL

docs.title: Images pulled at first startNext steps
docs.text:
Docker Compose deploymentKubernetes deployment with Helm

All images are pinned by tag in versions.env, at the root of the repository, and init.sh copies the pins into .env. The host must be able to reach Docker Hub at first start, directly or through a private registry mirror. Subsequent starts use the local cache.

Image Variable in versions.env Approximate size docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow thehive_flow_image_version ~100 MB docker.io/library/postgres postgresql_image_version ~400 MB docker.io/temporalio/server temporal_image_version ~200 MB docker.io/temporalio/admin-tools temporal_image_version ~300 MB docker.io/library/nginx nginx_image_version ~60 MB docker.io/chrislusf/seaweedfs seaweedfs_image_version ~90 MB

The total pull is approximately 1 GB. The init.sh script pulls the nginx image before anything else, to read the group of the Docker socket from a throwaway container.

The two code transformation language images are also pulled at the first start of the thehive-flow service, which refuses to start if a pull fails:

Image Approximate size gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 ~20 MB gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian12 ~60 MB

Both are pinned by immutable digest in the application itself rather than in versions.env. On a host that can't reach gcr.io, they must be mirrored to an internal registry and their references overridden through modules.codex.languages in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml.

The thehive-flow service also pulls docker.io/testcontainers/ryuk, approximately 10 MB, pinned by immutable digest in the application too. It runs the reaper container that removes orphaned code transformation containers after a crash. A failed pull doesn't stop the service: the reaper is then unavailable, and orphaned containers are removed at the next start only.

The cluster must be able to reach the following registries at install time and first start, directly or through a private registry mirror.

Image Version Purpose docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow The chart appVersion, which is the released version TheHive Flow application image docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow-assistant The chart appVersion, which is the released version Helper containers of the code transformation jobs docker.io/temporalio/server 1.32.0, set by the Temporal subchart Temporal Server subchart docker.io/temporalio/admin-tools 1.32.0 by the Temporal subchart, 1.32.1 for the readiness wait Temporal schema migrations and namespace creation, and the wait-temporal init container of the application pod docker.io/library/busybox 1.38.0 The wait-postgres init container of the application pod and of the database migrations Job docker.io/curlimages/curl 8.22.0 The helm test probe pod only ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgresql The default of the CloudNativePG operator 0.29.1 PostgreSQL deployed by the cnpg deployment scenario docker.io/chrislusf/seaweedfs Set by the SeaweedFS chart 4.48.0 Object storage deployed by the seaweedfs deployment scenario

The versions come from the chart and the deployment scenarios, which pin the following releases:

Component Pinned version Set by Temporal subchart 1.7.0, shipping Temporal Server 1.32.0 The chart dependencies CloudNativePG operator chart 0.29.1 The helm upgrade --install cnpg command of the cnpg scenario SeaweedFS chart 4.48.0 The helm upgrade --install seaweedfs command of the seaweedfs scenario

The code transformation language images are pulled from gcr.io on demand. On an air-gapped cluster, they must be mirrored to an internal registry and referenced through codex.languageImages.

docs.title: TheHive Flow System Requirements
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow hardware and storage requirements depend on the deployment method: a Docker Compose stack on a single Linux host, separate from the host running TheHive, or a Helm chart on a Kubernetes cluster.

No package installation for TheHive Flow

Unlike TheHive, TheHive Flow isn't distributed as Linux packages and can't be installed with a package manager. The only supported deployment methods are Docker Compose and Kubernetes, whatever the method used to install TheHive itself.

A single TheHive Flow instance

TheHive Flow can't run as a cluster: deploy one instance only. A TheHive cluster is supported in front of this single instance.

docs.title: Hardware requirements
docs.text:
Docker Compose deploymentKubernetes deployment with Helm

The stack deploys the following services on the host:

The chart and its deployment scenarios deploy the following on the cluster:

docs.title: Deployment profiles
docs.text:
Two deployment profiles are available in the StrangeBee Docker Compose repository. Both deploy the same services and differ in the resources allocated to each one.

Profile Usage Recommended memory Recommended CPU Disk Production environment #1, prod1-thehive-flow Standard production workload 8 GB RAM 4 vCPUs 50 GB Production environment #2, prod2-thehive-flow High-performance or resource-intensive workload 16 GB RAM 8 vCPUs 100 GB

These figures are what the stack itself needs. They come on top of the operating system and any other services running on the same host. The disk figures are a starting point: see Data storage for what drives the growth.

docs.title: Memory limits per service
docs.text:
The docker-compose.yml file of each profile defines a memory limit and a CPU limit for each service, under deploy.resources.limits. The file also sets memswap_limit to the same value as the memory limit, so that a container can't swap instead of being stopped. These are hard limits enforced by the Docker runtime. The out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminates a container that exceeds its memory limit.

Service Profile #1 Profile #2 Notes postgresql 1 GB, 2 CPUs 4 GB, 4 CPUs Hosts three databases: thehive_flow, temporal, and temporal_visibility. Profile #2 also sets shared_buffers to 1 GB and effective_cache_size to 3 GB temporal 1 GB, 2 CPUs 2 GB, 4 CPUs Workflow engine thehive-flow 1 GB, 2 CPUs 2 GB, 4 CPUs Stateless server with low RAM usage. The limit is a safety cap. Also carries GOMEMLIMIT, described in the next section s3-store 512 MB, 1 CPU 1 GB, 2 CPUs SeaweedFS S3-compatible object storage holding the blobs nginx 512 MB, 1 CPU 1 GB, 1 CPU Reverse proxy that typically uses under 50 MB temporal-admin 256 MB 256 MB Only active during admin operations such as schema migrations and namespace creation init-s3-store 256 MB 256 MB One-shot container that provisions the S3 bucket at startup, then exits Stack total ~4 GB ~10 GB On top of the operating system and any other services on the host

Adjust limits in docker-compose.yml based on observed usage with docker stats, then apply them with docker compose up -d. Keep memswap_limit equal to the memory limit.

docs.title: Go memory limit of the thehive-flow service
docs.text:
The thehive-flow container carries a second ceiling: the GOMEMLIMIT environment variable, set in docker-compose.yml to 85% of the memory limit of the service. That's 870MiB for the 1 GB limit of profile #1 and 1740MiB for the 2 GB limit of profile #2. The Go garbage collector doesn't read the container limit on its own. Without GOMEMLIMIT, it would let the heap grow until the OOM killer terminates the container. Because a single process both handles incoming requests and runs the workflows, that kill restarts the whole application rather than a single step.

When raising the thehive-flow memory limit, raise the memory limit, memswap_limit, and GOMEMLIMIT together, keeping at least 128 MiB between GOMEMLIMIT and the memory limit. Only Go binary suffixes are valid, such as 870MiB. With a malformed value such as 870MB, the container exits immediately.

docs.title: Code transformation containers
docs.text:
TheHive Flow runs Python and JavaScript code transformations in disposable containers launched on the host Docker daemon, outside the stack and its memory limits. Three properties matter for host sizing:

  • No resource limits: The containers run without a memory or CPU cap, so a memory-hungry script competes with the stack and the operating system for host RAM.
  • No fixed concurrency ceiling: One container runs per executing transformation step, so the count follows how many runs execute transformations at the same time.
  • Short-lived: Each container is removed as soon as its script exits.

A small ryuk reaper container also runs on the host daemon for the life of the thehive-flow service, and removes orphaned script containers after a crash.

The recommended profile sizing above covers typical transformation workloads. For workflows running many concurrent transformations, or scripts processing large inputs in memory, budget extra RAM on top of the stack total. The transformation language images add approximately 80 MB to the Docker image cache.

docs.title: Chart sizing defaults
docs.text:
The chart and the deployment scenarios ship the following defaults. Every pod of the chart gets a CPU request but no CPU limit, so pods can burst into spare CPU. The data storage growth drivers apply unchanged. Plan for approximately 1 MB per workflow run in the thehive_flow database, and two to five times that for the Temporal history, depending on retention. The blob store size follows the run retention, as described in Blob store volume sizing.

Component Default Tuning TheHive Flow pod Requests 250m CPU and 512 MiB of memory, limited to 1 GiB of memory The resources.* values. The Go memory limit is derived as 85% of the memory limit through goMemLimitPercent, so raising resources.limits.memory raises it too. The chart refuses to render when the derived margin falls under 128 MiB Database migrations job Requests 100m CPU and 128 MiB of memory, limited to 256 MiB of memory The migrations.resources.* values PostgreSQL cluster One instance and 10 GiB of storage on the default storage class, with no resource requests or limits The scenarios/cnpg/postgres-cluster.yaml manifest: set instances: 3 for high availability, set storageClass, add resources, and grow the storage for production, following the PostgreSQL volume sizing baseline Temporal Five pods, one per service, requesting 550m CPU and 1.3 GiB of memory in total, limited to 2.75 GiB of memory in total. See Temporal services for the per-service values. History shards: 512, immutable for the cluster's life The temporal.server.<service>.resources and temporal.admintools.resources values. temporal.server.config.persistence.numHistoryShards sets the shard count: change it before the first installation or not at all Object storage One SeaweedFS pod with a 10 GiB persistent volume claim on the default storage class, with the resource defaults of the SeaweedFS chart The scenarios/seaweedfs/seaweedfs-values.yaml file: allInOne.data.size for the volume, allInOne.resources for the pod. For more than one replica, use the distributed mode of the SeaweedFS chart instead of allInOne Code transformation jobs No CPU or memory constraints, a 2 GiB cap on the working directory, and a 24-hour cap on a job's run time codex.kubernetes.resources for requests and limits, codex.kubernetes.ephemeralStorage to change the cap on the working directory, codex.kubernetes.activeDeadlineSeconds to shorten the cap on a job's run time, and codex.maxConcurrentActivityExecutionSize to cap how many jobs one language runs at once

docs.title: Temporal services
docs.text:
The bundled Temporal runs as five pods. History gets the largest share because it caches workflow histories across the 512 history shards, so under load it's the first service to need more memory. The admin-tools pod only runs operational commands and is mostly idle. Keep these defaults unless the OOM killer terminates a Temporal pod.

Service Role CPU request Memory request Memory limit Values key Frontend gRPC entry point for TheHive Flow 100m 256 MiB 512 MiB temporal.server.frontend.resources History Workflow state and event histories 200m 512 MiB 1 GiB temporal.server.history.resources Matching Task queues dispatching work to the worker of TheHive Flow 100m 256 MiB 512 MiB temporal.server.matching.resources Worker Internal Temporal system workflows 100m 256 MiB 512 MiB temporal.server.worker.resources Admin tools Operations CLI 50m 64 MiB 256 MiB temporal.admintools.resources

docs.title: Data storage
docs.text:
The following table lists the locations where the Docker Compose stack stores data and what drives their growth. The two data directories live in the profile directory, so the filesystem holding the repository clone is the one to size and watch. The Docker image cache and the daemon log files live under /var/lib/docker, and the backup root wherever backup.sh is pointed at.

Location Content Growth driver ./postgresql/data All PostgreSQL data: the thehive_flow database, Temporal history, and Temporal visibility index Number of workflow runs and history retention period ./s3-store/data Blob store contents: files ingested through webhooks or runs, and activity outputs promoted out of the database Volume and size of the files the workflows handle, and the run retention period. See Blob store volume sizing Docker image cache Pinned images for all services Static after the initial pull, approximately 1 GB total. Grows with each upgrade until docker image prune runs Backup root, /opt/backups/thehive-flow in the examples Backup folders produced by backup.sh: a full copy of the two data directories above, the configuration, and .env Operator retention policy multiplied by the size of the data directories Docker daemon log files Container stdout and stderr in JSON format Log rotation configuration

docs.title: PostgreSQL volume sizing
docs.text:
Use the following planning baseline:

  • Plan for approximately 1 MB per workflow run in the thehive_flow database. This covers definitions, run state, variables, and the run and step execution history.
  • Temporal history is typically two to five times the size of the thehive_flow database, depending on workflow complexity and the configured retention period.

For example, 10,000 workflow runs per month over 12 months, at a 3 MB average, results in approximately 360 MB for the thehive_flow database and approximately 1 GB for Temporal. Adjust for the actual workload.

To check the actual directory and database sizes, see Monitor TheHive Flow.

docs.title: Blob store volume sizing
docs.text:
Both blob store back ends follow the same sizing rules. The blobs live in the ./s3-store/data directory with the default s3 back end, and in the configured blob directory with the local back end.

The blob store holds whole files, so its growth follows what the workflows carry rather than how many times they run. Content is deduplicated within an organization: two runs in the same organization handling the same file store it once, because blobs are addressed by organization and SHA-256 hash. The same file handled by two different organizations is stored twice, by design. The organization boundary is a tenancy boundary, not a caching one.

Files follow the run retention, 30 days by default. The purge runs at every startup of TheHive Flow, then periodically. When it deletes a run, the files the run references are queued, and a deletion job removes them shortly after the startup purge and at regular intervals afterward. A file is deleted only when no run of the same organization still references it and nobody has stored the same content in the last 24 hours. Files that no run references are never deleted, such as an upload whose request failed after the file was stored. With modules.runs.retention: 0, nothing is purged, so no file is deleted.

Watch the size of the directory and add a host-level disk alert, as described in Monitor TheHive Flow. If it approaches the disk budget, provision more disk or shorten modules.runs.retention. Read Temporal workflow history retention first: shortening the retention deletes history.

The s3-store container is capped at 512 MB of RAM in profile #1 and 1 GB in profile #2, regardless of how much data it stores. The store keeps an on-disk index rather than an in-memory catalog, so memory tracks concurrent request volume, not object count. The single-node profile of the stack has one client, TheHive Flow, so the cap is sized for that. If the OOM killer terminates the container, see Troubleshoot TheHive Flow.

docs.title: Recommended operating systemsNext steps
docs.text:
The Docker Compose host is officially supported on the following distributions:

  • Debian 12
  • Ubuntu 22.04
  • RHEL 9
  • TheHive Flow Software Requirements
  • Deploy TheHive Flow with Docker Compose
  • Deploy TheHive Flow on Kubernetes

docs.title: Upgrade TheHive Flow with Docker Compose
docs.text:
6.0 One

Upgrade an existing TheHive Flow Docker Compose deployment to a new version. TheHive Flow is released with TheHive and carries the same version number: upgrade both to that version in the same maintenance window. Upgrade TheHive Flow first, while TheHive is stopped. The upgrade preserves all your data.

Before you begin

To ensure a smooth upgrade, make sure you have:

  • A cold backup of the stack, taken with backup.sh. It captures the databases, the blobs of the shipped object storage, the configuration, and .env together, which is what a rollback needs. With an external object storage or the local filesystem back end, capture the blobs at the same time with your own tooling.
  • A scheduled maintenance window. The upgrade stops TheHive and TheHive Flow.
  • A time when as few workflows as possible are running. The upgrade doesn't wait for running workflows to finish: the new version resumes them from their recorded execution history.
  • TheHive release notes of the target version, to identify changes that may affect your deployment.

The commands below run from the profile directory, prod1-thehive-flow or prod2-thehive-flow, inside the clone of the StrangeBee Docker Compose repository.

docs.title: Step 1: Stop TheHive
docs.text:
Stop TheHive before touching TheHive Flow, with the command matching how TheHive is deployed. TheHive stays stopped until TheHive Flow runs the new version.

Cluster deployments

For cluster deployments, stop all TheHive nodes.

Package installationDocker Compose deploymentKubernetes deployment with Helm 
sudo systemctl stop thehive

docker compose down

Scale TheHive Deployment down to zero replicas:

kubectl -n <thehive_namespace> scale deployment <thehive_deployment> --replicas=0

docs.title: Step 2: Get the new deployment files
docs.text:
StrangeBee releases a new version by moving the image versions pinned in versions.env, at the root of the repository. The same change can also touch docker-compose.yml, the scripts, the nginx template, the Temporal configuration, and the shipped thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml.

  1. Pull the new files into the clone:

    git pull

    The files you own aren't tracked by git and stay in place: .env, the data directories, thehive-flow/secret/, certificates/, nginx/certs/, and the rendered temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml. If you edited a tracked file, such as thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml or nginx/templates/default.conf.template, git pull refuses to overwrite it: run git stash, pull again, then git stash pop and resolve any conflict.

  2. Compare the new pins with the versions the stack runs, which init.sh copied into .env at the last initialization:

    grep _image_version ../versions.env
grep _image_version .env

    Note which of temporal_image_version and postgresql_image_version change: they decide whether Step 4 applies.

docs.title: Step 3: Stop TheHive Flow
docs.text:
Stop the application and nginx. PostgreSQL, Temporal, and the object storage keep running for the next steps:

docker compose stop thehive-flow nginx

docs.title: (Optional) Step 4: Upgrade the Temporal schema
docs.text:
Skip this step when temporal_image_version keeps the same minor version, such as 1.32.1 to 1.32.2. A new Temporal minor version requires a database schema upgrade before the new server starts, and Temporal supports moving one minor version at a time only. StrangeBee moves the pin one minor version per release. If you skipped releases and the new pin is more than one minor version ahead of the running server, upgrade through each intermediate minor version, repeating this step and the next with each one.

Run the schema upgrade tool from the admin-tools image of the new version, against both Temporal databases. The version is passed on the command line, because .env still carries the old one until Step 5:

TEMPORAL_DB_PASSWORD=$(grep '^temporal_db_password=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

temporal_image_version=<new_temporal_version> docker compose --profile admin run --rm --no-deps \
  -e SQL_PASSWORD="${TEMPORAL_DB_PASSWORD}" temporal-admin \
  temporal-sql-tool --plugin postgres12 --ep postgresql -p 5432 -u temporal --db temporal \
  update-schema -d /etc/temporal/schema/postgresql/v12/temporal/versioned

temporal_image_version=<new_temporal_version> docker compose --profile admin run --rm --no-deps \
  -e SQL_PASSWORD="${TEMPORAL_DB_PASSWORD}" temporal-admin \
  temporal-sql-tool --plugin postgres12 --ep postgresql -p 5432 -u temporal --db temporal_visibility \
  update-schema -d /etc/temporal/schema/postgresql/v12/visibility/versioned

Replace <new_temporal_version> with the temporal_image_version value of versions.env. The schema upgrade is backward compatible, so the running Temporal server keeps working until it's recreated at the next step. For the details of the Temporal procedure, see Upgrade Temporal Server in the Temporal documentation.

PostgreSQL major versions

This procedure covers PostgreSQL minor and patch upgrades, which keep the data directory as is. A PostgreSQL major version change isn't covered: it changes the data directory format and requires a pg_upgrade or a dump and restore procedure, described in Upgrading a PostgreSQL Cluster. Run it before applying a pin that moves the major version.

docs.title: Step 5: Apply the new versions
docs.text:
Run the initialization script again:

bash ./scripts/init.sh

On an initialized stack, the script keeps every secret in .env, offers the current server name, TheHive URL, and TheHive addresses as defaults for its three questions, and performs the following tasks:

1/ Rewrites .env from dot.env.template with the image versions now pinned in versions.env.

2/ Renders temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml again, in case its template changed.

3/ Installs the custom TLS certificate from ./certificates/, or generates a new self-signed one.

4/ Recreates the postgresql and temporal containers when their image version changed, and waits for both to be healthy. The Temporal schema and namespace already exist, so the script leaves them alone.

The script rewrites .env from the template: a line you added to .env by hand, outside the keys the template declares, doesn't survive. Set extra container variables in the environment: block of the service instead, as described in Environment variable overrides.

With a self-signed certificate, the new one replaces the previous, and nginx serves it from Step 6. If TheHive trusts the specific certificate, as described in Option B, copy the new nginx/certs/server.crt to TheHive host before upgrading TheHive at Step 8. See TLS certificate renewal.

docs.title: Step 6: Start the stack
docs.text:
Start all services. Docker Compose pulls the images whose version changed and recreates their containers:

docker compose up -d

TheHive Flow applies its database migrations at startup, then becomes ready. The init-s3-store container runs again and exits once it has verified the object storage identity and bucket.

docs.title: Step 7: Reconcile the configuration
docs.text:
A new version can introduce configuration blocks in the shipped thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml. They arrive with git pull, unless you stashed your own changes to the file at Step 2: in that case, compare your version with the shipped one and add what's missing. See TheHive Flow Application Configuration.

To apply a change to the file, recreate the thehive-flow service:

docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow

The --force-recreate flag is required. The file is mounted into the container, and Docker Compose doesn't detect changes to mounted files, so a plain docker compose up -d leaves the container running with the previous configuration.

docs.title: Step 8: Upgrade TheHive
docs.text:
Once TheHive Flow runs the new version, upgrade TheHive to the same version.

  • For a package or Docker Compose installation: follow Upgrade from TheHive 6.x.
  • For a Kubernetes release, upgrade the release as described in Deploy TheHive on Kubernetes. The helm upgrade command restores the replica count set in your values. When thehive.autoscaling.enabled is true, the chart doesn't set the replica count, so scale the Deployment back up with kubectl scale.

docs.title: Step 9: Verify the upgrade
docs.text:
On TheHive Flow host, check that all containers are running and that the health endpoints respond:

docker compose ps -a
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/livez
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz
docker compose logs --tail=50 thehive-flow

Then, in TheHive, sign in with an account that has the predefined Org-Admin profile and select the health indicator at the bottom of the sidebar menu. It covers every configured connector: TheHive Flow, Cortex, Malware Information Sharing Platform & Threat Sharing (MISP), and Email Intake. Its color reflects all of them at once. It turns green when every configured connector is healthy, and red when at least one is in error. Its Flow section shows TheHive Flow URL and its own status, OK or ERROR. TheHive probes TheHive Flow every minute by default, so allow that long for the status to reflect the restart.

Finally, go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu and check that it displays the workflow list. An error notification over an empty workflow list means TheHive can't reach TheHive Flow: see Troubleshoot TheHive Flow.

Once everything checks out, remove the images the previous version used:

docker image prune -f

docs.title: Roll backNext steps
docs.text:
To roll back, return the repository to the previous revision, then restore the cold backup taken before the upgrade. The backup holds the .env file of the previous version, so the stack restarts on the previous images:

git log --oneline -- ../versions.env
git checkout <previous_commit>
docker compose down
bash ./scripts/restore.sh . ./backup/<backup_folder>

The data directories must be empty before the restore, as described in Restore. Restoring is required, not optional. TheHive Flow database migrations are forward-only, and Temporal schema migrations are never reverted: the previous version can't run on a database migrated by the new one. Workflow runs started under the new version are lost with the restore, and runs started under the previous version resume from the backup state.

To retry the upgrade later, return to the main branch with git checkout main and start again from Step 2.

  • Maintain TheHive Flow
  • TheHive Flow Security Maintenance
  • Back Up and Restore TheHive Flow
  • Troubleshoot TheHive Flow

docs.title: Upgrade TheHive Flow on Kubernetes
docs.text:
6.0 One

Upgrade an existing TheHive Flow Helm release to a new version. TheHive Flow is released with TheHive and carries the same version number: upgrade both to that version in the same maintenance window. Upgrade TheHive Flow first, while TheHive is stopped. The upgrade preserves all your data.

Before you begin

To ensure a smooth upgrade, make sure you have:

  • A backup of PostgreSQL and of the object storage, captured together, because the database references files by content hash. See Configuration and operations on Kubernetes.
  • A scheduled maintenance window. The upgrade stops TheHive and TheHive Flow.
  • A time when as few workflows as possible are running. The upgrade doesn't wait for running workflows to finish: the new version resumes them from their recorded execution history.
  • TheHive release notes of the target version, to identify changes that may affect your deployment.

The examples below use the thehive-flow namespace and the thehive-flow release name, which are the names the deployment scenarios use. Adapt them to your cluster conventions.

docs.title: Step 1: Stop TheHive
docs.text:
Stop TheHive before touching TheHive Flow, with the command matching how TheHive is deployed. TheHive stays stopped until TheHive Flow runs the new version.

Cluster deployments

For cluster deployments, stop all TheHive nodes.

Package installationDocker Compose deploymentKubernetes deployment with Helm 
sudo systemctl stop thehive

docker compose down

Scale TheHive Deployment down to zero replicas:

kubectl -n <thehive_namespace> scale deployment <thehive_deployment> --replicas=0

docs.title: Step 2: Get the chart of the new version
docs.text:
Each version of the chart is published in the StrangeBee Helm repository added at installation time. Its appVersion is the released TheHive Flow version, and the image tags default to it, so upgrading with the new chart moves the images.

  1. Refresh the repository index and list the chart versions, with the version of TheHive Flow each one ships in its APP VERSION column:

    helm repo update
helm search repo strangebee/thehive-flow --versions

  2. Note the chart version whose APP VERSION is the target TheHive Flow version. The commands below refer to it as <chart_version>.

If you installed with the deployment scenarios, also refresh the clone of the GitHub repository with git pull, from the chart directory. A new version can change the scenario values files you pass to the chart.

docs.title: Step 3: Review the values file
docs.text:
Reuse the values files passed at installation time: a helm upgrade renders the chart from the values passed on its command line, not from the ones stored in the release. Check the following before upgrading:

  • config.api.public.url must still be set: the chart refuses to render without it.
  • On a cluster that pulls from a private mirror, mirror the new docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow and docker.io/strangebee/thehive-flow-assistant images at the new version. When their pinned versions changed, also mirror the code transformation images and the other images the chart pulls.
  • If your values file pins image.tag or codex.kubernetes.assistantImage.tag, set them to the new version: a pinned tag doesn't follow the chart appVersion. Left empty, both follow it.
  • Compare your values with the defaults of the new chart for keys introduced by the new version, with helm show values strangebee/thehive-flow --version <chart_version>. The application configuration lives in the config.* values, so there's no configuration file to reconcile on the cluster.

The Secrets provisioned at installation time stay in place. Keep the JWT signing key stable: changing it invalidates every token already issued.

docs.title: Step 4: Render the chart
docs.text:
Render the chart before upgrading. This catches a missing config.api.public.url and any PostgreSQL address mismatch between TheHive Flow and the Temporal subchart, without touching the cluster:

helm template thehive-flow strangebee/thehive-flow --version <chart_version> \
  --namespace thehive-flow --values <values_file> > /dev/null && echo OK

With the deployment scenarios, replace --values <values_file> with the three -f scenarios/... files passed at installation time.

docs.title: Step 5: Upgrade the release
docs.text:
Upgrade the release with the new chart:

helm upgrade thehive-flow strangebee/thehive-flow --version <chart_version> \
  --namespace thehive-flow \
  --values <values_file> \
  --wait --timeout 10m

The upgrade runs the following, in order:

1/ A pre-upgrade Job runs TheHive Flow database migrations, so the schema is current before the application rolls. The Job pulls TheHive Flow image at the new version, so the cluster must be able to pull it. On a private mirror, the pull secret must already exist.

2/ The Temporal subchart runs its schema upgrade as a pre-upgrade hook, so the Temporal Server schema is current before the new server starts. The Temporal Server version is pinned in the chart and moves with it.

3/ The thehive-flow Deployment rolls: the current pod stops, then the new pod starts and verifies that the schema is current. The startup probe holds the liveness and readiness probes until the application first answers on /livez.

The --wait flag makes the command return once the Deployment is available again. If either pre-upgrade Job fails, the upgrade stops before the Deployment rolls and the previous version keeps running. When TheHive Flow migration Job fails, Helm prints its logs, and the Job stays in place for 10 minutes, for inspection with kubectl -n thehive-flow logs job/thehive-flow-migrations. When the Temporal schema Job fails, TheHive Flow database migrations have already been applied, and the previous pod isn't restarted. That state isn't supported: the pod only checks at startup that the schema isn't behind its own migrations, so it can't tell that the schema is now ahead. The previous version then runs against a database it doesn't know. Restore the thehive_flow database from the backup taken before the upgrade, then fix the cause and run the upgrade again.

docs.title: Step 6: Upgrade TheHive
docs.text:
Once TheHive Flow runs the new version, upgrade TheHive to the same version.

  • For a package or Docker Compose installation: follow Upgrade from TheHive 6.x.
  • For a Kubernetes release, upgrade the release as described in Deploy TheHive on Kubernetes. The helm upgrade command restores the replica count set in your values. When thehive.autoscaling.enabled is true, the chart doesn't set the replica count, so scale the Deployment back up with kubectl scale.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify the upgrade
docs.text:
Run the chart test, which probes the version endpoint from a throwaway pod:

helm test thehive-flow -n thehive-flow --logs

Then check that the pods are running and that the application logs show no unexpected errors:

kubectl -n thehive-flow get pods
kubectl -n thehive-flow logs deploy/thehive-flow --tail=50

To check the health endpoints directly, forward the observability port and query it. /readyz confirms TheHive Flow can reach its database and the Temporal workflow engine, and returns 503 naming the failing check otherwise:

kubectl -n thehive-flow port-forward deploy/thehive-flow 9090:9090
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

Then, in TheHive, sign in with an account that has the predefined Org-Admin profile and select the health indicator at the bottom of the sidebar menu. It covers every configured connector: TheHive Flow, Cortex, Malware Information Sharing Platform & Threat Sharing (MISP), and Email Intake. Its color reflects all of them at once. It turns green when every configured connector is healthy, and red when at least one is in error. Its Flow section shows TheHive Flow URL and its own status, OK or ERROR. TheHive probes TheHive Flow every minute by default, so allow that long for the status to reflect the restart.

Finally, go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu and check that it displays the workflow list. An error notification over an empty workflow list means TheHive can't reach TheHive Flow: see Troubleshoot TheHive Flow.

docs.title: Roll backNext steps
docs.text:
A rollback restores the databases first, then redeploys the previous chart. helm rollback alone isn't a supported rollback: it reverts neither TheHive Flow database schema nor the Temporal Server schema, and the previous pod starts anyway. Its startup check only detects a schema that's behind its own migrations, not one that's ahead. TheHive Flow database migrations are forward-only, and Temporal schema migrations are never reverted, so the previous version can't be trusted on a database migrated by the new one.

  1. Scale TheHive Flow down, so that nothing writes to the databases during the restore:

    kubectl -n thehive-flow scale deployment thehive-flow --replicas=0

  2. Restore the thehive_flow, temporal, and temporal_visibility databases and the object storage from the backup taken before the upgrade, with the tooling described in Configuration and operations on Kubernetes. Restore the databases and the object storage together: the database references files by content hash.

  3. List the revisions of the release and roll back to the one before the upgrade. Helm keeps the history of the release, and the rollback redeploys the previous chart and images:

    helm history thehive-flow -n thehive-flow
helm rollback thehive-flow <revision> -n thehive-flow --wait

Workflow runs started under the new version are lost with the restore, and runs started under the previous version resume from the backup state.

  • Deploy TheHive Flow on Kubernetes
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Monitor TheHive Flow
  • Troubleshoot TheHive Flow

docs.title: Back Up and Restore TheHive Flow
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow keeps its state in two directories of the profile directory, mounted into the containers: postgresql/data, holding the databases, and s3-store/data, holding the blobs. The configuration, the TLS certificates, and the .env file sit beside them, so the whole profile directory is the unit to back up.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: What's backed up
docs.text:
The backup.sh script copies the following folders and files of the profile directory:

Data Folder Notes The thehive_flow database postgresql/data Workflows, runs, variables, webhook configuration, run and step execution history Temporal persistence postgresql/data The temporal and temporal_visibility databases, holding the in-flight workflow state. Captured with the database above, as one PostgreSQL data directory Blob store contents s3-store/data Files ingested through webhooks or runs, and promoted activity outputs, in the shipped object storage Application configuration and secrets thehive-flow/ thehive-flow.yml, TheHive API key file, and the SMTP password file of an email server override Temporal configuration temporal/ Including the rendered temporal-server.yaml, which holds the Temporal database password Nginx configuration and TLS material nginx/, certificates/ The template, the certificate, and the private key Environment file .env, stored as dot.env Every secret of the stack, the image versions, and the runtime parameters. The databases can only be restored together with it

Two kinds of data fall outside the script:

  • An external S3-compatible object storage, configured as described in S3 back end. Back it up with the tooling of the storage service.
  • A blob directory of the local filesystem back end located outside the profile directory. Capture it with your own tooling.

In both cases, capture the blobs and the PostgreSQL data at the same time, for the reason below.

The database and the blobs are one unit

Rows in the thehive_flow database reference blobs by content hash. Restoring the database against a blob store that doesn't hold the referenced content leaves dangling references that TheHive Flow can't detect. A workflow reading such a file fails at run time, not at restore time. The coupling holds in both directions: files are deleted once their runs are purged, so a database older than the blob store references files deleted since. Whichever method you use, capture both together.

Backups carry every secret of the stack

A backup holds .env, the rendered Temporal configuration, the API key file, the TLS private key, the S3 identity the object storage stores in its data, and the database with the organization secret variables and the settings pushed by TheHive. The script creates each backup folder readable by its owner only. Treat the backup location with the same care as .env, and encrypt the backups before shipping them off-host.

docs.title: Step 1: Choose a backup method
docs.text: Method When TheHive Flow downtime Consistency Method 1: Instance or volume snapshot Single-node host on a platform that offers snapshots, the common case None: the stack keeps running Guaranteed by the platform: the whole profile directory is captured at one point in time Method 2: Cold backup with backup.sh No snapshot facility available, a portable copy restorable on another host, or before a risky operation such as an upgrade The whole stack is stopped for the duration of the copy, proportional to the size of the data directories Guaranteed by the script: everything is stopped before the copy

docs.title: Step 2: Run the backup
docs.text: Run the method you chose at Step 1.

docs.title: Method 1: Instance or volume snapshot
docs.text:
Use a snapshot when your host runs on a platform that offers snapshots: it's the simplest option and requires no downtime. A snapshot taken while the stack runs captures postgresql/data, s3-store/data, and .env at the same instant, so the database, the Temporal persistence, and the blobs can't drift apart.

Use your platform's own tooling, such as AWS EBS snapshots, hypervisor snapshots, or LVM. Nothing in the stack is needed, and the stack doesn't interfere with it.

Two caveats:

  • A snapshot of a running PostgreSQL is a crash-consistent image, not a clean copy: PostgreSQL replays its write-ahead log on restore, which is supported but isn't the same guarantee as a copy taken while the service is stopped. For a guaranteed-clean copy, take a cold backup as well.
  • Snapshot size follows the data directories. See Blob store volume sizing.

docs.title: Method 2: Cold backup
docs.text:
Maintenance window required

This procedure involves changing configuration files and restarting services. Schedule a maintenance window to prevent service disruption.

Use a cold backup when no snapshot facility is available, when you want a copy restorable on any host running the same profile, or before a risky operation such as an upgrade.

Run the script from the profile directory, with the path of the profile directory and the root folder of the backups. Without arguments, the script prompts for both, with . and ./backup as defaults. Prefer a dedicated location with enough space, such as a mounted backup volume:

bash ./scripts/backup.sh . /opt/backups/thehive-flow

What the script does:

1/ Creates the backup folder, <backup_root>/<timestamp>/, readable by its owner only, and starts a log file next to it, backup_log_<timestamp>.log.

2/ Stops every service of the stack with docker compose stop.

3/ Copies the postgresql, s3-store, thehive-flow, temporal, nginx, and certificates folders with rsync, preserving ownership and permissions.

4/ Copies .env as dot.env.

5/ Restarts the stack with docker compose up -d. The restart also runs when a copy fails, so a failed backup doesn't leave the stack stopped.

The backup folder mirrors the profile directory:

/opt/backups/thehive-flow
├── 20260115-0200-0100
│   ├── certificates
│   ├── dot.env
│   ├── nginx
│   ├── postgresql
│   ├── s3-store
│   ├── temporal
│   └── thehive-flow
└── backup_log_20260115-0200-0100.log

The stack is unavailable for the whole copy. The duration is proportional to the size of postgresql/data and s3-store/data: on an installation handling large files, measure it once before scheduling, with time bash ./scripts/backup.sh . /opt/backups/thehive-flow.

Runs in flight when the services stop don't fail: Temporal keeps their state in the copied databases and they resume once the stack restarts. TheHive Flow detects a step still executing at that moment as interrupted shortly after. It then re-runs it from the start if it has retries configured, and fails it otherwise.

docs.title: (Optional) Step 3: Ship the backups off-host
docs.text:
This step applies to the folders produced by method 2. The platform stores method 1 snapshots.

Ship the backup folders off-host using your existing tooling: the stack doesn't handle this automatically. Ship whole folders: a database directory without its dot.env or its blobs can't be restored.

Recommended options:

  • Copy the backups to a backup server with rsync:

    rsync -az /opt/backups/thehive-flow/ <backup_server>:/srv/backups/thehive-flow/

  • Upload them to S3:

    aws s3 sync /opt/backups/thehive-flow/<timestamp> s3://<bucket>/thehive-flow/<timestamp>/

  • Encrypt them before shipping, as one archive per backup folder:

    tar czf - -C /opt/backups/thehive-flow <timestamp> \
  | gpg --encrypt --recipient <recipient> -o /opt/backups/thehive-flow-<timestamp>.tar.gz.gpg

docs.title: (Optional) Step 4: Schedule automated backups
docs.text:
The cron example below schedules method 2. For method 1, configure the cadence and retention in your platform's snapshot tooling instead. Because method 2 stops the stack, schedule it when as few workflows as possible run, and account for the downtime in the service expectations of TheHive Flow. Webhook calls arriving during the copy are refused, and TheHive reports the connection as down.

The recommended retention is daily backups for 30 days, with at least one weekly backup shipped to a geographically separate location.

Size the retention against the data directories: a backup is a full copy, and the blob store is usually by far the larger half. Measure one backup before committing to a retention window, and prefer snapshots if the platform offers them.

Example cron entries, running daily at 2 AM and keeping 30 days of backups. Pass both arguments to the script: without them, it prompts and the job hangs.

0 2 * * * cd <profile_directory> && bash ./scripts/backup.sh . /opt/backups/thehive-flow >> /var/log/thehive-flow-backup.log 2>&1
0 3 * * * find /opt/backups/thehive-flow -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -mtime +30 -exec rm -rf {} +
0 3 * * * find /opt/backups/thehive-flow -maxdepth 1 -name 'backup_log_*.log' -mtime +30 -delete

docs.title: Step 5: Restore
docs.text:
Maintenance window required

This procedure involves changing configuration files and restarting services. Schedule a maintenance window to prevent service disruption.

The restore.sh procedure below restores a backup folder produced by method 2, on a host running the same profile. To restore a method 1 snapshot, use your platform's snapshot tooling instead.

  1. Stop the stack. The script refuses to run while any service is up:

    docker compose down

  2. Empty the data directories. Pre-existing files can conflict with the restored ones:

    rm -rf ./postgresql/data/* ./s3-store/data/*

  3. Run the restore, with the path of the profile directory and the backup folder to restore. Without arguments, the script prompts for both:

    bash ./scripts/restore.sh . /opt/backups/thehive-flow/<timestamp>

What the script does:

1/ Checks that the backup folder exists and holds a dot.env file, and that no service is running.

2/ Copies the postgresql, s3-store, thehive-flow, temporal, nginx, and certificates folders back into the profile directory with rsync, overwriting what's there.

3/ Restores dot.env as .env. The restored file carries the secrets that match the restored databases and the object storage identity, and the image versions the backup was taken with.

4/ Starts the stack with docker compose up -d, and logs the whole operation in restore_log_<timestamp>.log in the current directory.

Because the Temporal persistence is restored together with the thehive_flow database, the two stores are consistent. Runs that were in flight at backup time resume where they were, and nothing that happened after the backup remains.

Restoring on another host

The restored .env carries the user and group identifiers, the Docker socket group, and the server name of the host the backup was taken on, and restore.sh starts the stack with them. On another host, fix them right after the restore:

  1. Stop the stack the script started:

    docker compose down

  2. Make the two data directories owned by the user who runs the stack. This is needed when the restore ran as root, because the directories then keep the ownership of the original host. The init.sh script doesn't check these two directories:

    sudo chown -R <uid>:<gid> ./postgresql/data ./s3-store/data

  3. Run bash ./scripts/init.sh to detect the identifiers and the Docker socket group again, and confirm the server name and TheHive settings. The script keeps the restored secrets. Without a custom certificate, it generates a new self-signed certificate for the new host, so a TheHive that trusts the specific certificate needs the new one: see TLS certificate renewal.

  4. Start the stack:

    docker compose up -d

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the restoreNext steps
docs.text:
Check that all containers are running and that the health endpoints respond:

docker compose ps -a
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

Then, in TheHive, go to the Flow view and check that the workflows and the run history of the backup are back.

docs.title: Authentication Between TheHive Flow Components
docs.text:
6.0 One

Every channel between TheHive Flow, TheHive, and the services of the stack carries its own authentication mechanism.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

The following diagram shows each channel and its mechanism. Blue arrows mark the services TheHive Flow needs to start: Temporal, PostgreSQL, and the blob store. The yellow arrows are used at run time only, when users work in the Flow view or when workflows run. Dashed arrows carry no authentication and rely on the isolation of the thehive-flow-network Docker network.

docs.title: Authentication matrix
docs.text: Channel Mechanism Direction Where configured TheHive → TheHive Flow JWT HS256, symmetric TheHive signs, TheHive Flow validates jwt_signing_key in the .env file of TheHive Flow, and TH_FLOW_KEY or flow.jwt_signing_key in TheHive External system → Webhook trigger Per-webhook method: none by default, Basic Auth, header key, or JWT The caller authenticates each request, unless the method is None The authentication section of the Webhook trigger TheHive Flow → TheHive, Analyzer and Responder nodes API key, bearer token TheHive Flow signs each request thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key, or thehive_api_key in .env TheHive Flow → TheHive, TheHive node Bearer token set in the node, usually a secret global variable TheHive Flow signs each request The Authentication section of the TheHive integration node TheHive Flow → PostgreSQL Username and password Connects as the thehive_flow role flow_db_password in .env, expanded into the connection string of thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml Temporal → PostgreSQL Username and password Connects as the temporal role temporal_db_password in .env, rendered into temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml by init.sh TheHive Flow → Blob store S3 access key and secret with the s3 back end. Filesystem ownership and permissions with the local back end TheHive Flow signs each S3 request, or writes as the container user s3_access_key_id and s3_secret_access_key in .env, or the blobstore.local.path directory TheHive Flow → Docker engine Membership of the group owning the Unix socket TheHive Flow starts and removes the code transformation containers The socket mount and the docker_gid group of the thehive-flow service in docker-compose.yml. See Docker engine access TheHive Flow → Third-party APIs Per-node method, such as an API key, a bearer token, or Basic Auth TheHive Flow authenticates each request The Authentication section of each integration node, or the Authentication option of each HTTP request node TheHive Flow → LLM provider API key of the provider, when it requires one TheHive Flow authenticates each request of an AI node The LLM providers configured in TheHive, which TheHive pushes to TheHive Flow TheHive Flow → SMTP server SMTP username and password, when the server requires them TheHive Flow authenticates the session of each Send email node The SMTP configuration in TheHive, which TheHive pushes to TheHive Flow, or the email server override in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml TheHive Flow → Temporal None Trust through network isolation The thehive-flow-network Docker bridge Nginx → TheHive Flow None Trust through network isolation The thehive-flow-network Docker bridge

docs.title: JWT between TheHive and TheHive Flow
docs.text:
Both services use the same algorithm: HS256, an HMAC-SHA256 signature with a symmetric key.

  • The init.sh script generates the key with openssl rand -hex 32 and stores it in .env as jwt_signing_key.
  • The thehive-flow service receives it through the BEEFLOW_SECRET_JWT_SYMMETRIC_KEY environment variable set in docker-compose.yml.
  • TheHive must be configured with the same value: through the TH_FLOW_KEY environment variable, or through flow.jwt_signing_key in the mounted application.conf when TheHive runs with --no-config.

There's no automated key exchange or rotation protocol. The key is set once at install time and rotated manually. A key you set yourself must be at least 32 characters long.

Tokens expire 1 minute after signing, with a 30-second validation leeway in TheHive Flow. Keep the clocks of both hosts synchronized with NTP: a larger clock skew makes TheHive Flow reject every token as expired.

Common pitfall: Docker Compose environment variable syntax

With the list syntax, quotes become part of the value and cause a token signature is invalid error:

environment:
  - TH_FLOW_KEY="<jwt_signing_key>"

Use the mapping syntax instead, where YAML strips the quotes:

environment:
  TH_FLOW_KEY: "<jwt_signing_key>"

The list syntax also works without quotes:

environment:
  - TH_FLOW_KEY=<jwt_signing_key>

docs.title: Direct calls to TheHive Flow
docs.text: Calling the /api/ paths of TheHive Flow directly, without going through TheHive, isn't a supported integration. The shipped nginx only forwards TheHive requests from the addresses listed in nginx_thehive_addresses in .env: a request from any other address receives a 403 before reaching TheHive Flow. To start workflows from your own systems, use Webhook triggers instead: they enter through nginx on port 443 and carry their own authentication method, independent of the JWT.

docs.title: TheHive API key
docs.text:
TheHive Flow uses a bearer token to authenticate the requests that Analyzer and Responder nodes send to TheHive. TheHive Flow reads the token from the BEEFLOW_SECRET_THEHIVE_API_KEY environment variable, filled from thehive_api_key in .env, and falls back to the thehive-api-key file inside the configured secret_path when the variable is empty: /secret in the container, mapped from ./thehive-flow/secret/ on the host.

The TheHive integration node doesn't use this token. It authenticates with the bearer token set in its own Authentication section, usually stored in a secret global variable.

The file contains the raw token, and stays readable by its owner only, like the other secret files of the stack:

printf '%s' '<thehive_api_key>' > ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key
chmod 600 ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key

See the secrets inventory.

Whitespace is trimmed from every secret

The loader trims leading and trailing whitespace and newlines from all secrets it resolves, whether from a file or a BEEFLOW_SECRET_* environment variable. This includes the JWT signing key, TheHive API key, and any Docker registry credentials such as passwords and identity or registry tokens. A trailing newline in a secret file is therefore harmless, and a secret value that must contain leading or trailing whitespace isn't supported.

docs.title: PostgreSQL authentication
docs.text: The init.sh script creates the thehive_flow and temporal database roles when they're missing, with the passwords of .env, and aligns the roles with those passwords at each later run. The passwords are stored in .env and in temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml, both readable by their owner only and covered by .gitignore. They're never embedded in tracked configuration files.

docs.title: Key rotationNext steps
docs.text:
See Rotate secrets for the procedure of each key.

docs.title: Manage TheHive Flow Logs
docs.text:
6.0 One

Every service in a TheHive Flow deployment logs to its container output, collected by the Docker daemon.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Access the logs
docs.text:
To read the last 200 lines of a specific service:

docker compose logs --tail=200 thehive-flow
docker compose logs --tail=200 temporal
docker compose logs --tail=200 postgresql
docker compose logs --tail=200 nginx

To follow a service in real time:

docker compose logs -f thehive-flow

To read all services since a point in time, for example 2h for the last 2 hours:

docker compose logs --since <duration>

docs.title: Interpret the logs of each service
The thehive-flow service
docs.text:
The thehive-flow service logs structured JSON. Every log line has at minimum time, level, and msg.

HTTP request lines add server_name, http_method, and url_path. Error lines add error.cause, error.error, and error.stack.

The access log line closing each request, whose msg is HTTP request handled, adds http_status_code and duration. When the request was rejected, it also carries the reason under error.

A rejected request is client behavior, so the service logs that line at INFO, not ERROR. Filtering on ERROR alone shows server faults and hides every rejection.

Depending on how the error was built, the rejection reason sits under error.msg or error.cause.msg: read both, as the second recipe below does.

To list server faults with jq:

docker compose logs --no-log-prefix thehive-flow 2>&1 \
  | grep '"level":"ERROR"' \
  | jq '{time, msg, error: (.error.error // .error.msg)}'

To list rejected requests, with both places the reason can sit:

docker compose logs --no-log-prefix thehive-flow 2>&1 \
  | grep '"msg":"HTTP request handled"' \
  | jq -c 'select(.http_status_code >= 400)
           | {time, http_status_code, url_path,
              reason: .error.msg, cause: .error.cause.msg}'

The --no-log-prefix flag is required: without it, Compose prefixes every line with the service name followed by |, and jq fails to parse.

Some rejections, such as an unrouted 404 or a 405, carry no error field at all, so reason is null. A 429 from the webhook rate limiter does carry its reason.

docs.title: Change the log level
docs.text:
Set the BEEFLOW_LOG_LEVEL environment variable on the thehive-flow service, in the environment: block of docker-compose.yml or in a docker-compose.override.yml file, as described in Environment variable overrides. The value is a threshold: the service logs every line at that severity and above, so setting warn keeps the warning and error lines and drops the rest. The accepted values, from most to least verbose, are:

  • debug: Adds verbose diagnostic detail, for investigation sessions
  • info: Default value. Routine operations, including the request lines and rejection reasons described above
  • warn: Warnings, such as the periodic retention sync warning
  • error: Server faults only
services:
  thehive-flow:
    environment:
      BEEFLOW_LOG_LEVEL: "warn"

Apply the change by recreating the service, because a plain restart doesn't re-read the file:

docker compose up -d thehive-flow

To change the level without recreating the container, call the /loglevel endpoint of the observability listener from the host:

curl -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"level":"debug"}' http://127.0.0.1:9090/loglevel

The new level applies at once, and the change is logged as log level changed at runtime. It doesn't survive a restart of the container, which goes back to BEEFLOW_LOG_LEVEL. To read the current level, run curl http://127.0.0.1:9090/loglevel.

Raising the log level hides rejection reasons

Raising the level above INFO silences the rejection reasons in the container output. Server faults keep their ERROR line, and a configured OTLP logs export still receives everything, because the level applies per destination.

docs.title: The temporal service
docs.text:
The temporal service logs structured JSON in the Temporal schema. Watch for the following events:

  • history size exceeds warn limit: A workflow history passed 10 MB. See Troubleshoot TheHive Flow
  • history size exceeds error limit: A workflow history passed 50 MB, and Temporal terminated the workflow
  • Errors about updating or locking a shard: Temporal can't write its state to PostgreSQL, which points to a database issue

A workflow task that a worker takes but doesn't finish in time doesn't produce a log line. It shows as a WorkflowTaskTimedOut event in the workflow history.

docs.title: The postgresql service
docs.text:
PostgreSQL logs connection errors, authentication failures, and slow queries when configured. Turn on slow query logging by adding the following flags to the command of the postgresql service in docker-compose.yml. The Production environment #2 profile already defines a command with memory settings: append the flags to it rather than replacing it.

services:
  postgresql:
    command:
      - postgres
      - -c
      - log_min_duration_statement=1000
      - -c
      - log_connections=on
      - -c
      - log_disconnections=on

Apply the change. Recreating the database container briefly interrupts the whole stack:

docker compose up -d postgresql

docs.title: The nginx service
docs.text: The access log format is IP - - [timestamp] "METHOD path HTTP/version" status bytes "referer" "user-agent" "x-forwarded-for". The error log includes TLS handshake failures and upstream connection errors. At start, the 40-thehive-allow.sh lines list the addresses nginx allows and skips for TheHive requests.

docs.title: The object storage services
docs.text: The s3-store service logs the availability and storage errors of the object storage. The one-shot init-s3-store container logs the provisioning of the S3 identity and the bucket, with any failure prefixed with FATAL:. Read it with docker compose logs init-s3-store.

docs.title: Collect logs during an incident
docs.text:
Failing to collect these logs is the primary reason post-mortems can't determine a root cause. Collect the logs of all services as soon as you detect an incident.

Service Why it matters thehive-flow Workflow run traces, JWT validation errors, HTTP errors, Temporal client errors temporal Workflow scheduling decisions, retry history, timeouts, task queue depth postgresql Connection errors, slow queries, schema migration status nginx Client IP, URL, HTTP status, TLS errors, upstream 502 and 504 errors s3-store Blob store availability and storage errors init-s3-store Provisioning errors on the S3 identity and the bucket, prefixed with FATAL:

Collect a wider window than you think you need, at least 2 hours before the incident, because Temporal workflows can have long delays between task scheduling and execution. The following commands gather the logs of every service over the last 24 hours, the container state, and the versions, into one folder:

mkdir thehive-flow-diagnose-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ) && cd $_
docker compose -f ../docker-compose.yml logs --since 24h --no-color --timestamps > compose-logs.txt 2>&1
docker compose -f ../docker-compose.yml ps -a > compose-ps.txt
docker compose -f ../docker-compose.yml images > compose-images.txt
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz > readyz.json
grep _image_version ../.env > versions.txt
cp ../thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml .

The application logs don't carry secrets, but review thehive-flow.yml before sharing the folder, and never include .env, the files of thehive-flow/secret/, or the rendered Temporal configuration, which hold the secrets of the stack. Attach the folder, as an archive, to every support ticket.

docs.title: Configure Docker log rotation
docs.text:
Configure the Docker daemon to prevent log files from filling the disk. The configuration below caps each container at 300 MB of logs, three files of 100 MB. Apply it before starting the stack on a new host, because it only takes effect for newly created containers.

  1. Create or edit /etc/docker/daemon.json:

    {
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "100m",
    "max-file": "3"
  }
}

  2. Restart Docker. Restarting the Docker daemon restarts every container of the stack, so schedule it like any other maintenance operation:

    systemctl restart docker

  3. Verify that rotation is active:

    docker inspect thehive-flow \
  | jq '.[0].HostConfig.LogConfig'

    Rotation is active when the output shows the configured limits:

    {
  "Type": "json-file",
  "Config": {
    "max-file": "3",
    "max-size": "100m"
  }
}

    An empty Config object means the container was created before the daemon configuration: recreate it with docker compose up -d so the setting applies.

docs.title: Retain and archive the logsNext steps
docs.text:
The rotation configured above deletes the oldest log lines once a container reaches its cap, so the host only ever holds the recent history. The minimum recommended retention for incident investigation is 30 days. A busy deployment can fill its 300 MB cap in far less time. To keep the full window, archive the logs off the host.

The Docker daemon log files are on the host filesystem under /var/lib/docker/containers/<container_id>/. For long-term retention or centralized log management, ship them to your SIEM or log aggregator, such as Loki, Elastic, or Splunk. Use a log shipper such as Promtail, Filebeat, or Fluentd.

  • Monitor TheHive Flow
  • Troubleshoot TheHive Flow
  • TheHive Flow System Requirements

docs.title: Maintain TheHive Flow
docs.text:
6.0 One

Routine maintenance of a TheHive Flow deployment covers tuning the run retention, keeping the disk under control, and upgrading the services.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Upgrade TheHive Flow
docs.text:
To upgrade TheHive Flow and the other services of the stack, see Upgrade TheHive Flow with Docker Compose. The other services are PostgreSQL, Temporal, the object storage, and nginx. Their versions are pinned together in versions.env, at the root of the repository clone.

After an upgrade, check that your thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml carries the blocks of the shipped one at the new version. modules.runs.sync_temporal_retention is one such block, and without it the run list and the Temporal history expire on different clocks. See Temporal workflow history retention.

docs.title: Log rotation
docs.text:
Log rotation is configured once at the Docker daemon level. See Docker log rotation.

Check that rotation is active after installing or reinstalling Docker on a host:

docker inspect thehive-flow | jq '.[0].HostConfig.LogConfig'

docs.title: PostgreSQL routine maintenance
docs.text:
PostgreSQL runs autovacuum by default, so no manual table maintenance is required for normal operation.

Monitor table bloat periodically:

docker compose exec postgresql psql -U postgres -d thehive_flow -c "
  SELECT schemaname, tablename, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup,
         round(n_dead_tup::numeric / nullif(n_live_tup,0) * 100, 1) AS dead_pct
  FROM pg_stat_user_tables
  ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
  LIMIT 10;"

A dead_pct above 20% on a large table may indicate that autovacuum isn't keeping up. Force a manual vacuum if needed:

docker compose exec postgresql psql -U postgres -d thehive_flow \
  -c "VACUUM ANALYZE;"

docs.title: Temporal workflow history retention
docs.text:
Run retention has one knob: modules.runs.retention in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml, with a default of 30 days. It governs three things at once:

  • How long a run stays in the run list
  • How long the blob store keeps the files those runs reference
  • How long Temporal keeps its execution history, because the stack enables modules.runs.sync_temporal_retention

TheHive Flow applies the value to the default namespace at startup and checks it again periodically. It also purges the runs older than the retention at every startup, then periodically, so frequent restarts don't postpone the purge.

A change takes effect for executions that complete after it's applied. It isn't retroactive in either direction. Raising the retention doesn't bring back history Temporal has already deleted. Those runs stay in the run list until modules.runs.retention expires their rows, with their details replaced by the message This execution log is not available anymore. There's no way to remove them earlier.

The key is absent from the shipped file. For the first change, add it under modules.runs, then recreate the thehive-flow service. A value of 168h is 7 days. Omit the key entirely to keep the 30-day default.

modules:
  runs:
    retention: 168h

docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow

Before shortening the retention

This includes the first restart after adding sync_temporal_retention. The sync is symmetric: it aligns the namespace down as readily as up, and shortening a namespace retention deletes the history beyond the new window. If your namespace currently holds more than modules.runs.retention, set modules.runs.retention to that longer value first, then recreate the service. Check what the namespace holds today with the namespace describe command below.

The minimum accepted value is 24h. Below that, the run-list purge would delete runs whose Temporal history is still live, so TheHive Flow refuses to start rather than let the two stores diverge. TheHive Flow enforces that floor, which matches the minimum retention Temporal accepts for a namespace. Setting 0 turns retention off entirely, with no purge and no namespace sync.

Setting the retention on the namespace directly with temporal operator namespace update --retention isn't supported. TheHive Flow periodically converges the namespace back to modules.runs.retention. Two stores holding two different retentions is the state to avoid, because whichever one purges first leaves the other serving runs it can no longer describe.

Raising the retention keeps proportionally more Temporal history in PostgreSQL: a 30-day window holds roughly 10 times the history of a 72-hour one. Size the disk accordingly, per PostgreSQL volume sizing, or lower modules.runs.retention. It also keeps more files in the blob store. See Blob store volume sizing.

Check the current setting:

docker compose --profile admin run --rm temporal-admin \
  temporal operator namespace describe -n default --address temporal:7233

docs.title: Docker image cleanup
docs.text:
To remove dangling images after upgrades:

docker image prune -f

To show disk usage by Docker objects:

docker system df -v

The data of the stack lives in the ./postgresql/data and ./s3-store/data directories of the profile directory, mounted into the containers, not in Docker volumes. docker volume prune and docker compose down -v therefore don't touch it. Check the size of the two directories with:

du -sh ./postgresql/data ./s3-store/data

The reset script deletes everything

bash ./scripts/reset.sh stops the stack and deletes the two data directories, the rendered Temporal configuration, TheHive API key file, the TLS certificates, and .env with every secret. It asks for confirmation, and nothing it deletes is recoverable except from a backup. Use it to start over on a test host only.

docs.title: Backup rotation
docs.text:
Delete backup folders older than 30 days, along with their log files:

find /opt/backups/thehive-flow -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -mtime +30 -exec rm -rf {} +
find /opt/backups/thehive-flow -maxdepth 1 -name 'backup_log_*.log' -mtime +30 -delete

Schedule this alongside the backup cron. See Schedule automated backups.

docs.title: Health check cadenceNext steps
docs.text:
Run these checks after every maintenance operation, and verify that all services are healthy, that TheHive Flow is live and ready, and that the logs show no unexpected errors:

docker compose ps -a
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/livez
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz
docker compose logs --tail=50 thehive-flow
