docs.title: Monitor TheHive Flow
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow exposes health endpoints and Prometheus metrics. The Docker Compose stack ships built-in Docker health checks for its services. Dashboards and alerts come from your own monitoring platform, fed by these metrics.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Health endpoints
docs.text:
The thehive-flow service exposes its health on port 9090, published on loopback only: 127.0.0.1:9090. There's no application-level authentication on this listener, so protect it with a host firewall if needed.

Endpoint What it checks Expected response GET /livez HTTP server is up 200 with an empty body GET /readyz Internal modules, database connection, and Temporal client 200, or 503 with a JSON body naming each failing check GET /metrics Prometheus metrics exposition 200 with text metric lines 
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/livez
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

A failing /readyz indicates that TheHive Flow is still starting or is shutting down, or that PostgreSQL or the Temporal frontend is unreachable. Startup can keep /readyz at 503 for several minutes. The first start pulls the code transformation images before the service reports ready, and any start can wait on the rebuild of the variable reference index. The response body reports a coarse status for each of the db, modules, and temporal checks, and deliberately leaves out the underlying error:

  • modules reports not ready until startup completes, and again once shutdown begins.
  • db and temporal report a status such as unreachable, timeout, or error.

Check docker compose logs thehive-flow for the specific error, and see Troubleshoot TheHive Flow for the common failure signatures.

The blob store isn't part of /readyz. It's checked once at startup, with a HeadBucket request on the s3 back end and a real write test on the local back end. A failed check aborts the boot. Storage that breaks later shows up as failing runs rather than as a failing probe. Watch the s3-store container health and its disk instead, or the disk holding the local blob directory.

docs.title: Disk alerting for the blob store
docs.text:
Files are deleted once the runs that use them are purged, but the blob store can still fill up. Causes include a burst of large files, a long modules.runs.retention, or deletions that keep failing. Nothing in the stack alerts on its size: TheHive Flow exposes no metric for the space left, and a full disk surfaces as blob writes failing mid-run. Whichever back end holds the blobs, a host-level disk alert is the only signal, so treat it as mandatory rather than as a hardening step.

With the default s3 back end, put the alert on the filesystem holding the ./s3-store/data directory, the same one you'd use for ./postgresql/data. Check their current size with:

du -sh ./postgresql/data ./s3-store/data

With the local filesystem back end, put it on the filesystem holding the blobstore.local.path directory.

Also alert on the deletion job's error lines in the thehive-flow logs. A pass that fails to delete files logs blob-drain: could not delete file at the error level, once per kind of failure, with a hint when the storage refused the permission. A database failure stops the pass with blob-drain: could not process queued file deletions, at the error level too. The summary line of each pass, blob-drain: processed queued file deletions, carries the files_deleted, files_kept, files_skipped, files_recent, files_failed, and files_pending counters.

docs.title: Docker health checks
docs.text:
Docker monitors PostgreSQL, Temporal, and the object storage automatically. These health checks gate service startup: the thehive-flow service doesn't start until PostgreSQL and Temporal are healthy and the object storage has been provisioned.

Service Check command Interval Retries Start period postgresql pg_isready -U postgres -d postgres 5 s 12 30 s temporal nc -z 127.0.0.1 7233 10 s 30 60 s s3-store curl -sf http://localhost:8333/healthz 5 s 10 10 s init-s3-store None. One-shot container, gated on its exit code — — — thehive-flow None. Distroless image without a shell — — — nginx None — — —

The object storage is gated differently from the other services: the thehive-flow service waits for init-s3-store to complete successfully, not only for s3-store to be healthy. A healthy s3-store service whose bucket doesn't exist isn't enough, because the blob store performs a HeadBucket request at startup and fails fast. The init-s3-store container runs to completion and exits, so Exited (0) is its normal steady state, not a failure.

View the current health status:

docker compose ps -a

docs.title: Prometheus scraping
docs.text:
Add the following job to your Prometheus configuration:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: thehive-flow
    scrape_interval: 30s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["<flow_host>:9090"]

Port 9090 is loopback-only by default. If it isn't reachable from your Prometheus server, publish it on an address your Prometheus server can reach, by changing the ports: entry of the thehive-flow service in docker-compose.yml:

services:
  thehive-flow:
    ports:
      - "<host_ip>:9090:9090"

Apply the change:

docker compose up -d thehive-flow

Make the change in docker-compose.yml rather than in a docker-compose.override.yml file: Compose adds the ports of an override file to those of the base file instead of replacing them.

docs.title: Application metrics
docs.text:
Besides standard instrumentation for the REST server, the PostgreSQL connection pool, and the Temporal SDK client, the /metrics endpoint exposes the following application metrics:

Metric Type Labels Purpose thehive_flow_activity_calls_total Counter activity_type, outcome Workflow step executions. outcome is success, error, or canceled: alert on the error rate to catch failing steps thehive_flow_activity_duration_seconds Histogram activity_type, outcome Duration of workflow step executions thehive_flow_cache_hits_total, thehive_flow_cache_misses_total, thehive_flow_cache_evictions_total Counter cache_name In-process cache behavior

Labels are bounded by design: metrics never carry run, workflow, or organization identifiers. To follow an individual run, use the execution logs instead. No dashboard or alert rule ships with the stack, so alerts on these metrics are yours to define.

As a starting point, the following Prometheus rule fires when more than 5% of workflow step executions fail:

groups:
  - name: thehive-flow
    rules:
      - alert: FlowActivityErrorRateHigh
        expr: >
          sum(rate(thehive_flow_activity_calls_total{outcome="error"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(thehive_flow_activity_calls_total[5m]))
          > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: More than 5% of TheHive Flow step executions are failing

To alert per step type instead of on the overall rate, aggregate with sum by (activity_type) in both halves of the expression.

docs.title: Temporal metrics
docs.text:
The temporal service exposes its own Prometheus metrics on port 8000, configured in temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml.template. They cover the internals of the workflow engine, such as persistence latency and task backlog. The port is internal to the Docker network and isn't published on the host.

To scrape Temporal with your Prometheus, publish the port by adding a ports: entry to the temporal service in docker-compose.yml, binding it to an address your Prometheus server can reach. Use 127.0.0.1 if Prometheus runs on the same host.

services:
  temporal:
    ports:
      - "<host_ip>:8000:8000"

Apply the change:

docker compose up -d temporal

Then add the scrape target to your Prometheus configuration:

- job_name: temporal
  static_configs:
    - targets: ["<flow_host>:8000"]

The following Temporal signals are worth a dashboard panel or an alert on a single-node stack:

Signal Why it matters Server-wide gRPC success rate The single health signal for Temporal that alerts can act on Persistence request success rate and latency Persistence errors are the most likely failure mode with a co-tenanted PostgreSQL, and slow persistence shows up in latency before it shows up as errors Task schedule-to-start latency, by task type Primary signal that TheHive Flow workers can't keep up and a backlog is building, split by Workflow versus Activity task type Available worker task slots Capacity headroom explaining why schedule-to-start latency trends up Shard lock latency Shard-info lock contention in the history service, an early precursor to persistence slowdowns

docs.title: Conditions to alert on
docs.text:
Nothing in the stack sends notifications. The following conditions are worth an alert in your monitoring platform, with tooling such as node-exporter or cAdvisor for the host and container signals:

Condition How to detect Severity TheHive Flow not ready /readyz returns non-200 for more than 5 minutes, the time a startup can take Critical TheHive Flow not live /livez returns non-200 for more than 30 seconds Critical Workflow steps failing More than 5% of thehive_flow_activity_calls_total with outcome="error" over 5 minutes, as in the rule above Warning PostgreSQL, Temporal, or the object storage unhealthy docker compose ps shows unhealthy Critical Disk above 80% on the filesystem holding ./postgresql/data or ./s3-store/data df -h on the filesystem Warning Container terminated by the OOM killer Docker oom event Critical Temporal persistence error rate above 1%, or persistence latency above 1 s Temporal metrics on port 8000 Critical, Warning

Alerting in air-gapped networks

In an air-gapped network, SaaS notification channels are unreachable. Point the notification channel of your monitoring platform at something that already lives inside the boundary instead, such as an internal SMTP relay or a webhook into a ticketing or SIEM system already running, for example TheHive itself. That internal system then owns whatever happens next, and the alert never needs to leave the network.

docs.title: Check service statusNext steps
docs.text:
To check all services at once:

docker compose ps -a

To check detailed resource usage:

docker stats --no-stream

To check the PostgreSQL connectivity from the host:

docker compose exec postgresql pg_isready -U postgres

To check the database sizes:

docker compose exec postgresql psql -U postgres -c "\l+"

To check the Temporal connectivity:

docker compose --profile admin run --rm temporal-admin \
  temporal operator cluster health --address temporal:7233

docs.title: TheHive Flow Security Maintenance
docs.text:
6.0 One

Keeping a TheHive Flow deployment patched relies on the image versions StrangeBee pins in versions.env, at the root of the StrangeBee Docker Compose repository, and on the upgrade route of each component.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Component upgrade route
docs.text:
Every image of the stack is pinned by tag in versions.env. StrangeBee moves the pins, and the upgrade procedure applies them: git pull, then bash ./scripts/init.sh to copy the new versions into .env, then docker compose up -d. The constraints below decide what else the upgrade of a component involves.

Component Variable in versions.env Constraint TheHive Flow thehive_flow_image_version Database migrations run at startup and are forward-only. Rolling back doesn't revert the schema: undoing a schema change requires restoring the backup taken before the upgrade Nginx nginx_image_version No schema and no state, so fully independent PostgreSQL, minor or patch version postgresql_image_version Data is preserved in ./postgresql/data. Minor and patch versions are safe PostgreSQL, major version postgresql_image_version Breaking change requiring pg_upgrade or a dump and restore procedure outside the stack, before the pin moves Temporal, patch version temporal_image_version The temporalio/server and temporalio/admin-tools images share the pin and always move together Temporal, minor version temporal_image_version Requires the Temporal schema upgrade before the new server starts, one minor version at a time SeaweedFS object storage seaweedfs_image_version The s3-store and init-s3-store services share the pin. Data is preserved in ./s3-store/data. Stop the thehive-flow service before recreating the store, because recreating it under a running instance makes workflow steps fail on blob reads

docs.title: Version coupling between Temporal and TheHive Flow
docs.text: The Temporal Server version must be compatible with the Temporal SDK version embedded in TheHive Flow binary. Check TheHive Flow release notes before moving the Temporal pin yourself. Upgrading Temporal independently is safe as long as the server stays within the SDK supported range, typically within two minor versions.

docs.title: Respond to a CVE
docs.text: The patched version of an image usually reaches versions.env with the next release: run the upgrade procedure to apply it. To apply a patch before StrangeBee publishes the pin, move the pin yourself in versions.env, run bash ./scripts/init.sh to copy it into .env, then recreate the affected service as described below. Without a custom certificate, each run of init.sh also generates a new self-signed certificate: see TLS certificate renewal. The next git pull then reports a conflict on versions.env: discard your local change with git checkout -- ../versions.env before pulling, since the upstream pin is at least as recent.

docs.title: CVE in TheHive Flow binary
docs.text:
Move thehive_flow_image_version, run init.sh, then recreate the service:

docker compose up -d thehive-flow

Downtime is brief. Database migrations, if the new version carries any, run at startup.

docs.title: CVE in nginx
docs.text:
Move nginx_image_version, run init.sh, then recreate nginx only:

docker compose up -d nginx

Docker recreates the nginx container, which is the only entry point of the stack. TheHive requests and webhook calls are refused for a few seconds, and long-running requests still in progress are cut. The other services keep running.

docs.title: CVE in the object storage
docs.text:
Move seaweedfs_image_version, run init.sh, then stop the thehive-flow service, recreate the store, and provision it again:

docker compose stop thehive-flow
docker compose up -d init-s3-store
docker compose up -d thehive-flow

Blobs survive: they live in ./s3-store/data, not in the image. Downtime lasts as long as the store restart plus provisioning. The init-s3-store container asserts that the identity and the bucket exist before exiting 0. A failed provisioning therefore shows up as a non-zero exit rather than as a thehive-flow service that crash-loops later. To check the result, read the container logs:

docker compose logs --tail=50 init-s3-store

docs.title: CVE in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
For a minor or patch version, move postgresql_image_version, run init.sh, then recreate the service:

docker compose up -d postgresql

The ./postgresql/data directory is preserved. Expect a brief downtime while TheHive Flow and Temporal reconnect.

docs.title: CVE in Temporal
docs.text:
For a patch version, move temporal_image_version, run init.sh, then recreate the server:

docker compose up -d temporal

Temporal retries in-flight workflow tasks automatically after the restart. For a new minor version, follow the Temporal schema upgrade first.

docs.title: CVE in a base OS image
docs.text:
The maintainers of the PostgreSQL, Temporal, nginx, and SeaweedFS images rebuild them with OS patches under the same tag. Because the pins are tags, pulling the image again fetches the rebuilt one:

docker compose pull <service>
docker compose up -d <service>

docs.title: Version pinning policy
docs.text:
Every image of the stack is pinned by tag in versions.env, and init.sh copies the pins into .env, which docker-compose.yml reads. The latest tag is never used.

  • StrangeBee maintains the pins. Operators move them by pulling the repository, not by editing image references in docker-compose.yml.
  • The image of TheHive Flow follows TheHive releases: TheHive and TheHive Flow are released together and carry the same version number.
  • A pin moved by hand, as described in Respond to a CVE, is a temporary measure until the next release.

Check that the running stack matches the pins:

grep _image_version ../versions.env
grep _image_version .env
docker compose images

docs.title: TLS certificate expiry
docs.text:
Self-signed certificates generated by init.sh are valid for 365 days. Monitor the expiry:

openssl x509 -in ./nginx/certs/server.crt -noout -dates

Renew the certificate before it expires, as described in TLS certificate renewal.

For production deployments, use certificates signed by a trusted certificate authority (CA) and integrate with your certificate lifecycle management tooling, such as certbot or Vault PKI.

docs.title: Audit checklistNext steps
docs.text:
Run the following checks periodically. Monthly is recommended.

  • The pins in .env match the ones in versions.env, and the repository clone is up to date with the latest release
  • The nginx/certs/server.crt expiry is more than 60 days away
  • The .env permissions are 600: ls -la .env
  • The thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key and nginx/certs/server.key permissions are 600, and bash ./scripts/check_permissions.sh reports no deviation
  • nginx_thehive_addresses in .env lists only the addresses TheHive currently calls from, and the 40-thehive-allow.sh lines of docker compose logs --no-log-prefix nginx show what nginx allows and skips
  • No secrets appear in the docker compose logs output
  • The Temporal namespace retention matches modules.runs.retention: docker compose --profile admin run --rm temporal-admin temporal operator namespace describe -n default --address temporal:7233
  • Docker log rotation is configured: docker inspect thehive-flow | jq '.[0].HostConfig.LogConfig'
  • Backup folders exist and are recent: ls -lt /opt/backups/thehive-flow | head -5
  • Maintain TheHive Flow
