  • Back Up and Restore TheHive Flow

docs.title: TheHive Flow Security
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow generates and stores several secrets on its host, isolates its services on an internal Docker network, and terminates TLS at the nginx entry point.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: Secrets inventory
docs.text:
Secret Location on host Generated by PostgreSQL superuser password .env init.sh thehive_flow database password .env init.sh temporal database password .env, and its copy in temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml init.sh JWT signing key .env init.sh S3 secret access key .env, and its copy in the identity the object storage keeps in s3-store/data init.sh TheHive API key thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key, or .env Operator SMTP password of an email server override, when one is defined The file of thehive-flow/secret/ named in its password key Operator TLS private key nginx/certs/server.key init.sh or operator Secret variables and settings pushed by TheHive The thehive_flow database, in postgresql/data TheHive and the users Copies of all the above The backup folders of backup.sh backup.sh

All generated secrets are 256-bit random values produced by openssl rand -hex 32. None are committed to git: .env, thehive-flow/secret/*, the rendered Temporal configuration, the certificate files, and the data directories are all covered by .gitignore.

The postgresql, temporal, s3-store, and thehive-flow services run as the user who ran init.sh, so the secret files can stay readable by their owner only. Nginx runs as root inside its container and reads the TLS certificate files regardless of their mode. The script sets .env, temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml, and the TLS private key nginx/certs/server.key to mode 600. The check_permissions.sh script, which init.sh runs first, expects the files of thehive-flow/secret/ and the private keys of nginx/certs/ and certificates/ at mode 600 too. The backup.sh script creates each backup folder at mode 700.

docs.title: Organization secret variables
docs.text: Organization secret variables live in the PostgreSQL database, not on the host filesystem. Their values are never displayed in the interface, and execution logs don't record them among the resolved inputs of a node. A workflow can't reference a secret in a value that's stored or returned, such as a run label, a workflow output, or the value of a Set local variable node. Code nodes are the exception: they receive secrets in clear and can print them, as described in Code transformation isolation. Their only copy outside the database is the database backup, covered in the warning below.

docs.title: Settings pushed by TheHive
docs.text:
TheHive pushes its license token and three of its own settings to TheHive Flow, which stores the settings in the PostgreSQL database and uses them to open the connections itself:

  • The SMTP configuration, including the SMTP password, used by Send email nodes.
  • The LLM providers, including their API keys, used by AI nodes.
  • The outbound proxy settings, including the proxy password.

The database stores these values unencrypted. Anyone who can read the database or its backup can read them, so restrict access to the PostgreSQL service and protect the backups as described in the warning below. Change these settings in TheHive, not in TheHive Flow. The only exception is SMTP: an email server override defined in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml replaces the SMTP configuration pushed by TheHive. Its password lives in a file of thehive-flow/secret/ or in the BEEFLOW_SECRET_MAILER_PASSWORD environment variable, not in the database.

docs.title: External secret managers
docs.text:
Secrets don't have to stay in .env. Docker Compose reads a variable from the shell that runs it before falling back to .env, so an external secret manager can export jwt_signing_key, thehive_api_key, s3_secret_access_key, flow_db_password, temporal_db_password, and postgres_password at deploy time. Inside the container, TheHive Flow resolves every BEEFLOW_SECRET_* variable from its environment first and falls back to the file in /secret. A variable set to an empty value counts as unset, and the file fallback engages.

Two limits apply. The init.sh script writes every secret it generates into .env regardless, so the file has to be protected either way. And the Temporal database password always lands on disk: temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml holds it, rendered by init.sh.

The Docker registry credentials of custom code transformation images and the password of an email server override aren't declared in .env or in docker-compose.yml. Pass them through the environment: block of the thehive-flow service, as described in Environment variable overrides.

Backup folders carry secrets

The object storage keeps its own S3 identity in cleartext inside s3-store/data, both the access key and the secret key. The database holds the organization secret variables and the settings pushed by TheHive, with the SMTP password, the LLM provider API keys, and the proxy password. And every backup holds .env, the API key file, and the TLS private key. The backup.sh script therefore creates its folders at mode 700. Treat the backup location with the same care as .env: encrypt the backups before shipping them off-host, and don't relax the permissions to make them easier to copy.

docs.title: Network isolation
docs.text:
Users never reach TheHive Flow directly. The browser talks to TheHive, which forwards the calls of the Flow view to TheHive Flow with a JWT and streams the live execution updates back to the browser. TheHive Flow calls TheHive back with an API key to run Cortex analyzers and responders. Webhook callers are the only other traffic that reaches the host, and all of it enters through nginx on port 443.

  • thehive-flow-network is an isolated Docker bridge. No port is reachable from the host unless explicitly declared with ports:.
  • The thehive-flow service on port 8081 isn't published on the host: all traffic enters through nginx on port 443.
  • Nginx forwards TheHive requests only from the addresses listed in nginx_thehive_addresses in .env, set by init.sh. A request from any other address receives 403, and so does every request while the list is empty. Webhook calls stay open to any caller. See TheHive address filtering.
  • The observability listener on port 9090 is published on loopback only, 127.0.0.1:9090, so operators can reach /livez and /readyz from the host. It has no application-level authentication: protect it with host firewall rules if the /metrics data is sensitive.
  • PostgreSQL, Temporal, and the object storage aren't published on the host at all. The S3 API on port 8333 is reachable only from inside thehive-flow-network.
  • Outbound connections opened by workflow nodes go through an egress guard that blocks non-public addresses, so a workflow can't probe the internal network. Internal targets must be explicitly allowlisted: see Egress allowlist. Code transformation nodes are the exception: see Code transformation isolation.

docs.title: TheHive address filtering
docs.text:
TheHive is the only client of the /api/ paths, and it enforces the security of these routes: a call that reaches them without going through TheHive bypasses it. Nginx therefore forwards /api/ only from the addresses in nginx_thehive_addresses, and answers 404 to every path other than /api/ and /webhook/.

List every node of a TheHive cluster. When TheHive goes through an outbound proxy or a Network Address Translation (NAT) device, nginx sees the address of that device. Listing it opens TheHive requests to every other client of that device too.

At start, nginx logs each entry it allows, and each entry it skips with the reason: an entry that isn't an IPv4 address or range, or an entry that covers the Docker network gateway. The filter relies on nginx seeing the real address of the caller. With the default Docker port publishing on Linux, it does. docker-proxy relays the connection instead for a client connecting over IPv6, with rootless Docker, or with "iptables": false in the Docker daemon configuration. In these cases, nginx sees the gateway of thehive-flow-network, the .1 address of the network, for every such caller. Allowing that address would open TheHive requests to all of them, so nginx skips any entry that covers it. If the nginx log shows the gateway as the client: of refused TheHive requests, make TheHive reach the host over a path that keeps its address, such as IPv4, instead of changing the list.

docs.title: Code transformation isolation
docs.text:
On Kubernetes, see Code transformation isolation on Kubernetes.

Python code and JavaScript code nodes run the script a workflow author wrote. Every user holding the manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows permission can therefore run arbitrary code on the deployment, and the script runs with the same trust as that user. Grant the permission accordingly.

Each script runs in a disposable container on the host Docker daemon, launched from a distroless image for the run and removed as soon as the script exits or its node timeout expires. A small ryuk reaper container also runs on the host daemon for the life of the thehive-flow service, and removes orphaned script containers after a crash. To launch these containers, the thehive-flow service mounts the Docker socket of the host, which grants it root-equivalent access to the host, as mounting the socket in Cortex does for analyzers. Inside the script container, the deployment doesn't restrict the script further:

  • Network: The container joins the default Docker bridge, not thehive-flow-network. The script can reach the internet and every address the host can reach, including services on the local network. The egress guard doesn't apply to it, and the egress allowlist has no effect on it. The stack's internal services stay out of reach by name, since they only live on thehive-flow-network.
  • User: The script runs as the user of the image, which is root for the two default images, with the default Docker capability set.
  • Resources: No CPU, memory, or process limit is set on the container. A runaway script competes with the rest of the host until the node timeout stops it.
  • Secrets: A secret variable the script references is handed to it in clear, and nothing prevents the script from printing it. Printed values land in the script_out output and in the execution logs, which don't redact them.

To reduce the exposure:

  • Restrict the manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows permission to the profiles that need it, and review the code nodes of imported workflows before running them.
  • Filter the outbound traffic of the default bridge with host firewall rules, for example in the DOCKER-USER chain, to keep scripts away from the internal network.
  • Build a custom execution image that runs as a non-root user when the scripts don't need root.
  • Keep the node timeout short, since it's the only bound on a script's run time.

docs.title: Webhook exposure
docs.text:
Webhook triggers are the one entry point designed to be called by external systems. They don't go through TheHive. They enter through nginx on port 443, under the /webhook/ path prefix of the public URL. The authentication method configured on each webhook controls who can start the workflow, so select one for any webhook reachable from outside your network.

Two network-level restrictions narrow the exposure further:

  • Host firewall: When every caller is known, restrict inbound port 443 to their source addresses. TheHive reaches TheHive Flow on the same port, so keep TheHive host among the allowed sources.

  • Nginx: To restrict only the webhook paths while TheHive requests stay restricted to nginx_thehive_addresses, add access rules to the existing location /webhook/ block of the nginx configuration template, above its proxy_pass line. Then restart nginx with docker compose restart nginx. The server-level proxy directives are inherited, so the block only needs the access rules and proxy_pass:

    location /webhook/ {
    allow <caller_cidr>;
    deny  all;
    proxy_pass http://thehive-flow/webhook/;
}

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
A dedicated rate limiter protects each webhook. It applies before authentication, so it rejects a flood of requests without spending authentication work or reading any payload. The limiter is a token bucket kept in memory by the thehive-flow service, keyed by webhook and client IP address. It allows 120 requests per minute by default: the bucket starts full, refills continuously, and holds at most 1 minute of traffic, which is also the tolerated burst. A request over the limit receives a 429 response with a Retry-After: 60 header.

By default, the client IP address used as the key is the address of the TCP connection, not the X-Forwarded-For header, which a caller could forge. Requests reach the thehive-flow service through the shipped nginx and therefore all carry the proxy address. In practice, the limit is a per-webhook limit, shared by every caller of that webhook. To key the limit on the real caller instead, list the range of thehive-flow-network under api.public.trusted_proxies in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml. TheHive Flow then reads the caller address from the X-Forwarded-For header that nginx sets, as described in Trusted proxies.

The value of the limit can't be changed: every webhook applies the default of 120 requests per minute.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Nginx terminates TLS on port 443. Two modes are available, selected by init.sh:

  • Self-signed certificate, the default: init.sh generates a 365-day, 2048-bit RSA certificate for the configured nginx_server_name. Clients must either trust the certificate or turn off certificate verification.
  • Custom certificate: Place server.crt, server.key, and ca.pem in ./certificates/ before running init.sh. init.sh copies the files to nginx/certs/ and turns on the ssl_trusted_certificate directive automatically in the nginx configuration.

Internal service-to-service communication, from the thehive-flow service to PostgreSQL, Temporal, and the object storage, uses plain TCP on the isolated Docker network. The S3 endpoint is plain HTTP. No mTLS is used between internal services.

docs.title: Certificate for external webhook callers
docs.text:
As soon as a webhook is called from outside, the certificate nginx presents must be signed by an authority the caller trusts. That's a public certificate authority (CA) for a cloud service, or the internal certificate authority of your organization for an internal sender. Most senders refuse the self-signed certificate init.sh generates by default. Provide your own certificate, and renew it as described in TLS certificate renewal.

A recommended topology puts a reverse proxy or a load balancer of your own in front of TheHive Flow host: it carries the public certificate and forwards only /webhook/<id>. Set flow_public_url to its address so that webhook URLs point at it. TheHive keeps calling nginx directly: don't list the address of that proxy in nginx_thehive_addresses.

docs.title: TLS toward TheHive
docs.text:
When flow_thehive_url is an https:// address, the thehive-flow service validates TheHive certificate against the system trust store of its image, so a certificate signed by a public CA works as is. There's no option to turn off certificate verification on this channel.

For a certificate signed by an internal CA, mount the CA bundle into the container and point the SSL_CERT_FILE variable at it, in the thehive-flow service of docker-compose.yml or in a docker-compose.override.yml file. Then apply with docker compose up -d thehive-flow:

services:
  thehive-flow:
    volumes:
      - /path/to/internal-ca.pem:/etc/ssl/internal-ca.pem:ro
    environment:
      SSL_CERT_FILE: /etc/ssl/internal-ca.pem

The file replaces the system trust store for the whole process, so it must hold every CA the service needs to trust, including the public CAs used by the external systems your workflows call.

docs.title: Rotate secrets
docs.text: There's no scheduled rotation, and no tooling automates one: init.sh generates every secret once, and the procedures below rotate them manually.

docs.title: JWT signing key
docs.text:
The JWT key must be the same on TheHive Flow and TheHive simultaneously. In-flight requests fail during the brief rotation window.

  1. Generate a new key with openssl rand -hex 32.
  2. Update jwt_signing_key in .env.
  3. Update the TheHive configuration with the new key.

  4. Apply the change on both sides at the same time. Recreate the containers rather than restarting them, because a plain docker compose restart doesn't re-read .env. On TheHive Flow host:

    docker compose up -d thehive-flow

    On TheHive host:

    docker compose up -d thehive

docs.title: TheHive API key
docs.text:
Update the secret file, keeping it readable by its owner only:

printf '%s' '<thehive_api_key>' > ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key
chmod 600 ./thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key

Alternatively, update the value in .env:

thehive_api_key=<thehive_api_key>

The command that applies the change depends on where you put the key. After editing the secret file, restart the service so the file is read again:

docker compose restart thehive-flow

After editing .env, recreate the container, because a plain restart doesn't re-read .env:

docker compose up -d thehive-flow

docs.title: PostgreSQL passwords
docs.text:
The init.sh script aligns the thehive_flow and temporal database roles with the passwords in .env at each run, and renders the Temporal one into temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml. Rotating either password therefore takes an edit and a run of the script, during a short stop of the stack:

  1. Stop the services that use the passwords:

    docker compose stop thehive-flow temporal

  2. Set a new value for flow_db_password, temporal_db_password, or both in .env: openssl rand -hex 32 produces one.

  3. Run the script again. It keeps the other secrets, alters the roles, renders the Temporal configuration, recreates PostgreSQL, whose container carries the role passwords, and starts Temporal. Without a custom certificate, it also generates a new self-signed certificate: see TLS certificate renewal.

    bash ./scripts/init.sh

  4. Start the rest of the stack:

    docker compose up -d

The superuser password is different: PostgreSQL reads postgres_password at its first start only, and the script doesn't alter the postgres role. To rotate it, alter the role first, then update .env and recreate the container:

docker compose exec postgresql psql -U postgres -c "ALTER ROLE postgres PASSWORD '<new_password>';"

docs.title: TLS certificate renewal
docs.text:
For the self-signed certificate, which expires after 365 days, run init.sh again: when ./certificates/ holds no custom certificate, the script generates a new one at each run. Then restart nginx, which reads the certificate files from the mounted nginx/certs/ directory:

bash ./scripts/init.sh
docker compose restart nginx

For a custom certificate, place the new server.crt, server.key, and ca.pem set in ./certificates/, then run the same two commands: the script copies the files to nginx/certs/. Replacing the files in ./nginx/certs/ directly and restarting nginx works too. In both directories, keep server.key at mode 600. No other service downtime is required.

Every run of init.sh renews a self-signed certificate

The script doesn't check whether a self-signed certificate already exists. Every run without a custom certificate in ./certificates/ generates a new one, including the runs of an upgrade, a PostgreSQL password rotation, or a restore on another host. Nginx serves the new certificate at its next start. A TheHive configured to trust the specific certificate then rejects TheHive Flow until the new nginx/certs/server.crt is copied to TheHive host and TheHive restarted. Webhook callers that pin the certificate need the new one too. A custom certificate avoids the churn: the script copies the same files at each run.

docs.title: S3 secret access key
docs.text:
The key exists in two places that must agree: .env, which the thehive-flow service reads, and the S3 identity stored inside the object storage itself, which init-s3-store provisioned. Updating only .env leaves TheHive Flow authenticating with a key the storage rejects.

Update s3_secret_access_key in .env, then provision the identity on the store again and recreate the thehive-flow container so it picks up the new value:

docker compose up -d init-s3-store
docker compose up -d thehive-flow

up -d runs the provisioning container again even though it has already run and exited. Compose restarts a stopped one-shot service, and recreates it outright when its environment changed, which is the case here. Stored blobs are unaffected, because the identity governs access, not the content.

Rotating the secret under the same access key ID replaces it, and the previous secret stops working: that's the rotation path the stack supports. Changing s3_access_key_id instead adds a second access key: the provisioning step never removes a credential you stop referencing, so the previous key stays active on the store indefinitely, with its old secret. To retire an access key ID entirely, remove it explicitly.

The following command drops the identity and every access key under it. The -apply flag is required: without it, s3.configure runs in simulation mode and changes nothing.

docker compose exec s3-store \
  sh -c 'echo "s3.configure -user thehive-flow -delete -apply" | weed shell -master s3-store:9333'

Then provision the identity you want to keep:

docker compose up -d init-s3-store

Verify what the store holds before and after. The output contains secret keys in cleartext, so don't paste it into a ticket:

docker compose exec s3-store \
  sh -c 'echo "s3.configure" | weed shell -master s3-store:9333'
Next steps
  • Authentication Between TheHive Flow Components
  • TheHive Flow Environment Variables
  • TheHive Flow Application Configuration
  • Monitor TheHive Flow
  • Troubleshoot TheHive Flow

docs.title: Troubleshoot TheHive Flow
docs.text:
6.0 One

When a TheHive Flow deployment misbehaves, run the first steps below to locate the failing component, then look up your symptom in the tables.

Docker Compose deployment

The settings and procedures below apply to the Docker Compose deployment of TheHive Flow. On a Kubernetes deployment, see Configuration and operations on Kubernetes instead.

docs.title: First steps for any incident
docs.text:
1. Check the container state:

    docker compose ps -a

  2. Check the readiness:

    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz

  3. Check the recent logs:

    docker compose logs --tail=100 thehive-flow

  4. Collect the logs of every service, as described in Collect logs during an incident.

docs.title: Startup and initialization
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix init.sh stops with Invalid TheHive URL The prompt for TheHive URL was left empty, or the value isn't an http:// or https:// address Run bash ./scripts/init.sh again and enter TheHive address as reachable from the thehive-flow container, for example http://<thehive_host>:9000 init.sh stops with Cannot read the Docker socket group The user running the script can't run Docker commands, or the Docker socket isn't at /var/run/docker.sock Check that docker run hello-world works for that user, then run the script again init.sh stops with Initialisation did not complete due to permissions issue The files of the profile directory aren't owned by the user running the script, or their permissions are off, and the fix was declined Run bash ./scripts/check_permissions.sh and accept the fix, or run init.sh again and answer y The thehive-flow service can't reach TheHive flow_thehive_url is wrong TheHive Flow reaches TheHive over an explicit URL, without a shared Docker network. Set flow_thehive_url to TheHive address in .env, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow to recreate the container with the new value An Analyzer or Responder action node fails on a DNS error flow_thehive_url points at a host name that doesn't resolve The /readyz endpoint doesn't probe TheHive, so it stays 200 and the stack looks healthy. Fix the value in .env, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow The thehive-flow service exits at startup with invalid api.public.url flow_public_url in .env isn't an absolute http or https URL, or it carries credentials, a query, or a fragment Fix the value as described in Public URL, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow A webhook caller receives a 404 response, or can't connect, on the webhook URL The public URL doesn't match the address callers reach TheHive Flow at, typically behind another reverse proxy or a path prefix Set flow_public_url in .env to the public address, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow The thehive-flow service exits at startup because no TheHive API key is set Neither the thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key file nor thehive_api_key in .env holds a key. The init.sh script warns about it at the end of its run Provision the key, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow The temporal service exits with no usable database connection found temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml is missing or holds a stale password Run bash ./scripts/init.sh again: it renders the file from its template with the current password. Verify with ls -la temporal/config/temporal-server.yaml: the file must exist, at mode 600, owned by the user the stack runs as The thehive-flow service logs Namespace default is not found The Temporal default namespace wasn't created during init Run bash ./scripts/init.sh again, or create it manually: docker compose --profile admin run --rm temporal-admin temporal operator namespace create -n default --address temporal:7233 The thehive-flow service exits with in-memory blob store is a unit-test-only backend The blobstore: block is missing from thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml, or was overridden to memory TheHive Flow requires a durable back end, s3 or local. Restore the shipped blobstore: block and run docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow The thehive-flow service exits at startup on a blobstore.local.path error The back end is local and the path is missing, relative, or points to a directory that doesn't exist or isn't writable The local filesystem back end creates nothing itself: the path must be absolute, and the directory must exist, be writable by TheHive Flow, and pass the write test performed at startup. Fix the volume mount or its permissions, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow A run stays in the run list but opening it shows This execution log is not available anymore, and the log repeats hourly: retention sync: Temporal namespace retention differs from runs.retention thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml lost the modules.runs block. The Temporal namespace therefore keeps a shorter retention than the run list, and Temporal deletes the history first. Nothing crashes: the only signal is the hourly warning Restore the modules.runs block and run docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow. Runs whose history is already deleted stay listed, without their details, until modules.runs.retention expires them. Raising the retention doesn't bring their history back The thehive-flow service exits at startup on a bucket or credentials error init-s3-store didn't complete, or the credentials in .env no longer match the identity stored on the object storage Check docker compose logs init-s3-store. Provision again with docker compose up -d init-s3-store, then docker compose up -d thehive-flow init-s3-store logs FATAL: s3.configure failed The s3-store service rejected the identity setup Check docker compose logs s3-store: the service must be healthy first. Then run docker compose up -d init-s3-store init-s3-store logs FATAL: the thehive-flow S3 access key is absent from the store The identity setup reported no error but the access key isn't there Check docker compose logs s3-store. If the store is healthy, recreate it and provision again: docker compose up -d --force-recreate s3-store && docker compose up -d init-s3-store init-s3-store logs FATAL: bucket thehive-flow does not exist Bucket creation silently failed: the store answered but didn't create it Check docker compose logs s3-store and the free space of the disk holding ./s3-store/data, then run docker compose up -d init-s3-store init-s3-store shows Exited (0) in docker compose ps -a Normal. It's a one-shot provisioning container: it configures the identity, asserts the bucket exists, then exits Nothing to do. Only a non-zero exit code is a failure init-s3-store never finishes and shows no exit code It can't reach the s3-store master. Each provisioning call is bounded by a timeout Check docker compose logs s3-store and docker compose ps s3-store. The FATAL message appears once the timeout fires

docs.title: Docker engine access
docs.text:
TheHive Flow launches containers on the host Docker daemon to run Python and JavaScript code transformations. See Docker engine access for how the socket is shared with the container.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A code transformation fails with permission denied on the Docker socket The group of the Docker socket changed since the initialization, so docker_gid in .env no longer matches it Run bash ./scripts/init.sh again to detect the group, then docker compose up -d thehive-flow A code transformation fails with Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock The socket isn't mounted, or the Docker daemon doesn't listen on /var/run/docker.sock on this host Run docker inspect thehive-flow and verify the socket appears under Mounts. The shipped docker-compose.yml mounts /var/run/docker.sock: on a host whose daemon listens elsewhere, point the volume entry of the thehive-flow service at the actual socket path

docs.title: Authentication and JWT
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix The log shows token signature is invalid JWT key mismatch Verify both sides use the exact same jwt_signing_key value, and check for stray quotes in the Docker Compose environment variable syntax Requests from TheHive are rejected with an expired token error Clock skew between TheHive and TheHive Flow hosts Tokens expire 1 minute after signing, with a 30-second leeway. Compare date on both hosts and synchronize them with NTP An Analyzer or Responder action node fails with 401 The API key that TheHive Flow uses to call TheHive is wrong or revoked Check that thehive-flow/secret/thehive-api-key holds a valid TheHive API key, then run docker compose restart thehive-flow. If thehive_api_key is set in .env, it wins over the file: fix it there and run docker compose up -d thehive-flow instead TheHive can't reach TheHive Flow over HTTPS with a self-signed certificate The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) running TheHive rejects the untrusted certificate See TLS with a self-signed certificate: turn off certificate verification or trust the specific certificate

docs.title: HTTP errors
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix A 500 response returns only {"message":"Internal Server Error"} with no detail By design, 5xx bodies hide internals in production to avoid leaking sensitive data The real cause is always in the logs: docker compose logs --tail=200 thehive-flow. To surface the full error over HTTP without turning off authentication, temporarily add BEEFLOW_VERBOSE_ERRORS: "true" to the environment: block of the thehive-flow service, then run docker compose up -d thehive-flow. This is a debug aid: remove it once done

docs.title: Health and readiness
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix /readyz returns 503 TheHive Flow is still starting or is shutting down, or PostgreSQL or Temporal isn't reachable If the response body reports modules as not ready and the other checks as ok, startup is still in progress, which can take several minutes: wait and retry. Otherwise, check docker compose logs thehive-flow for readyz check failed lines: their check field names the failing dependency, db or temporal. At startup, the same failures appear as failed to ping database or failed to create temporal client. Also check docker compose ps for unhealthy services /livez returns connection refused The thehive-flow container is down or crashed Run docker compose up -d thehive-flow and check docker compose logs thehive-flow for crash details The thehive-flow container restarts in a loop Startup error, such as a database that isn't healthy yet, a missing API key, or a configuration error Check docker compose logs thehive-flow for the failed to start line, logged at ERROR level: its error field gives the cause. Look it up in Startup and initialization

docs.title: Check the path from TheHive host
docs.text:
When TheHive reports TheHive Flow in error, start from TheHive host and call the version endpoint through nginx. The endpoint needs no token, so the check isolates the network and nginx from the JWT and TheHive configuration:

curl -sk https://<nginx_server_name>/api/v1/version
  • A JSON document whose version field holds the version of TheHive Flow means the path is open. The problem is on TheHive side: see Authentication and JWT, and check flow.url in TheHive configuration.
  • A 403 means the address TheHive host calls from isn't in nginx_thehive_addresses: see the first rows of the table below. With a TheHive cluster, run the check from every node.
  • A connection error means nginx isn't reachable: see the last rows of the table below.
  • Without -k, a failure before the request is sent means curl doesn't trust the certificate. TheHive hits the same failure: see TLS with a self-signed certificate.

Expected output

The version endpoint returns the version of TheHive Flow and the versions of the services it reached, trimmed here to the relevant fields:

{"version":"6.0.0","dependencies":{"postgresql":"...","docker":"...","temporal":"..."}}

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix TheHive can't reach TheHive Flow and nginx answers 403 to TheHive requests while webhooks work nginx_thehive_addresses in .env is empty, doesn't list the address TheHive calls from, or lists only entries nginx skipped because they cover the Docker network gateway Set nginx_thehive_addresses to the addresses TheHive calls from, then run docker compose up -d --no-deps nginx. The 40-thehive-allow.sh lines of docker compose logs --no-log-prefix nginx show what nginx allowed and skipped The nginx log shows access forbidden by rule for TheHive requests The client: address of that log line isn't in nginx_thehive_addresses If it's the gateway of thehive-flow-network, see the next row. Otherwise, add that address to nginx_thehive_addresses in .env, then run docker compose up -d --no-deps nginx The client: of refused TheHive requests in the nginx log is the .1 address of thehive-flow-network Docker relays the connection through docker-proxy and masks the source address Don't add that address: nginx skips it. See TheHive address filtering At start, nginx logs skipping '<entry>' An entry of nginx_thehive_addresses isn't an IPv4 address or range, or covers the Docker network gateway Fix the entry in .env, then run docker compose up -d --no-deps nginx Nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway The thehive-flow service isn't running or isn't ready yet Run docker compose restart thehive-flow and wait for /livez to return 200 Nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway right after a restart of the thehive-flow service Nginx still uses the IP address it resolved before the restart, for up to 10 seconds Wait a few seconds and retry. You don't need to restart nginx Nginx returns 504 Gateway Timeout The request took longer than 600 s Check the workflow run duration. If the duration is legitimate, increase proxy_read_timeout in nginx/templates/default.conf.template An interrupted upload returns an HTML error page instead of a JSON error Nginx buffers request bodies, so it absorbs a stalled upload at its own client_body_timeout and answers before TheHive Flow sees it This is expected in this topology. TheHive Flow returns the JSON 408 for a stalled body transfer only when it's exposed directly, or behind a proxy configured to stream request bodies through TLS handshake error in the browser The browser doesn't trust the self-signed certificate Accept the browser security warning, or deploy a certificate signed by a certificate authority (CA) Port 443 isn't reachable from outside the host The port isn't open in the host firewall Open the port: firewall-cmd --add-port=443/tcp --permanent && firewall-cmd --reload on RHEL, or ufw allow 443 on Debian and Ubuntu

docs.title: Outbound connections
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix A workflow step fails with egress guard: outbound connection to non-public address blocked, for example an HTTP request node calling TheHive on a private network, or an AI node calling a locally hosted LLM provider The step targets an address that resolves to a non-public IP address. By design, nodes that open outbound connections can't reach loopback, link-local, private, carrier-grade NAT, or reserved addresses unless the range is allowlisted Add the target range to the egress allowlist in thehive-flow/config/thehive-flow.yml, then run docker compose up -d --force-recreate thehive-flow

docs.title: Temporal and workflows
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix The temporal service exits with sql schema version compatibility check failed: version mismatch The Temporal Server image moved to a new minor version without the schema upgrade Run the Temporal schema upgrade for the new version, then docker compose up -d temporal A workflow run is stuck indefinitely The Temporal worker isn't polling the task queue Run docker compose restart thehive-flow. If the issue persists, check the Temporal logs for the workflow history The Temporal logs show history size exceeds warn limit A workflow history passed 10 MB, for example through a large loop. Above 50 MB, Temporal logs history size exceeds error limit and terminates the workflow itself No action is needed: above 50 MB, Temporal terminates the workflow. To stop it sooner, terminate it: docker compose --profile admin run --rm temporal-admin temporal workflow terminate --workflow-id <workflow_id> --reason "history limit" --address temporal:7233. If a workflow regularly reaches the warning, reduce the data it carries between steps With the blob store on the local back end, workflow steps reading files fail with a file-not-found error The processes don't all see the same directory, because the deployment splits them across hosts or volumes, or the database was restored without the matching blob directory Nothing detects this at startup. The local filesystem back end requires every process to share one directory on one host. Back up and restore the database and the blob directory together

docs.title: Disk and resources
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Disk full on the host The PostgreSQL data, the blob store data, Docker logs, or backup folders grow unbounded Check du -sh ./postgresql/data ./s3-store/data and docker system df. Rotate old backups. Shorten run retention by lowering modules.runs.retention: read the warning there first, because shortening deletes history. Configure Docker log rotation The blob store directory keeps growing Files follow run retention, so a long retention or a burst of large files fills the directory. Deletions may also be failing, for example when the S3 identity lacks the delete permission Check with du -sh ./s3-store/data. Look for blob-drain: could not delete file in docker compose logs thehive-flow, and for files_failed and files_pending on the blob-drain: processed queued file deletions lines. See Blob store volume sizing The OOM killer terminates a container The memory limit is too low for the workload Check docker stats --no-stream, raise the memory limit of the affected service in docker-compose.yml, under deploy.resources.limits.memory and memswap_limit together, then run docker compose up -d <service>. For the thehive-flow service, raise GOMEMLIMIT with them The OOM killer terminates the s3-store container Concurrent request volume exceeded the memory limit of the service, which is unrelated to how much data the store holds Confirm with docker inspect thehive-flow-s3-store --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'. Raise deploy.resources.limits.memory and memswap_limit together in docker-compose.yml: raising only the first lets the container swap instead of failing loudly

docs.title: Get supportNext steps
docs.text:
If the steps above don't resolve the issue, collect the logs of every service as described in Collect logs during an incident, and open a ticket with the archive attached. Describe the symptom, when it started, and the steps that reproduce it. Never attach .env, the files of thehive-flow/secret/, or the rendered Temporal configuration.

  • Monitor TheHive Flow
  • Deploy TheHive Flow with Docker Compose
  • TheHive Flow Environment Variables

docs.title: About TheHive Flow
docs.text:
6.0 One

Security operations involve repetitive and time-sensitive tasks: creating alerts from external events, triaging alerts, enriching observables, and notifying teams. TheHive Flow is the workflow orchestrator integrated with TheHive. It automates these tasks so your team can focus on investigation instead of manual coordination. Using a visual editor, you connect trigger, flow, transformation, action, and integration nodes into automated pipelines that run when events occur.

Relationship to existing automation features

TheHive Flow workflows cover most of the use cases handled by existing automation features in TheHive, including notifications, alert feeders, functions, and Cortex responders. These features remain available and usable on their own. TheHive Flow adds multi-step logic, conditional branching, scheduled execution, and a visual workflow editor, all natively within TheHive, without requiring code or an external tool.

docs.title: Managing workflows
docs.text:
Workflows are organized within organizations and displayed in the Flow view. They're shared across the organization and visible to all members with sufficient permissions. There's no personal or user-isolated workspace. You can tag workflows to categorize them, and set their status:

  • Enabled: Runs automatically when triggered, and on demand from the workflow editor or a case or alert page.
  • Disabled: Never runs. Its triggers are ignored and manual runs are unavailable, so it can be edited without affecting production. A Subworkflow node calling it fails. Turning off a workflow doesn't delete it. Its configuration is fully preserved, so turning it off is the recommended way to pause a workflow during maintenance or testing.

No versioning

There's no workflow versioning. Any modification is applied immediately to the active workflow. Duplicate a workflow before making significant changes. To keep a history, export your workflows and version them in a Git repository.

Workflows from other TheHive instances or organizations can be imported. To start from a working example instead of building from scratch, import one of the ready-made workflow templates covering common security automation scenarios.

docs.title: Workflow components
docs.text:
Every workflow follows the same structure: it starts with a trigger, optionally passes through flow and transformation nodes to route and reshape data, and ends with action or integration nodes that produce results.

  • Trigger: Starts the workflow when an event occurs. Every workflow has exactly one trigger node.
  • Flow: Controls execution paths by branching on conditions, looping over lists, pausing, or calling another workflow.
  • Transformation: Processes data between steps by setting local variables or running Python or JavaScript scripts.
  • Action: Performs generic operations such as sending HTTP requests, emails, or chat messages, running Cortex analyzers and responders, or calling an LLM.
  • Integration: Performs operations in TheHive or a third-party product through its API.

Each node receives input from the previous step and passes output to the next. Outputs are JSON values, so they can be reused anywhere downstream as output variables and read or reshaped with jq expressions.

Example: Automated alert creation and triage

docs.title: Trigger nodes
docs.text:
Every workflow requires a trigger node. TheHive automatically creates one when you create a workflow. Only one trigger node exists per workflow, but multiple triggers can be configured within this node to provide different entry points for workflow execution. Multiple triggers work as OR conditions: any one of them independently starts the workflow.

Available triggers are:

  • Webhook: Listens for incoming HTTP requests from external systems or TheHive itself, and automatically starts the workflow when the webhook URL receives a request. Accepts the GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, and OPTIONS methods unless you restrict the accepted methods. The webhook URL points at TheHive Flow, not at TheHive, and is reachable without signing in to TheHive, so the trigger carries its own authentication method.
  • Scheduler: Starts the workflow on a recurring schedule. A trigger node can carry multiple scheduler blocks, each running independently on its own schedule.

Calling a workflow from another workflow

To call a workflow from another workflow of the same organization, use a Subworkflow flow node. To start a workflow of another organization, use an HTTP request action node to send a request to the webhook URL of that workflow.

Regardless of trigger configuration, enabled workflows can always be run manually from the workflow editor or from a case or alert page in TheHive.

docs.title: Flow nodes
docs.text:
Flow nodes control how workflows branch, loop, process multiple items, pause, or call another workflow.

Available flows are:

  • For each: Iterates over each item in an array or object that matches a jq expression, and executes the same sequence of nodes for each entry. Supports sequential or parallel execution modes. In sequential mode, the loop stops on the first error. In parallel mode, iterations run concurrently up to a configurable limit. The first failure cancels the remaining iterations. The node waits for the running ones to stop, then reports the errors from all failed iterations together.
  • If: Evaluates a jq expression and directs execution down two branches based on the boolean result, true or false. The node produces an output after one branch finishes, so the workflow can continue after the conditional logic.
  • Sleep: Pauses the execution path for a specified duration, then continues with the next node.
  • Subworkflow: Calls another workflow of the same organization and waits for it to finish. Passes values to the input variables of the called workflow, along with the trigger payload of the calling workflow. Returns the exit variables of the called workflow as outputs.

An execution path ends when it reaches a node with no next step.

docs.title: Transformation nodes
docs.text:
Transformation nodes process or manipulate data within workflows. They perform custom operations that modify, extract, or format information as it moves through the workflow.

Available transformations are:

  • Set local variable: Creates local variables. Returns the assigned value as an output.
  • Python code: Executes Python scripts within the workflow. Returns the script output, exit code, and any variables you expose with flow.set() as outputs.
  • JavaScript code: Executes JavaScript scripts within the workflow. Returns the script output, exit code, and any variables you expose with flow.set() as outputs.

docs.title: Action nodes
docs.text:
Action nodes perform operations that interact with TheHive or external systems. They change the environment or trigger downstream processes.

Available actions are:

  • HTTP request: Sends HTTP requests to external APIs, or to TheHive API for endpoints the TheHive integration node doesn't cover, using any standard HTTP method. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Send email: Sends emails using the SMTP configuration from TheHive.
  • Analyzer: Triggers Cortex analyzers on observables. Lists analyzers available across all configured Cortex instances for the organization, automatically filtered by observable type. If the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) or Permissible Actions Protocol (PAP) level of the observable isn't compatible with the analyzer, Cortex returns an error at execution. Returns analyzer reports as outputs.
  • Responder: Triggers Cortex responders on alerts, cases, observables, tasks, or task logs. Lists responders available across all configured Cortex instances for the organization, automatically filtered by entity type. If the TLP or PAP level of the entity isn't compatible with the responder, Cortex returns an error at execution. Returns responder execution reports as outputs.
  • AI: Sends a message to a large language model (LLM) using one of the LLM providers configured in TheHive by an administrator, and returns its response, optionally constrained to a structured output schema. Returns the response text, structured result, finish reason, and token usage as outputs.

docs.title: Integration nodes
docs.text:
Integration nodes perform operations in TheHive or third-party products. Each integration node targets one product API and exposes its operations as dedicated actions selected within the node. Integrations tagged Beta were built from the provider's API documentation, not tested against a live environment: check them before using them in production. If you have access to a live environment, help validate the integration and share your feedback with the StrangeBee Support team.

Available integrations are:

  • TheHive: Performs operations in TheHive through TheHive API, such as creating, updating, querying, or deleting cases, alerts, tasks, and observables, managing comments and task logs, or starting a Cortex job. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs. To perform an operation this node doesn't manage, use the HTTP request action node instead.
  • Splunk: Performs operations through the Splunk REST API, such as creating and following search jobs, running searches, listing indexes and fired alerts, submitting events, and updating Splunk Enterprise Security findings and investigations. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Microsoft Defender for Endpoint: Performs operations through the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API, such as listing, retrieving, and updating alerts, running response actions on devices, and creating indicators. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Microsoft Defender (Graph Security API): Performs operations through the Microsoft Graph security API, such as listing, retrieving, and updating Microsoft Defender XDR alerts and incidents. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Microsoft Entra ID: Performs operations through the Microsoft Graph API, such as looking up users, sign-ins, audit logs, devices, and risk detections, and taking account actions such as Disable User or Force Password Reset. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Microsoft Sentinel: Performs operations through the Microsoft Sentinel REST API, such as listing, retrieving, and updating incidents, managing incident comments, and listing or writing watchlists. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Recorded Future: Performs operations through the Recorded Future API, such as enriching and triaging indicators in bulk, looking up domains, IP addresses, hashes, and URLs, and searching analyst notes and threat maps. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • VirusTotal: Performs operations through the VirusTotal API, such as scanning URLs and files, and retrieving domain, IP address, file, and analysis reports. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Beta CrowdStrike Falcon: Performs operations through the CrowdStrike Falcon APIs, such as querying devices and vulnerabilities, running response actions on hosts, querying and updating alerts, and looking up threat intelligence indicators. It also manages custom indicators of compromise (IOCs) and detonates file samples in the Falcon sandbox. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Elastic Security: Performs operations through the Elasticsearch API, such as searching and indexing documents, running ES|QL queries, and listing Elastic Security detection alerts. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • HarfangLab EDR: Performs operations through the HarfangLab API, such as searching and isolating endpoints, managing alerts, running jobs on agents, searching telemetry, managing IOC rules, and listing Sigma rules. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Jira Cloud: Performs operations through the Jira Cloud platform REST API, such as creating, editing, transitioning, and searching issues, managing comments, attachments, worklogs, watchers, and votes, and browsing projects and issue metadata. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Slack: Performs operations through the Slack Web API, such as posting, updating, and deleting messages, managing reactions, reading threads and channel history, and looking up channels and users. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Beta Microsoft Teams: Performs operations through the Microsoft Graph API, such as sending, replying to, updating, and deleting channel messages, and sending chat messages. It also creates chats and channels, adds team and channel members, and lists teams, channels, and messages. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • ServiceNow: Performs operations through the ServiceNow Table and Attachment APIs, such as creating and updating incidents and change requests, and searching configuration items, users, and user groups. It also manages record attachments, and reads and writes records in any table. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • OpenCTI: Performs operations through the OpenCTI GraphQL and TAXII 2.1 APIs, such as searching entities, observables, indicators, and relationships, and creating observables, indicators, reports, incidents, relationships, and sightings. It also manages labels, markings, and notes, and requests enrichment from connectors. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.
  • Wazuh: Performs operations through the Wazuh server API, such as listing, adding, restarting, and deleting agents, and running active responses and file integrity monitoring scans. It also reads security configuration assessment results, rules, CDB lists, and manager logs. Returns the response body, status code, and headers as outputs.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Workflows in TheHive Flow support seven types of variables:

Type Scope Displayed reference Description Input variables Single workflow $input.<field_name> Input values passed into the workflow when it starts. Declare and assign them in the Workflow input section when configuring a Webhook trigger, with a jq expression applied to the incoming request. A Subworkflow node in another workflow can also assign them when it calls the workflow. Use the workflow settings to manage input variables for all nodes of the workflow, for example to rename, describe, or delete them. A run from a case or alert page assigns the entity identifier to the case_id or alert_id input variable when the workflow declares it. Trigger payload Single workflow $input.payload Built-in variable automatically available in every run, carrying the data received by the trigger that started the run, such as the JSON body, headers, and query parameters of a webhook request, or the case or alert identifier of a run from a case or alert page. Requires no declaration and no assignment. See Access the Trigger Payload for the available fields. Exit variables Single workflow — Output values the workflow computes when it completes, stored with the run. Declared in workflow settings as named jq expressions that are evaluated at the end of the run. When the workflow is called by a Subworkflow node, they're returned to the calling workflow as outputs of that node. Local variables Single workflow $<node_name>.<field_name> User-defined values scoped to a single workflow run, created during execution with a Set local variable transformation node. Output variables Single workflow $<node_name>.<output_name> Values a node produces automatically when it runs, available to every later node. The available outputs depend on the node type. See each node's configuration page for details. In a For each loop, the current item and its key are available as the item and idx outputs of the loop node, within the Loop branch only. Loop output variables Single workflow $<node_name>.<variable_name> Values declared on a For each node to collect results across iterations. Each is a named jq expression evaluated after every iteration, and the values are aggregated across all iterations and available in the nodes that follow the loop. Global variables Organization Visible: $global.<variable_name> / Secret: $secret.<variable_name> Values defined once at the organization level and shared across all workflows. Managed from the Global variables tab and can't be modified within workflows. They can be visible or secret. Secret variables hold sensitive data such as API keys, passwords, or SSL/TLS certificates. Their values are never displayed in the interface and never appear in execution logs or API responses.

Insert variables with the $var button, or enter $ in a field and start entering the variable name to filter the suggestions. In both cases, select one of the suggestions to insert the reference. It can't be entered in full manually.

An inserted variable is highlighted in the field. How you read a nested field from it depends on its type:

  • A direct variable, highlighted in green: Appears in the condition of an If node, the Field to iterate over and the loop output variables of a For each node, and the exit variables of a workflow. Read a nested field by entering .<field_name> right after the reference, directly in the field.
  • A jq expression, highlighted in blue: The variable wrapped in a jq expression. To read a nested field or transform the value, select the expression and edit the jq inside it. The available functions are listed in Jq Functions. Always add fields inside the expression itself. Text entered after the expression is treated as literal text, not as part of the expression, and the node fails at execution with a type mismatch. You can also select the + button to write the variable and the field together in one step.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Workflows pass JSON values between nodes. Some values don't fit that model well: a large API response, a binary download, or a document uploaded to a webhook. TheHive Flow stores these values as files and passes a file reference between nodes instead of the content itself. In most workflows, this is invisible: reading a variable returns its value whether it's stored inline or as a file.

A value is stored as a file in the following cases:

  • Large node outputs: By default, any node output whose content reaches 1 MiB is automatically stored as a file. Below that size, the value is stored inline.
  • Binary or multipart HTTP responses: An HTTP request node response body that isn't valid text is stored as a file regardless of its size. Parts of a multipart/* response body that are large or not JSON are stored as files too.
  • Files uploaded to a webhook: A file sent with the HTTP request that triggers a Webhook trigger is stored as a file. Declare an input variable of type Raw in the workflow settings, then assign it with $request.files.<field> in the Workflow input section of the trigger, so that its metadata is available in the variable suggestions.
  • Files written by code nodes: A file registered with flow.set_file_from_path() in a Python code or JavaScript code node.

Stored files are capped at 25 MiB by default. A value above that limit is rejected.

Reading a variable whose value is stored as a file works the same way as reading any other variable, within a size limit:

  • If the file content is JSON and doesn't exceed 1.5 MiB, the default limit, referencing the variable returns its content transparently. Nested fields can be read as usual, for example $<node_name>.body.<field_name>.
  • If the file content is larger than 1.5 MiB or isn't JSON, referencing the variable returns the file reference itself, a small object describing the file, instead of the content. In that case, read the file in a code node with flow.get_file_path(). You can also forward the reference as is to a node that accepts files, such as the Multipart parts field of an HTTP request node.

docs.title: File metadata
docs.text:
Every value stored as a file exposes its metadata through the read-only $files namespace, which mirrors the node outputs and input variables:

  • $files.<node_name>.<output_name>: Metadata of a node output stored as a file.
  • $files.input.<field_name>: Metadata of an input variable stored as a file.

The metadata contains the following fields:

Field Type Description name string The file name. size number The file size in bytes. content_type string The MIME type of the file content. sha256sum string The SHA-256 checksum of the file content. created_at string When the file was stored. created_by string The node that produced the file.

The $files namespace never holds file content. Reading content goes through the regular variable reference, as described above.

In the variable suggestions, these metadata references appear in a dedicated Files group. The group lists an entry for every output that could be stored as a file. TheHive Flow decides whether to store a value as a file only when the workflow runs, based on the size and format of the real value.

Files entries resolve to nothing for inline values

A $files reference returns metadata only when the value is stored as a file. For a value stored inline, the common case for small JSON, the same reference resolves to nothing. To read the value itself, always pick the suggestion from the node's own group, not from the Files group. The exception is a field that takes a file, such as the File field of an integration action: there, both groups insert the file itself.

docs.title: Timeout, retry, and backoff configuration
docs.text:
• A timeout defines the maximum duration an operation is allowed to run before it's automatically stopped and marked as timed out. Timeouts can be configured at both the workflow level and the node level. When both levels define a timeout, the shortest duration applies.

  • A retry defines the number of times a failed node execution is attempted again. A retry delay specifies the wait time between retry attempts. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Retries can be configured only at the node level.

  • A backoff defines the coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt. Backoff can be configured only at the node level.

docs.title: Execution mode
docs.text:
When several branches converge on the same node, its execution mode controls whether the node runs for each branch or once for all of them:

  • Execute once per branch: The node runs once for each incoming branch. This is the default when the execution mode isn't configured.
  • Wait for all branches: The node waits for all incoming branches to complete, then runs once.

The execution mode is configured in the Add options of the node, under Execution configuration. It's available on most action, integration, and transformation nodes.

docs.title: Execution tracking
docs.text:
Executions are asynchronous: triggering a workflow doesn't block TheHive interface.

Each workflow execution generates an execution record that captures the status of the workflow and each of its nodes. Execution logs are available in three places:

  • The Execution Logs tab in the Flow view lists the executions of every workflow in the organization for the configured retention period. Use it to spot failures and open a specific run.
  • The Executions tab inside a workflow shows the runs of that workflow in detail. Select a node to display its start and end dates, duration, status, and input and output data.
  • The Automations tab of a case or alert in TheHive lists the runs launched on that case or alert.

docs.title: PermissionsNext steps
docs.text:
• Only users with the manageOrchestrator/readWorkflows permission can access the Flow view and see workflows.
  • Only users with the manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows permission can create, modify, or run workflows in TheHive Flow.
  • Only users with the manageOrchestrator/deleteWorkflows permission can delete workflows in TheHive Flow.
  • Only users with the manageOrchestrator/readVariables permission can access the Global variables tab and see global variables.
  • Only users with the manageOrchestrator/writeVariables permission can create or modify global variables in TheHive Flow.
  • Only users with the manageOrchestrator/deleteVariables permission can delete global variables in TheHive Flow.

The Flow entry in the sidebar, and the Workflows and Execution Logs tabs, require the manageOrchestrator/readWorkflows permission.

docs.title: Access the Trigger Payload
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Every workflow run in TheHive Flow, whatever started it, exposes a built-in $input.payload variable carrying the data received by the trigger that started the run. Unlike input variables, it requires no declaration and no assignment. Insert it in a node with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting it from the suggestions. An inserted reference is displayed as $input.payload.

docs.title: Fields available in every run
docs.text:
• trigger_kind: How the run started, with webhook for a Webhook trigger, schedule for a Scheduler trigger, or user for a manual run from the workflow editor or a case or alert page
  • trigger_id: The identifier of the trigger that started the run, or of the user for a manual run
  • triggered_at: The UTC timestamp of when the run was triggered

A Scheduler trigger adds no fields beyond these.

docs.title: Additional fields from a Webhook trigger
docs.text:
• body: The JSON body of the incoming request
  • headers: The request headers. Credential headers such as Authorization or Cookie are redacted.
  • query: The query string parameters of the webhook URL
  • method: The HTTP method of the request
  • form: The form fields of a request sent as multipart/form-data
  • body_kind: How the request body reached the payload

Secrets in the payload

The payload is stored with the run for the run retention period, and every user who can read workflows can see it. Only credential headers are redacted, including the header the webhook authenticates on. A secret sent in the body, the query string, or a form field is stored in clear.

The body field is present only when the request body is valid JSON small enough to stay inline. The body_kind field is always present and reports which of the four cases applies:

  • inline: The body is valid JSON small enough to stay inline, and body holds its parsed value.
  • promoted: The body isn't inline JSON, whether a non-JSON content type at any size, invalid JSON, JSON null, or JSON at or above the inline limit. body is absent.
  • empty: The request carried no readable body, either none at all or a multipart/form-data body, whose parts reach the payload as form instead. body is absent.
  • too_large: The whole payload exceeded its 256 KiB limit, so the body was dropped to fit. body is absent.

When the body isn't in the payload, assign it to an input variable with $request.body in the Workflow input section of the Webhook trigger instead.

docs.title: Additional fields from a manual run
docs.text:
A manual run adds the variables supplied with the run, by name. A run from a case or alert page adds the entity identifier. A run from the workflow editor adds nothing, because no input can be passed there.

  • payload_trimmed: Set to true when the supplied variables exceeded the payload size limit and some were dropped to fit. It reports that a drop happened, not which fields went, and it's absent when nothing was dropped.

docs.title: Payload of a called workflow
docs.text: A workflow called by a Subworkflow node has no trigger of its own for that run. It receives the payload of the calling workflow, whole and unchanged, including the trigger_kind, trigger_id, and triggered_at fields of the calling run. The calling workflow can't modify it. To send other values to the called workflow, use its input variables.

docs.title: Inspect the payload of a past runNext steps
docs.text:
To check the payload a manual or Webhook run received, open the run in the Executions tab of the workflow and select the trigger node. The Input section of its execution details displays the payload. The execution details of a Scheduler run don't display the payload, only the Current interval of the trigger. For more details, see Display Workflow Execution Logs.

  • Manage Input and Exit Variables

docs.title: Add a Trigger
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Define how your workflow automatically starts in TheHive Flow. A workflow can have multiple triggers configured simultaneously, working as OR conditions: any one of them independently starts the workflow.

Manual trigger from the workflow editor

The trigger node always lists a Manual entry, alongside any triggers you configure. It requires no configuration and can't be removed: you can manually run a workflow from the workflow editor even without configuring any triggers.

docs.title: Add a Webhook trigger
docs.text:
Configure a Webhook trigger that starts the workflow automatically when the webhook URL receives an HTTP request, from an external system or TheHive itself.

The webhook URL points at TheHive Flow, not at TheHive, so the calling system must be able to reach TheHive Flow.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. In the trigger node, select Add a trigger.

  4. In the Select a trigger drawer, select Webhook.

  5. Optional: In the Allowed HTTP methods field, select which of GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, and OPTIONS the webhook accepts.

    Leave the field empty to accept any of these methods. Once you restrict the list, the webhook rejects every other method with a 403 response.

  6. Copy the URL from the Webhook URL field.

  7. Configure the webhook URL in the appropriate location:

    • For external system events: Paste the copied webhook URL into your external system following its documentation.
    • For TheHive events: Create a notification with a Webhook notifier. When configuring the notifier, add a webhook endpoint and paste the copied webhook URL into the URL field.

  8. Optional: To assign values to the workflow's input variables, go to the Workflow input section. It lists every input variable declared for the workflow, each with its own field. To declare a new input variable, select , enter its name in the Input variable field, select its type, then select Save. The Raw type isn't available here. To receive a file uploaded with the request, declare a Raw input variable in the workflow settings first, then assign it with $request.files.<field>.

    Edit input variables

    The Workflow input section declares new input variables and assigns their values. To manage input variables for all nodes of the workflow, for example to rename, describe, or delete them, use the workflow settings.

    In the field of each input variable, enter a jq expression that defines what value to assign from the incoming request. You can transform the value with the functions listed in Jq Functions. The incoming request exposes the following references:

    • $request.body: The entire request body
    • $request.body.<field>: A specific field
    • $request.headers["<header_name>"]: A specific HTTP header from the request. Enter the header name with a capital letter at the start of each hyphen-separated part, for example X-Api-Key.
    • $request.query.<parameter_name>: A specific query string parameter from the webhook URL
    • $request.method: The HTTP method of the request
    • $request.form.<field>: A specific form field, for a request sent as multipart/form-data
    • $request.files.<field>: A file uploaded with the request, as a file reference

    Once mapped, reference input variables in workflow nodes with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting the variable from the suggestions. An inserted reference is displayed as $input.<variable_name>.

    Accessing the request without an input variable

    Every run also exposes the incoming request through the built-in $input.payload variable, with no declaration or assignment required. The name payload is reserved for this variable and can't be used as an input variable name.

  9. Recommended: In the Authentication section, select a Method * to control who can start the workflow.

    The webhook URL is reachable without signing in to TheHive, and the endpoint applies no other authentication. The method you select here is what protects the workflow. Regardless of the method, each webhook accepts up to 120 requests per minute by default. TheHive Flow rejects requests beyond that limit with a 429 response carrying a Retry-After: 60 header. For how the limit works, see Rate limiting.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    Method Fields Description None — No authentication. Anyone who knows the webhook URL can start the workflow. This is the default. Basic Auth Username *, Password * The caller sends the credentials in an Authorization header using the HTTP Basic scheme. Key / Header Auth Header name *, Header value * The caller sends the header you define, with an exact, case-sensitive value. Use it for a shared secret or an API key, for example an X-Api-Key header. JWT Token Secret key *, Algorithm *, Require token expiration The caller sends a signed token in an Authorization header using the Bearer scheme. TheHive Flow validates the token against the secret key and the algorithm, and tolerates a clock difference of 30 seconds. In Algorithm, enter the HMAC algorithm the token is signed with, for example HS256, HS384, or HS512. Turn on Require token expiration to reject tokens that carry no expiration claim. It's turned off by default, so tokens that never expire are accepted.

    Leaving the method set to None

    With None, the webhook URL is the only secret protecting the workflow. The URL can't be rotated without recreating the trigger, and it leaks through access logs, proxy logs, the Referer header, and browser history. Select another method for any webhook reachable from outside your network.

    Keeping credentials out of the configuration

    Credential fields accept a reference to a secret global variable instead of a literal value. The reference resolves on every incoming request, so rotating the variable takes effect on the next call without editing the trigger.

docs.title: Add a Scheduler triggerNext steps
docs.text:
Configure a Scheduler trigger that starts the workflow automatically on a recurring schedule. A trigger node can carry multiple scheduler blocks, each with its own independent schedule.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. In the trigger node, select Add a trigger.

  4. In the Select a trigger drawer, select Scheduler.

  5. Select an interval type, then enter an interval time and any additional fields that appear.

    Available interval types and their fields:

    Interval type Interval value Additional fields Seconds 10 to 60 — Minutes 1 to 60 — Hours 1 to 24 Trigger at minute (0 to 59) Days 1 to 31 Trigger at hour (0 to 23), Trigger at minute (0 to 59) Weeks Fixed at 1 Trigger on day of the week, Trigger at hour (0 to 23), Trigger at minute (0 to 59) Months 1 to 12 Trigger at day of the month (1 to 31), Trigger at hour (0 to 23), Trigger at minute (0 to 59)

    Hours and minutes are in UTC.
