docs.title: Build Your First Workflow
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows manageOrchestrator/writeVariables One

Ready to see TheHive Flow in action? In this exercise, you'll build a complete workflow from scratch and learn why each piece works the way it does.

By the end, you'll have a working workflow that automatically converts CVEs from CIRCL for a specific vendor and product into alerts in TheHive. Along the way, you'll get hands-on with the core concepts you'll reuse in every workflow you build:

  • Connecting nodes to pass data from one action to the next
  • Fetching data from an external API using HTTP requests
  • Using variables to store and transform data throughout a workflow
  • Building loops to process multiple items automatically
  • Using conditions to filter and validate data
  • Creating alerts in TheHive from external data sources

You don't need any prior knowledge or access to external tools. You'll use publicly available CVE data throughout.

This exercise takes approximately 30 minutes to complete.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a workflow
docs.text:
Start by setting up a new workflow in TheHive Flow.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select .

  3. In the Workflow information drawer, enter the following information:

    - Name: Turn CIRCL CVEs into alerts

    - Description: Automatically fetch the latest CVEs from CIRCL and create security alerts in TheHive

    - Tags: cve

    - Timeout: 15 minutes

    The timeout defines the maximum allowed execution time for the entire workflow. You can also set a timeout at the node level. When both are defined, the shortest value applies.

  4. Select Save.

You'll arrive directly in the workflow editor. You can see that TheHive has created your workflow in a Disabled state with a default trigger node. The trigger node is the entry point that initiates workflow execution. Two triggers are available: Webhook, which starts the workflow when its URL receives an HTTP request, and Scheduler, which starts it on a recurring schedule. You can also run a workflow manually, from the workflow editor or from a case or alert page in TheHive, regardless of its trigger configuration.

For this exercise, skip the trigger configuration. You'll run the workflow manually later.

docs.title: Step 2: Set the vendor and product
docs.text:
You'll fetch CVEs for Apple macOS. Rather than hardcoding these values in the CIRCL API request, store them as local variables. They're scoped to a single workflow run and available to all subsequent nodes.

  1. In the workflow editor, drag the trigger node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

    The layout is free, so you can place nodes anywhere on the canvas.

  2. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Set local variable.

  3. Select in the Variables section.

  4. In the Set local variable drawer, enter the following information:

    - Name: vendor

    - Type: string

    - Value: apple

    Then, still in the drawer, select to add a second variable.

    - Name: product

    - Type: string

    - Value: macos

  5. Select the node title and rename it to Set vendor and product.

    Renaming nodes is optional but recommended. Descriptive names make your workflow easier to read at a glance. You can also add a description to a node, but it appears only in the node configuration drawer, not on the canvas.

  6. To exit the node configuration, select an empty space in the workflow editor or select .

    The workflow configuration is automatically saved at each step.

You now have two local variables that scope the CIRCL API query to a specific vendor and product.

docs.title: Step 3: Fetch the latest CVEs
docs.text:
Add an HTTP request node to fetch the latest CVEs for the vendor and product you set in the previous step.

  1. Add an HTTP request node by dragging the Set vendor and product node's connector to an empty area of the canvas and selecting HTTP request in the What is the next step? drawer.

  2. In the HTTP request drawer, enter the following information:

    - Method: GET

    - URL: https://cve.circl.lu/api/search/

    Position the cursor at the end of the URL, select the $var button, then select Set vendor and product > vendor.

    Enter / and select the $var button again to select Set vendor and product > product.

    Inserting variables

    Instead of the $var button, you can enter $ in the field, then the first characters of the variable name to filter the suggestions. Then select one of the suggestions to insert the reference. You can't enter the full reference manually.

    The final URL should look like this: https://cve.circl.lu/api/search/$set_vendor_and_product.vendor/$set_vendor_and_product.product

  3. Rename the node to Get CVEs.

  4. Select to view the available outputs.

    Output Type Description body object The response body returned by the server. Not set for a multipart response: use parts instead. code number The HTTP status code returned by the server. headers object The response headers returned by the server. parts object The parts of a multipart response body, keyed by part name. Each part carries its filename, content_type, size, and content. Empty when the response isn't multipart.

    These outputs are JSON values, automatically available as output variables in subsequent nodes. Because the workflow hasn't run yet, hovering over an output shows an example value. After the workflow has run, it shows the result from the last execution.

The HTTP request is now configured to fetch CVE data from CIRCL for Apple macOS. Before continuing, test what you've built so far.

docs.title: Step 4: Test the CVE retrieval
docs.text:
Testing as you build is a good habit in TheHive Flow. It helps you catch errors early and know exactly where they occurred. Execution logs are also available to help you understand why a workflow isn't working as expected. You'll use them in the final step of this exercise.

  1. To test a workflow, you need to enable it first. In the workflow editor, select Enable workflow.

  2. Select Run workflow.

  3. Select the Get CVEs node and then select .

  4. Hover over the body output to check that the node received data.

    Hovering over the output lets you inspect the data and its structure, which helps when you reference specific fields of the corresponding output variable in the next step.

If you see a list of CVE objects, your request is working correctly. You've fetched and stored the latest CVEs from CIRCL.

docs.title: Step 5: Extract the CVE list
docs.text:
Next, create another local variable to store the CVE list from the body response. You could reference the body output variable of the Get CVEs HTTP request node directly. Assigning it to a named local variable makes the intent explicit and the workflow easier to follow.

  1. Add a Set local variable node from the Get CVEs node.

  2. In the Set local variable drawer, select in the Variables section, then enter the following information:

    - Name: CVEList

    - Type: array

    - Value: Select the + button, enter $, select the Get CVEs > body variable, and add .results.nvd while still inside the jq expression.

    Select the suggestion from the Step variables group, not from the Files group. Entries in the Files group expose file metadata such as the file name and size, not the value itself, and resolve to nothing when the value isn't stored as a file.

    Add .results.nvd inside the inserted reference, not after it: select the reference to edit inside it. Text entered after the reference isn't part of the jq expression and makes the node fail at execution.

    You can also insert the variable with the $var button, then select the inserted reference to add a field.

    Add fields inside the reference

    For blue references, which are jq expressions, always add fields by editing the inserted reference, as described above. Text entered directly after a blue reference in the field value is treated as literal text, not as part of the jq expression, and the node fails at execution with a type mismatch.

    Case-sensitive field names

    Field names within variables are case-sensitive. Use the exact casing, or the expression won't work.

    The final value should look like this: $get_cves.body.results.nvd.

  3. Rename the node to CVE List.

You've now set up the data pipeline: the workflow fetches CVEs from CIRCL and stores them as a local array variable.

docs.title: Step 6: Process each CVE and filter by record type
docs.text:
Now loop over the CVE array and filter out entries that aren't valid CVE records before creating alerts in TheHive.

  1. Add a For each node from the CVE List node.

  2. In the For each drawer, select the CVE List > CVEList variable in the Field to iterate over field.

    Iterations run sequentially by default. For this exercise, leave them sequential and keep the Parallel execution toggle turned off.

    The Loop output variables section aggregates values produced inside the loop across all iterations, so nodes placed after the loop can use them. This exercise creates the alerts inside the loop itself and doesn't need them.

  3. Add a Set local variable node from the For each node.

    The For each node has two branches: the Loop branch and the Done branch. Use the Loop branch: .

  4. In the Set local variable drawer, select in the Variables section, then enter the following information:

    - Name: CVE

    - Type: json

    - Value: Select the + button, enter $, select the For each > item variable, and add [1] while still inside the jq expression.

    The final value should look like this: $for_each.item[1].

    In a For each node, item is the current iteration value and idx is its key. Here, CIRCL returns each entry as a two-element [id, CVE] pair, so item[0] is the CVE ID and item[1] is the CVE object you need.

  5. Rename the node to Set CVE occurrence.

  6. Add an If node from the Set CVE occurrence node.

  7. In the If drawer, select the Set CVE occurrence > CVE variable, then enter .dataType == "CVE_RECORD" directly after it.

    In an If node condition, the inserted reference is green because it's a direct variable. Unlike with blue references, text entered after a green reference isn't literal: it extends the expression. Entering text directly after it is correct here.

    The final value should look like this: $set_cve_occurrence.CVE.dataType == "CVE_RECORD".

You've set up the loop and filter logic for the workflow. Only CVEs with a dataType of CVE_RECORD move forward to the next step, where they're created as alerts in TheHive.

docs.title: Step 7: Create alerts in TheHive
docs.text:
To complete the workflow, you'll store your TheHive API key as a global variable, prepare the alert content from the CVE data, and create the alert in TheHive with a TheHive node.

Have your TheHive API key ready

To find it, see Manage User Accounts.

  1. From the workflow editor, select Workflows to go back to the workflow list.

  2. Select the Global variables tab.

    You manage global variables from this tab. Unlike local variables, global variables are defined once and shared across all workflows. They can be visible or secret.

  3. Select .

  4. In the Create a variable drawer, enter the following information:

    - Name: api_key_thehive

    - Secret: On

    - Value: string and paste your TheHive API key.

  5. Select Save.

  6. Select the Workflows tab and select your Turn CIRCL CVEs into alerts workflow.

  7. Add a Set local variable node from the If node.

    The If node has two branches: true and false. Use the true branch: .

  8. In the Set local variable drawer, select in the Variables section, then enter the following information:

    - Name: alertTitle

    - Type: string

    - Value: Enter New CVE:, then select the + button, enter $, select Set CVE occurrence > CVE, and add .cveMetadata.cveId while still inside the jq expression.

    The final value should look like this: New CVE: $set_cve_occurrence.CVE.cveMetadata.cveId

    Then, still in the drawer, select to add a second variable.

    - Name: alertDescription

    - Type: string

    - Value: Select the + button, enter $, select Set CVE occurrence > CVE, and add .containers.cna.descriptions[0].value while still inside the jq expression.

    The final value should look like this: $set_cve_occurrence.CVE.containers.cna.descriptions[0].value

  9. Rename the node to Set alert title and description.

  10. Add a TheHive node from the Set alert title and description node.

  11. In the TheHive drawer, enter the following information:

    - Base URL: https://<thehive_host>

    Replace <thehive_host> with the host name or IP address of your TheHive instance.

    - Bearer token: In the Authentication section, select the api_key_thehive global variable.

    - Organization: Enter the name of the organization where the alert is created. If left empty, the node uses the default organization of the account that owns the API key.

    - Action: Select Create Alert.

    Then fill in the fields for the action:

    - Type: CVE

    - Source: flow

    - Source ref: Select the + button, enter $, select Set CVE occurrence > CVE, and add .cveMetadata.cveId while still inside the jq expression.

    - Title: Select the $var button and select Set alert title and description > alertTitle.

    - Description: Select the $var button and select Set alert title and description > alertDescription.

    The Create Alert action offers more fields, but these are all you need for this exercise.

  12. Rename the node to Create alert.

Your workflow is now complete. The workflow sends each CVE that passes the CVE_RECORD filter to TheHive as a new alert, with a structured title and description taken from the CVE data.

docs.title: Step 8: Run the workflow
docs.text:
With the workflow fully built, run it and verify that it creates alerts in TheHive.

After Step 4, your workflow should still be enabled. If you turned it off, re-enable it before continuing.

  1. Go to the Executions tab and select Run workflow.

  2. Follow the execution of each node in real time.

    Nodes turn purple while running, green on success, red on failure, and stay gray if they aren't reached because of an upstream interruption. Select a red node to read the error message and fix the issue.

    The trigger node shows Manual because you started the run yourself. Select it to inspect the trigger payload the run received, displayed in Input.

    Nodes that run more than once inside the loop display a badge with the number of iterations. When some iterations succeed and others fail, two badges appear: one counts the successful iterations and the other the failed ones. A loop node turns red as soon as one iteration fails, even if the others succeeded.

  3. After the execution completes, go to the Alerts view and look for new alerts with the type CVE and the source flow.

If alerts appear in TheHive, your workflow is working end to end. You've built your first workflow in TheHive Flow!

Running the workflow more than once

TheHive rejects an alert when one with the same type, source, and source reference already exists in the organization. If you run the workflow again, the Create alert node fails with a 400 error for each CVE already imported. To run the exercise again, delete the previously created alerts in TheHive first.

Run a workflow on a case or an alert

You can also run a workflow from a case or alert page in TheHive. The run passes the case or alert identifier to the workflow in the trigger payload, and to the case_id or alert_id input variable when the workflow declares it. A workflow can then act on the entity it was launched from, for example to enrich a case or triage an alert.

docs.title: (Optional) Step 9: Clean upNext steps
docs.text:
This exercise creates real alerts in TheHive. Delete the alerts you no longer need and turn off the workflow. Deleting the alerts also lets you run the exercise again: TheHive rejects a new alert matching an existing one, whatever its status.

  1. In the Alerts view, filter on the source flow to isolate the alerts created by the workflow.

  2. Select in the column header to select all the alerts on the page, then select above the list.

  3. In the confirmation dialog, select OK.

  4. Go back to the Flow view, select the workflow, then select Disable workflow.

    No trigger is configured, so the workflow runs only when started manually. Turning it off prevents an accidental run from creating new alerts.

docs.title: Configure an Action Node
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Action nodes perform operations that interact with TheHive or external systems in TheHive Flow. They produce the workflow output by making changes in the environment or triggering downstream processes.

docs.title: Configure an HTTP request action node
docs.text:
An HTTP request action node sends HTTP requests to any API accessible from your TheHive instance:

  • ITSM tools
  • Threat intelligence platforms
  • Cloud services
  • Another TheHive Flow workflow with its Webhook trigger
  • TheHive API, for endpoints not covered by the TheHive integration node

Working with TheHive

To create, update, or query objects in TheHive, use the TheHive integration node, which exposes TheHive operations directly. Use an HTTP request node for TheHive API endpoints that the TheHive node doesn't cover, or for any other external API.

Targets on a private network

An HTTP request node can't reach non-public addresses, such as private, loopback, or link-local ranges: the step fails with an egress guard error. An administrator must first add the target range to the egress allowlist.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Actions.

  5. Select HTTP request.

  6. In the HTTP request drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Method *

    The HTTP method used for the request.

    - URL *

    The full endpoint URL.

    Examples:

    • https://<thehive_host>/api/v1/user
    • https://api.abuseipdb.com/api/v2/check?ipAddress=<ip_address>

    - Headers

    Select in the Headers section to add headers.

    Enter a header key and its corresponding value to include in the HTTP request. Use headers to define content types, expected response formats, or to include custom metadata required by the external system.

    - Body

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    The request body. Available for the POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE methods.

    - Multipart parts

    Key-value pairs sent as a multipart/form-data request, one part per pair. Leave Body empty when using this field. The node streams a value that's a file reference as a file part, and sends any other value as a plain form field. Available for the POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE methods.

  7. Optional: Select Add options to configure the following settings.

    - Authentication

    Configure how the node authenticates when calling the target API.

    Calling TheHive API

    If the HTTP request targets TheHive itself, make sure your TheHive authentication settings are compatible with the method you select in this node.

    Supported methods:

    • None: No authentication is added to the request.

    • Basic auth: Sends a username and password encoded in the Authorization header using the HTTP Basic scheme.

    Field Example Username * emma@example.com Password * $secret.api_password
    • Bearer token: Sends an access token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme.
    Field Example Token * $secret.api_token
    • OAuth 2.0: Authenticates with an access token, provided directly or obtained by exchanging a refresh token.
    Field With an access token With a refresh token Example Client ID Not used Required $global.oauth_client_id Client secret Not used Optional, for a confidential client $secret.oauth_client_secret Access token Required Not used $secret.oauth_access_token Refresh token Not used Required $secret.oauth_refresh_token Token URL Not used Required https://auth.example.com/oauth/token

    Access token or refresh token

    An access token is the short-lived key sent with each call to the service. A refresh token only serves to get new access tokens, and not every provider issues one.

    • Access token: Never renewed. Once it expires, calls fail until it's replaced. Suits a quick test.
    • Refresh token: Each node execution gets a fresh access token. Suits a workflow that runs over time. A new refresh token sent back by the provider isn't saved, so a provider that accepts each refresh token only once rejects the next execution.

    The form also shows Authorization URL and Token scopes, which have no effect: leave them empty.

    - Proxy

    Configure how the node connects to external services when a proxy is required.

    Nodes support three modes:

    • Disabled: No proxy is applied. All requests are sent directly.

    • Default: Uses the global proxy settings defined in TheHive application.conf. See proxy configuration in TheHive.

    • Enabled: Defines a custom proxy for this node, overriding the global configuration.

    Field Example Protocol https Address * proxy.example.com Port 8080 Proxy username $global.proxy_user Proxy password $secret.proxy_password

    Protocol defaults to https, and Port defaults to 8080.

    A custom proxy on a non-public address must first be added to the egress allowlist.

    - SSL

    Configure SSL settings for secure SSL/TLS communication with external services.

    Use this section when the external service relies on a private certificate authority (CA), requires client certificate authentication through mutual TLS, or uses a non-standard trust chain.

    Field Description Client certificate (mTLS) Turn on to authenticate with a client certificate (mutual TLS). Turned off by default. SSL key (PEM) The private key associated with the client certificate, in PEM format. Required only when Client certificate (mTLS) is turned on. SSL certificate (PEM) The client certificate to present during the SSL/TLS handshake, in PEM format. Required only when Client certificate (mTLS) is turned on. Certificate Authorities Server certificate verification mode. Default: uses the system's pre-installed certificate authorities. Custom: provide a CA certificate to verify the server. Disabled: skips server identity verification. Not recommended in production, as it exposes the connection to security risks. SSL CA certificate (PEM) The CA certificate used to verify the server's identity, in PEM format. Required only when Certificate Authorities is set to Custom.

    - Request timeout

    Maximum time for the HTTP call itself. When a node timeout is also set in Timeout & retry, the shorter of the two applies. The value can't exceed the node timeout or the workflow timeout. The node retries when it reaches the node timeout and retries are configured, but not when it reaches the request timeout.

    - Timeout & retry

    Configure how the node handles execution time limits and failure recovery.

    If the timeout is reached, the node fails.

    Global timeout vs. local timeout

    A timeout for the entire workflow is defined when creating the workflow. When both a node timeout and a workflow-level timeout are defined, the shortest timeout value applies.

    Field Description Timeout Maximum allowed execution time for the node, in seconds, minutes, or hours. The minimum value is 30 seconds. Retry attempts Number of times the node is retried on failure. Retry delay Time to wait between retry attempts, in seconds, minutes, or hours. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Backoff Coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt.

    Retries and timeouts

    If the node includes retry settings, the timeout applies to each attempt, not to the total duration of all attempts.

    Even without a node timeout, the HTTP call itself stops after the Request timeout, 30 seconds by default.

    - Execution configuration

    Set the Execution mode to control how the node behaves when several branches converge on it.

    Mode Behavior Execute once per branch The node runs once for each incoming branch. Applies when this section isn't configured. Wait for all branches The node waits for all incoming branches to complete, then runs once.

  8. Optional: Turn on Ignore HTTP errors to make the node succeed regardless of the response status code.

    By default, the node fails when the response returns a 4xx or 5xx error status code. With the option on, handle errors in the workflow, for example with an If flow node evaluating the code output.

    Two cases still fail the node:

    • A transport failure, such as a DNS, connection, TLS, or timeout error. The node sets no output.
    • A response announced as JSON that can't be parsed. The node sets the code and headers outputs but no body, and doesn't retry.

    When Ignore HTTP errors is off, the node retries a 408, 429, or 5xx response up to the number of times set in Retry attempts, under Timeout & retry. Any other 4xx response fails the node immediately, without retrying. When the called service includes a Retry-After header in its response, the node waits that long before the next attempt, up to a maximum of 5 minutes. This wait replaces the delay set by Retry delay and Backoff.

Execution outputs

When executed, the node returns the following outputs. Each output is a JSON value:

Output Type Description body any The response body returned by the target API. The node parses a response with a JSON content type to its value, and returns any other response as text. Not set for a multipart response: use parts instead. code number The HTTP status code returned by the server. headers object The response headers returned by the server. parts object The parts of a multipart response body, keyed by part name. Each part carries its filename, content_type, size, and content. Empty when the response isn't multipart.

A body that is large or binary, and a part content that is large or not JSON, are stored as files and returned as file references. A part stored as a file also carries a sha256sum field, and a part name reused across parts is suffixed with _2, _3, and so on.

To access outputs, select your HTTP request node and then select in the top-right corner of the screen. Hover over each output name to view its details.

These outputs can then be reused as output variables in subsequent nodes, using the $var button or by entering $ and selecting the output from the suggestions. Inserted references are displayed in the following form:

  • $<node_name>.body.<field_name>: to get a nested value from the response body
  • $<node_name>.code: to get the HTTP status code, for example to check whether the request succeeded
  • $<node_name>.headers.<header_name>: to get a specific response header
  • $<node_name>.parts.<part_name>.content: to get the content of one part of a multipart response

docs.title: Configure a Send email action node
docs.text:
A Send email action node sends an email using the SMTP configuration defined in TheHive, unless TheHive Flow has an email server override.

Prerequisite

Before using a Send email action node, you must configure an SMTP server in TheHive or set an email server override. The node can't send emails without a working SMTP configuration.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Actions.

  5. Select Send email.

  6. In the Send email drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - From *

    The email address used as the sender.

    - To *

    One or more recipient addresses, separated by commas.

    - Cc

    Additional recipients.

    - Bcc

    Hidden recipients.

    - Subject

    The email subject.

    - Body format

    Select how the message body is sent:

    • Text
    • HTML
    • Both: Sends both versions. This is the default, and it's recommended for maximum compatibility with email clients.

    - Text body

    The plain text content of the email.

    - HTML body

    The HTML content of the email.

  7. Optional: Select Add options to configure the following settings.

    - Timeout & retry

    Configure how the node handles execution time limits and failure recovery.

    If the timeout is reached, the node fails.

    Global timeout vs. local timeout

    A timeout for the entire workflow is defined when creating the workflow. When both a node timeout and a workflow-level timeout are defined, the shortest timeout value applies.

    Field Description Timeout Maximum allowed execution time for the node, in seconds, minutes, or hours. The minimum value is 30 seconds. Retry attempts Number of times the node is retried on failure. Retry delay Time to wait between retry attempts, in seconds, minutes, or hours. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Backoff Coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt.

    Retries and timeouts

    If the node includes retry settings, the timeout applies to each attempt, not to the total duration of all attempts.

    - Execution configuration

    Set the Execution mode to control how the node behaves when several branches converge on it.

    Mode Behavior Execute once per branch The node runs once for each incoming branch. Applies when this section isn't configured. Wait for all branches The node waits for all incoming branches to complete, then runs once.

docs.title: Configure an Analyzer action node
docs.text:
An Analyzer action node triggers a Cortex analyzer on a specific observable and makes the resulting report available as an output variable for use in subsequent workflow steps.

Prerequisite

To use an Analyzer action node, a Cortex server must already be connected to TheHive. If no Cortex instance is configured, follow the instructions in Add a Cortex Server before proceeding.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Actions.

  5. Select Analyzer.

  6. In the Analyzer drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Observable type *

    The type of observable to analyze. Two input modes are available:

    • Form: Select the type from a list.
    • Raw: Provide the type with a variable, when it's only known at runtime from a previous node's output.

    - Observable ID *

    The identifier of the observable to analyze.

    - Analyzer *

    Select the Cortex analyzer to run.

    The list shows only analyzers compatible with the selected observable type. Cortex checks the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) and Permissible Actions Protocol (PAP) levels of the observable at execution time: if they aren't compatible with the analyzer, it returns an error and the node fails.

    The list covers the analyzers of every Cortex instance connected to the organization. You don't select the instance: the node derives it from the analyzer you choose. When several instances host the same analyzer, the node uses the first one and gives no way to choose another. To target a specific instance, use the TheHive integration node with the Run Analyzer on Observable action, which takes the Cortex instance identifier as a value.

  7. Optional: Select Add options to configure the following settings.

    - Timeout & retry

    Configure how the node handles execution time limits and failure recovery.

    If the timeout is reached, the node fails.

    Global timeout vs. local timeout

    A timeout for the entire workflow is defined when creating the workflow. When both a node timeout and a workflow-level timeout are defined, the shortest timeout value applies.

    Field Description Timeout Maximum allowed execution time for the node, in seconds, minutes, or hours. The minimum value is 30 seconds. Retry attempts Number of times the node is retried on failure. Retry delay Time to wait between retry attempts, in seconds, minutes, or hours. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Backoff Coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt.

    Retries and timeouts

    If the node includes retry settings, the timeout applies to each attempt, not to the total duration of all attempts.

    - Execution configuration

    Set the Execution mode to control how the node behaves when several branches converge on it.

    Mode Behavior Execute once per branch The node runs once for each incoming branch. Applies when this section isn't configured. Wait for all branches The node waits for all incoming branches to complete, then runs once.

Execution output

When executed, the node runs the selected analyzer on the observable. The analyzer's report is available as an output object.

To access the output, select your Analyzer node and then select in the top-right corner of the screen. Hover over the output name to view its details.

This output can then be reused as an output variable in subsequent nodes, using the $var button or by entering $ and selecting the output from the suggestions. The inserted reference is displayed as $<node_name>.analyzer_report.

It contains the full report returned by Cortex, in the format specific to the analyzer that was run. Use a Set local variable node, a JavaScript code node, or a Python code node to extract specific fields from it.

docs.title: Configure a Responder action node
docs.text:
A Responder action node triggers a Cortex responder on a specific alert, case, observable, task, or task log. When the node runs, it executes the selected responder and makes the resulting report available as an output variable for use in subsequent workflow steps.

Prerequisite

To use a Responder action node, a Cortex server must already be connected to TheHive. If no Cortex instance is configured, follow the instructions in Add a Cortex Server before proceeding.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Actions.

  5. Select Responder.

  6. In the Responder drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Entity type *

    The type of entity on which the responder runs. Each entity type has its own value: alert for an alert, case for a case, case_artifact for an observable, case_task for a task, and case_task_log for a task log.

    Two input modes are available:

    • Form: Select the type from a list. The list is built from the entity types declared by the responders of the connected Cortex instances, so a type appears only when at least one enabled responder supports it.
    • Raw: Enter the type directly or provide it with a variable, when it's only known at runtime from a previous node's output or missing from the list.

    - Entity ID *

    The identifier of the entity to process.

    - Responder *

    Select the Cortex responder to execute.

    The list shows only responders compatible with the selected entity type. Cortex checks the TLP and PAP levels of the entity at execution time: if they aren't compatible with the responder, it returns an error and the node fails.

  7. Optional: Select Add options to configure the following settings.

    - Timeout & retry

    Configure how the node handles execution time limits and failure recovery.

    If the timeout is reached, the node fails.

    Global timeout vs. local timeout

    A timeout for the entire workflow is defined when creating the workflow. When both a node timeout and a workflow-level timeout are defined, the shortest timeout value applies.

    Field Description Timeout Maximum allowed execution time for the node, in seconds, minutes, or hours. The minimum value is 30 seconds. Retry attempts Number of times the node is retried on failure. Retry delay Time to wait between retry attempts, in seconds, minutes, or hours. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Backoff Coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt.

    Retries and timeouts

    If the node includes retry settings, the timeout applies to each attempt, not to the total duration of all attempts.

    - Execution configuration

    Set the Execution mode to control how the node behaves when several branches converge on it.

    Mode Behavior Execute once per branch The node runs once for each incoming branch. Applies when this section isn't configured. Wait for all branches The node waits for all incoming branches to complete, then runs once.

Execution output

When executed, the node runs the selected responder on the selected alert, case, observable, or task. The responder's report is available as an output object.

To access the output, select your Responder node and then select in the top-right corner of the screen. Hover over the output name to view its details.

This output can then be reused as an output variable in subsequent nodes, using the $var button or by entering $ and selecting the output from the suggestions. The inserted reference is displayed as $<node_name>.responder_report.

It contains the full report returned by Cortex, in the format specific to the responder that was run. Use a Set local variable node, a JavaScript code node, or a Python code node to extract specific fields from it.

docs.title: Configure an AI action nodeNext steps
docs.text:
An AI action node sends a message to a large language model (LLM) and returns its response. Use it to triage alerts, summarize case data, classify observables, or draft content as part of a workflow. The node calls an OpenAI-compatible LLM provider configured by your administrator.

Prerequisite

An administrator must configure at least one LLM provider before using an AI action node.

Locally hosted LLM providers

An AI node can't reach a provider on a non-public address: the step fails with an egress guard error. For a provider hosted on your internal network, an administrator must first add its address range to the egress allowlist.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Actions.

  5. Select AI.

  6. In the AI drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Role and context

    Defines the posture and context the AI adopts. For example: You are a security analyst specialized in alert triage.

    - Message *

    The concrete instruction to execute. Phrase the request here and inject the data to analyze from upstream nodes, for example Analyze this alert and decide whether to escalate or discard: $input.alert.

    - Provider *

    The LLM provider to use. Available providers depend on the configuration set by your administrator.

    - Model *

    The model that generates the response, selected from the models available for the chosen provider.

    - Output schema

    A JSON schema describing the expected output structure. When set, the AI constrains its response to match the schema, so downstream nodes can consume the fields individually. The field opens pre-filled with a schema declaring a single message string field. You can clear it: when the field is empty, the node produces no result output and only the raw response text is available.

  7. Optional: Select Add options to configure the following sections.

    - Model parameters

    Temperature: Controls how random the response is, from 0 to 2. Lower values make the response more focused and deterministic. Higher values make it more varied. Leave empty to use the model default.

    Max tokens: The maximum number of tokens in the response. Leave empty to use the provider default.

    Reasoning effort: How much reasoning the model spends before answering: None, Minimal, Low, Medium, High, Extra high, or Max. None turns reasoning off, and the levels a model accepts depend on the provider. Leave empty to use the configuration default, then the provider default.

    - Timeout & retry

    Configure how the node handles execution time limits and failure recovery.

    If the timeout is reached, the node fails.

    Global timeout vs. local timeout

    A timeout for the entire workflow is defined when creating the workflow. When both a node timeout and a workflow-level timeout are defined, the shortest timeout value applies.

    Field Description Timeout Maximum allowed execution time for the node, in seconds, minutes, or hours. The minimum value is 30 seconds. Retry attempts Number of times the node is retried on failure. Retry delay Time to wait between retry attempts, in seconds, minutes, or hours. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Backoff Coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt.

    Retries and timeouts

    If the node includes retry settings, the timeout applies to each attempt, not to the total duration of all attempts.

    - Execution configuration

    Set the Execution mode to control how the node behaves when several branches converge on it.

    Mode Behavior Execute once per branch The node runs once for each incoming branch. Applies when this section isn't configured. Wait for all branches The node waits for all incoming branches to complete, then runs once.

Execution outputs

When executed, the node returns the following outputs. Each output is a JSON value:

Output Type Description response string The raw text response from the LLM. result object The parsed structured output. Present only when an output schema is set. message object The raw assistant message returned by the LLM, including reasoning content when the model provides it. finish_reason string The reason the LLM stopped generating, for example stop, length, tool_calls, or content_filter. usage object Token usage for the call: prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, and total_tokens.

To access outputs, select your AI node and then select in the top-right corner of the screen. Hover over each output name to view its details.

These outputs can then be reused as output variables in subsequent nodes, using the $var button or by entering $ and selecting the output from the suggestions. Inserted references are displayed in the following form:

  • $<node_name>.response: to get the text response
  • $<node_name>.result.<field_name>: to get a field from the structured output when an output schema is set
  • $<node_name>.finish_reason: to check why the LLM stopped generating, for example in an If condition
  • $<node_name>.usage.total_tokens: to get the total token usage of the call

docs.title: Configure a Flow Node
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Flow nodes control how workflows branch, loop, process multiple items, pause, or call another workflow in TheHive Flow. An execution path ends when it reaches a node with no next step.

docs.title: Configure a For each flow node
docs.text:
A For each flow node iterates over each item in an array or object that matches a jq expression and executes the same sequence of nodes for each entry.

Each iteration is independent. To collect results across iterations, declare loop output variables when configuring the node, or process each result directly within the loop.

Nested loops

For each nodes can be nested: a For each node can contain another For each node in its body, to iterate over multi-level data structures.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Flows.

  5. Select For each.

  6. In the For each drawer, go to Field to iterate over and enter a jq expression that selects the items.

    The expression must return a JSON array or object. The node then iterates over each item in the result.

    You can select variables using the $var button. The functions available in expressions are listed in Jq Functions.

    Accessing a field from a variable

    To access a field, enter .<field_name> directly after the variable.

    Use an online jq playground to validate your expressions before adding them to the workflow.

    Examples

    • $<node_name>.body.items: Iterates over each item in the items array from the node's response body.
    • $<node_name>.body: Iterates over each item of a response body that is an array, for example the tasks listed by a TheHive integration node with the Post Query action.
    • $<node_name>.body | map(select(.status == "Waiting")): Filters the listed tasks with status "Waiting", then iterates over the result.
    • $<node_name>.body | map(select(.dataType == "ip" and (.tags | contains(["internal"]) | not))): Iterates over the listed IP observables that aren't tagged internal.
    • $<node_name>.body.alerts | sort_by(.severity) | reverse | .[0:5]: Iterates over the five alerts with the highest severity.
    • $<node_name>.body | unique_by(.data): Iterates over the listed observables, skipping duplicates that share the same value.
    • $<node_name>.body.events | group_by(.source.ip) | map({ip: .[0].source.ip, count: length}): Builds one item per source IP address with the number of events, then iterates over the result.
    • $<node_name>.body.message | split("\n") | map(select(test("^Failed login"))): Splits a text into lines and iterates over the lines that start with Failed login.

    The Key variable and Value variable fields are read-only: the current key is always available as idx and the current item as item in the Loop branch.

  7. Optional: Turn on the Parallel execution toggle to run iterations simultaneously instead of one at a time, then enter a Max parallelism value to cap how many run concurrently.

    • In sequential mode, the default, iterations run one at a time. The loop stops on the first error.
    • In parallel mode, iterations run concurrently up to the configured limit. The first failure cancels the remaining iterations. The node waits for the running ones to stop, then reports the errors from all failed iterations together.

  8. Optional: To collect results across iterations, go to the Loop output variables section and select .

    Enter a Variable name and a JQ value referencing an output of a node in the Loop branch. In the JQ value field, reference a variable with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting the variable from the suggestions. The node evaluates the expression after each iteration, aggregates the values across all iterations, and makes them available as loop output variables in the nodes that follow the loop. A loop output variable can't reference a secret global variable.

Branches

The For each node has two branches:

Branch Description Loop branch Connects to nodes that execute for each item in the collection. In all nodes on this branch, the item and idx output variables hold the current item and its key. Done branch Connects to nodes that execute once, after all iterations have completed.

docs.title: Configure an If flow node
docs.text:
An If flow node evaluates a jq expression and directs execution down two branches based on the boolean result: true or false.

Multiple conditions

The If node evaluates a single condition. To implement switch/case logic with multiple possible values, chain several If nodes in sequence, each handling one case on its false branch.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Flows.

  5. Select If.

  6. In the If drawer, enter your jq expression for the condition.

    The expression must evaluate to a boolean.

    You can select variables using the $var button. The functions available in expressions are listed in Jq Functions.

    Accessing a field from a variable

    To access a field, enter .<field_name> directly after the variable.

    Use an online jq playground to validate your expressions before adding them to the workflow.

    Examples

    • $<node_name>.code == 200: Returns true if the HTTP status code is 200.
    • $<node_name>.body.severity >= 3: Returns true if the severity of a case or alert returned by a TheHive integration node is High or Critical.
    • $<node_name>.body._id != null: Returns true if the field is present.
    • $<node_name>.body.tags | any(. == "phishing" or . == "malware"): Returns true if at least one tag is phishing or malware.
    • $<node_name>.body | map(select(.dataType == "ip")) | length > 10: Returns true if more than 10 IP observables are listed, for example by a Post Query action listing the observables of an alert.
    • $<node_name>.body.title | test("^\\[SOC\\]"; "i"): Returns true if the title starts with [SOC], regardless of letter case.
    • $<node_name>.body._createdAt > (now - 3600) * 1000: Returns true if the entity was created less than an hour ago. TheHive dates are Unix timestamps in milliseconds.
    • ($<node_name>.body.customFields | map(select(.name == "businessUnit")) | .[0].value) // "unknown" | IN("finance", "hr"): Returns true if the businessUnit custom field is finance or hr, treating a missing field as unknown.

Branches

The If node has two branches:

Branch Description true branch Connects to nodes that execute when the condition evaluates to true. false branch Connects to nodes that execute when the condition evaluates to false.

The two branches don't have to converge. All the following layouts are valid:

  • Configure only the true branch and leave the false branch empty. The workflow ends silently on that branch.
  • Merge both branches into a common node.
  • End each branch on a separate path.

docs.title: Configure a Sleep flow node
docs.text:
A Sleep flow node pauses the execution path for a specified duration. When the duration elapses, execution continues with the next node.

Use it to wait between two actions, for example to let an external system finish processing before querying its result.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Flows.

  5. Select Sleep.

  6. In the Sleep drawer, enter a Duration and select its unit: seconds, minutes, or hours.

    The minimum duration is 1 second.

    The duration can't exceed the workflow timeout

    If the duration is longer than the workflow timeout, the execution times out before the pause completes. The editor flags such a duration when you configure the node.

docs.title: Configure a Subworkflow flow nodeNext steps
docs.text:
A Subworkflow flow node calls another workflow of the same organization and waits for it to finish before continuing with the next node. Use it to reuse a sequence of nodes across workflows instead of rebuilding it in each one, for example a shared enrichment or notification routine.

The calling workflow passes values to the input variables of the called workflow, and the nodes that follow read its exit variables as outputs. The called workflow also receives the trigger payload of the calling workflow, unchanged. The other variables of the calling workflow aren't passed.

Before you begin

In the called workflow:

  • Enable the workflow.
  • Declare the input and exit variables in its settings.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Flows.

  5. Select Subworkflow.

  6. In the Subworkflow drawer, go to Select a workflow and select the workflow to call.

    The list contains the enabled workflows of the organization, except the one you're editing, so a workflow can't call itself.

  7. In the Subworkflow inputs section, enter a jq expression for each input variable of the called workflow.

    The section lists one field per input variable the called workflow declares. Leave a field empty to not assign that input variable.

    The calling workflow evaluates each expression when the run reaches the node, so it can reference any variable of the calling workflow, except a secret global variable. Reference a variable with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting the variable from the suggestions. The functions available in expressions are listed in Jq Functions.

    Examples

    • $input.alert_id: Passes the alert identifier the calling workflow received when it was run from an alert page.
    • $<node_name>.body._id: Passes the identifier of the case created by a TheHive integration node.
    • $<node_name>.item.data: Passes the value of the current observable, for a Subworkflow node placed in the Loop branch of a For each node that iterates over observables.
    • $<node_name>.body | map(.data): Passes the values of the observables listed by a TheHive integration node as an array, for example with the Post Query action.

  8. Optional: Select Add options to configure a Timeout.

    The timeout is the maximum time the calling workflow waits for the called workflow. The minimum value is 30 seconds. When the run reaches it, the called workflow stops and the node times out. Without a node timeout, the timeout of the called workflow applies. When both are set, the shorter one applies. A called workflow is never retried.

Once the node is configured, the nodes that follow it can use the exit variables of the called workflow. Reference them with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting the variable from the suggestions. An inserted reference is displayed as $<node_name>.<exit_variable_name>.

If the called workflow fails or times out, the Subworkflow node fails. The run of the called workflow is available only from the execution details of the node.

Changes to the called workflow

Changes to the called workflow affect the workflows that call it:

  • Turned off: The node fails when the run reaches it.
  • Input variable renamed or deleted: The value entered for it is kept and flagged. The calling workflow can't run until you move or remove the value.
  • Deleted: The calling workflow can't run until you select another workflow.

Indirect loops aren't detected

A workflow can't call itself directly, but nothing prevents a loop across several workflows, for example workflow A calling workflow B, which calls workflow A. Such a loop runs until the run reaches the first timeout in the chain.

docs.title: Configure an Integration Node
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Integration nodes perform operations in TheHive or third-party products in TheHive Flow. Each integration node targets one product API and exposes its operations as dedicated actions selected within the node. Integrations tagged Beta were built from the provider's API documentation, not tested against a live environment: check them before using them in production. If you have access to a live environment, help validate the integration and share your feedback with the StrangeBee Support team.

Products hosted on a private network

Integration nodes can't reach non-public addresses: the step fails with an egress guard error. To target a product hosted on your internal network, an administrator must first add its address range to the egress allowlist.

docs.title: Configure a TheHive integration node
docs.text:
A TheHive integration node performs operations in TheHive through TheHive API. It can create, retrieve, update, and delete cases, alerts, tasks, and observables. It can also add, update, and delete comments, create and update task logs, merge an alert into a case, or run a custom query. Each operation is a dedicated action selected within the node. The node can target the local TheHive instance or any other reachable TheHive instance.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Integrations.

  5. Select TheHive.

  6. In the TheHive drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Base URL *

    The URL of TheHive instance to call, for example https://<thehive_host>.

    - Authentication *

    In the Authentication section, provide the API key used as a bearer token to authenticate the request.

    - Organization

    The organization the action runs in, sent as the X-Organisation header with every action. If left empty, the action runs in the default organization of the user.

    - Headers

    Extra headers added to every request sent by the node. Select to add a header key and its value.

    Header values are stored in plaintext

    Header values appear in plaintext in the workflow execution history. Reference a secret global variable instead of pasting a credential directly.

    - Action *

    The operation to perform in TheHive. Available actions:

    Family Actions Cases Create Case, Get Case, Update Case, Close Case, Delete Case Alerts Create Alert, Get Alert, Update Alert, Delete Alert, Merge Alert with Case, Escalate Alert to Case Tasks Create Task in Case, Get Task, Update Task, Delete Task Observables Create Observable in Case, Create Observable in Alert, Get Observable, Update Observable, Delete Observable Comments Create Comment in Case, Create Comment in Alert, Update Comment, Delete Comment Attachments Add Attachment to Alert, Add Attachment to Case Task Logs Create Task Log, Update Task Log Page Templates Create Case Page Template Queries Post Query Cortex Run Analyzer on Observable, Run Responder

    After you select an action, the drawer displays the fields specific to that action. For the meaning and format of each field, see TheHive API documentation.

    Escalate Alert to Case compared to Merge Alert with Case

    Escalate Alert to Case promotes an alert into a new case. Merge Alert with Case merges an alert into an existing case instead.

    The Cortex actions compared to the Analyzer and Responder nodes

    The Run Analyzer on Observable and Run Responder actions start a Cortex job through TheHive API. Run Analyzer on Observable requires the analyzer, Cortex instance, and observable identifiers. Run Responder requires the responder identifier and the entity's type and identifier. Both return TheHive API response rather than the Cortex report.

    To pick an analyzer or a responder from a list filtered by observable or entity type, and to get the report itself as an output, use the Analyzer or Responder action node instead.

    The Add Attachment to Alert and Add Attachment to Case actions

    The File field takes a file reference produced by an earlier node, such as a file downloaded by an HTTP request action node or uploaded to the Webhook trigger, not literal text content. The field holds one reference and nothing else. Text around the reference or a second reference shows an inline error, because the run would fail. In this field, picking an entry from the Files group of the variable suggestions inserts the file itself, not its metadata.

    - Editor mode

    For actions that send a request body, select how to provide it:

    • Form: Fill in one field per body parameter.
    • Raw: Provide the whole request body in the Request body (raw) field.

    - Query parameters

    Optional query parameters sent with the request, entered as key-value pairs. Select to add a parameter. This section appears only for actions that accept query parameters.

    The Post Query action

    The Post Query action runs a TheHive query: an array of chained operations that search, filter, sort, and paginate data across any entity type. A pipeline starts with a primary operation that defines the initial set of entities. It can then chain a related object operation to navigate to associated entities, filter and sort steps to narrow and order the results, and a page step to paginate. Provide the pipeline in the Query field as a JSON array.

    For example, this query returns the first five in-progress tasks of case ~1234, sorted by due date from earliest to latest, with the assigned case template and the total count:

    [
  {"_name": "getCase", "idOrName": "~1234"},
  {"_name": "tasks"},
  {
    "_name": "filter",
    "_eq": {"_field": "status", "_value": "InProgress"}
  },
  {
    "_name": "sort",
    "_fields": [{"dueDate": "asc"}]
  },
  {
    "_name": "page",
    "from": 0,
    "to": 5,
    "extraData": ["caseTemplate", "total"]
  }
]

    For the full list of operations, filters, and computed fields, see Query and Export in TheHive API documentation.

  7. Optional: Configure the following settings.

    - SSL/TLS

    Configure SSL/TLS settings for secure communication with the external service.

    Use this section when the service relies on a private certificate authority (CA), requires client certificate authentication through mutual TLS, or uses a non-standard trust chain.

    Field Description Client certificate (mTLS) Whether the node authenticates with a client certificate (mutual TLS). Do not use a client certificate is the default. Select Provide a client certificate and key to fill in the two fields below. Client certificate (PEM) The client certificate to present during the SSL/TLS handshake, in PEM format. Required when Client certificate (mTLS) is Provide a client certificate and key. Client certificate key (PEM) The private key associated with the client certificate, in PEM format. Required when Client certificate (mTLS) is Provide a client certificate and key. Server verification How the node verifies the identity of the server. Uses the system's pre-installed certificate authorities is the default. Provide a custom CA certificate to verify the server uses the certificate in the next field. Do not verify the server's identity (not recommended for production) exposes the connection to security risks. CA certificate (PEM) The CA certificate used to verify the identity of the server, in PEM format. Required when Server verification is set to Provide a custom CA certificate to verify the server.

    - Proxy

    Configure how the node connects to the external service when a proxy is required.

    Select a Proxy mode:

docs.title: Configure a Microsoft Entra ID integration node
docs.text:
A Microsoft Entra ID integration node runs operations against the Microsoft Graph API. It can look up users and their licenses, group memberships, MFA methods, and directory roles. It can also list sign-ins, directory audit logs, managed devices, and risk detections, and take account actions such as Disable User, Revoke Sign-In Sessions, or Force Password Reset. Each operation is a dedicated action selected within the node.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Drag the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  4. In the What is the next step? drawer, select Integrations.

  5. Select Microsoft Entra ID.

  6. In the Microsoft Entra ID drawer, enter the following information:

    Variables

    Insert a variable with the $var button, or enter $ and select a variable from the suggestions. To access a field, select the variable to edit its jq expression, or use the + button to insert the variable and the field together.

    Inside the expression, jq functions transform the value before it's inserted in the field. The whole expression stays inside the blue reference, for example:

    • $<node_name>.body.results[0].id: Reads the first identifier of an API response.
    • $<node_name>.body.items | map(.name) | join(", "): Turns a list of objects into a comma-separated text.
    • $<node_name>.body.createdAt / 1000 | todate: Formats a TheHive date, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, as an ISO 8601 date.
    • $<node_name>.output.title | ascii_upcase: Converts a text to uppercase.

    See Jq Functions for the full list of available functions.

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Base URL *

    The URL of Microsoft Graph: https://graph.microsoft.com. The node targets the v1.0 version of Microsoft Graph.

    - Authentication *

    In the Authentication section, provide the Microsoft Entra ID application credentials. The node authenticates with the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow, so Authentication method is set to oauth2_client_credentials:

    Field Example Client ID * $global.entra_client_id Client secret * $secret.entra_client_secret Token URL * https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/oauth2/v2.0/token Token scopes https://graph.microsoft.com/.default

    Prerequisite

    Grant the application the Microsoft Graph application permissions matching the actions you use. The required permission varies per action. For example, reading user profiles, sign-in logs, or managed devices each needs its own permission. See the Microsoft Graph permissions reference.

    The account actions also need the application assigned an Entra administrator role, such as User Administrator. A Graph permission alone isn't sufficient for Enable User, Disable User, Force Password Reset, and Force Password Reset (with MFA).

    - Headers

    Extra headers added to every request sent by the node. Select to add a header key and its value.

    Header values are stored in plaintext

    Header values appear in plaintext in the workflow execution history. Reference a secret global variable instead of pasting a credential directly.

    - Action *

    The operation to perform in Microsoft Entra ID. Available actions:

    Family Actions Users Resolve User GUID, Get User, Get User License Details, Get User Group Memberships, Get User MFA Methods, Get User Directory Roles Sign-Ins List Sign-Ins Audit Logs List Directory Audit Logs Devices List Managed Devices Identity Protection List Risk Detections Account Actions Enable User, Disable User, Revoke Sign-In Sessions, Force Password Reset, Force Password Reset (with MFA)

    After you select an action, the drawer displays the fields specific to that action. For the meaning and format of each field, see the Microsoft Graph API documentation.

    Get User Directory Roles requires a Consistency Level field. Set it to eventual. The same field is optional on Resolve User GUID and List Directory Audit Logs: set it to eventual when the request uses $count, $search, $orderby, or an advanced filter.

    Identifying users

    Actions that take a user identifier accept either the object ID (GUID) or the user principal name (UPN), but not an email address. When a user's email address differs from their UPN, addressing them by email fails with a 404 response. Use Resolve User GUID to resolve an email address or alias to the object ID. Run it before List Risk Detections, whose $filter query parameter matches on the object ID, for example userId eq '<guid>'.

    - Editor mode

    For actions that send a request body, select how to provide it:

    • Form: Fill in one field per body parameter.
    • Raw: Provide the whole request body in the Request body (raw) field.

    - Query parameters

    Optional query parameters sent with the request, entered as key-value pairs. Select to add a parameter. This section appears only for actions that accept query parameters.

  7. Optional: Configure the following settings.

    - Proxy

    Configure how the node connects to the external service when a proxy is required.

    Select a Proxy mode:

    • Do not use a proxy: No proxy is applied. All requests are sent directly. This is the default.

    • Use the platform default proxy configuration: Uses the global proxy settings defined in TheHive application.conf. See proxy configuration in TheHive.

    • Configure a custom proxy: Defines a custom proxy for this node, overriding the global configuration.

    When Proxy mode is Configure a custom proxy, provide the following information:

    Field Example Protocol https Address * proxy.example.com Port 8080 Username $global.proxy_user Password $secret.proxy_password

    - SSL/TLS

    Configure SSL/TLS settings for secure communication with the external service.

    Use this section when the service relies on a private certificate authority (CA), requires client certificate authentication through mutual TLS, or uses a non-standard trust chain.

    Field Description Client certificate (mTLS) Whether the node authenticates with a client certificate (mutual TLS). Do not use a client certificate is the default. Select Provide a client certificate and key to fill in the two fields below. Client certificate (PEM) The client certificate to present during the SSL/TLS handshake, in PEM format. Required when Client certificate (mTLS) is Provide a client certificate and key. Client certificate key (PEM) The private key associated with the client certificate, in PEM format. Required when Client certificate (mTLS) is Provide a client certificate and key. Server verification How the node verifies the identity of the server. Uses the system's pre-installed certificate authorities is the default. Provide a custom CA certificate to verify the server uses the certificate in the next field. Do not verify the server's identity (not recommended for production) exposes the connection to security risks. CA certificate (PEM) The CA certificate used to verify the identity of the server, in PEM format. Required when Server verification is set to Provide a custom CA certificate to verify the server.

    - Error handling

    Configure whether the node fails on error responses.

    By default, the node fails when the response returns a 4xx or 5xx error status code. Turn on Ignore error status codes to make the node succeed regardless of the response status code. Then handle errors in the workflow, for example with an If flow node evaluating the code output. Error responses aren't retried when the option is on.

    Two cases still fail the node:

    • A transport failure, such as a DNS, connection, TLS, or timeout error. The node sets no output.
    • A response announced as JSON that can't be parsed. The node sets the code and headers outputs but no body, and isn't retried.

    When Ignore error status codes is off, the node retries a 408, 429, or 5xx response up to the number of times set in Retry attempts. Any other 4xx response fails the node immediately, without retrying. When the called service includes a Retry-After header in its response, the node waits that long before the next attempt, up to a maximum of 5 minutes. This wait replaces the delay set by Retry delay and Backoff.

  8. Optional: Select Add options to configure the following settings.

    - Timeout & retry

    Configure how the node handles execution time limits and failure recovery.

    If the timeout is reached, the node fails.

    Global timeout vs. local timeout

    A timeout for the entire workflow is defined when creating the workflow. When both a node timeout and a workflow-level timeout are defined, the shortest timeout value applies.

    Field Description Timeout Maximum allowed execution time for the node, in seconds, minutes, or hours. The minimum value is 30 seconds. Retry attempts Number of times the node is retried on failure. Retry delay Time to wait between retry attempts, in seconds, minutes, or hours. Without a delay, retries run 1 second apart by default. Backoff Coefficient applied to the retry delay to increase the wait time after each failed attempt.
