docs.title: Display Workflow Execution Logs
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/readWorkflows manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Use execution logs to inspect how a workflow ran for each node. They help debug a workflow that isn't behaving as expected.

Execution logs are available in three places:

  • The Execution logs tab in the Flow view gives an organization-wide overview of the runs of every workflow.
  • The Executions tab inside a specific workflow shows the runs of that workflow in detail and lets you run it and inspect each node.
  • The Automation Center of a case or alert in TheHive, in its Automations tab, lists the runs launched on that case or alert.

docs.title: Display execution logs for all workflows
docs.text:
The Execution logs tab in the Flow view lists the executions of every workflow in the organization for the configured retention period. It includes runs launched by a trigger, or manually from the workflow editor or a case or alert. It doesn't include the runs of workflows called by a Subworkflow node. Open those from the run of the calling workflow. Use it as a starting point to spot failures and jump into a specific run.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Go to the Execution logs tab.

    The tab lists the executions of all workflows, with the following columns:

    • Status: Whether the execution completed, failed, was canceled, terminated, timed out, or is still in progress
    • Workflow name: The workflow the execution belongs to
    • Execution ID: The unique identifier of the run
    • Trigger: An icon showing what started the run, either Manual, Webhook, or Scheduler
    • Duration: How long the execution took
    • Start date and end date: When the execution started and finished

  3. Select an Execution ID to open the detailed execution view for that run, where you can inspect each node as described in Display execution logs for a specific workflow.

This tab is a read-only overview. To run a workflow or step through its nodes, open the workflow and use its Executions tab.

docs.title: Display execution logs for a specific workflow
docs.text:
The Executions tab inside a workflow lists the runs of that workflow, whether launched by a trigger, or manually from the workflow editor or a case or alert. It doesn't include the runs in which the workflow was called by a Subworkflow node. Open those from the run of the calling workflow. Use it when you know which workflow to inspect. It lets you run the workflow and inspect the execution node by node on the canvas.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select the workflow whose execution logs you want to review.

  3. Go to the Executions tab.

    The tab lists the executions of the workflow from the last 30 days by default. Change the date range filter to see older ones still retained. Each run shows its status, start and end dates, unique ID, duration, and the trigger that started it. A run still in progress shows only its start date. You can filter by status and date range.

  4. Select Run workflow to follow the execution of each node in real time.

  5. Select a run to display its Run summary. It stays displayed until you select a node and includes:

    • Status, workflow ID, execution ID, start date, end date, and duration of the run
    • Failed steps: The nodes that failed, with their error message. Select one to open its execution details.
    • Workflow inputs: The value each input variable got for this run. Displayed only when the workflow declares input variables.
    • Workflow outputs: The value of each exit variable. Displayed only when the workflow declares exit variables and the run completed.

  6. Select a node to view its execution details:

    • Start date, end date, and duration: How long the node took to run
    • Status: Whether the node completed, failed, was canceled, or timed out. Nodes that didn't run stay gray on the canvas.
    • Error message: Displayed if the node encountered an error
    • Input and output data: The data passed into and returned by the node. The value of a secret global variable never appears in the execution data.

  7. Select the trigger node to see what started the run.

    On the canvas, the trigger node shows only the trigger that started the run, either Manual or the name of the Webhook or Scheduler trigger. Its execution details include the start date, end date, duration, and status, along with data that depends on how the run started:

    • Manual run: Input displays the raw data the run received when it started, known as the trigger payload. Output displays the value each input variable got for this run, which is what the next nodes receive.
    • Webhook trigger: The same data as a manual run, with a Response code. Only requests answered with 200 start a run, so the code is always 200.
    • Scheduler trigger: Current interval describes the schedule. It reflects the trigger's current configuration, so it no longer matches the run if the schedule was edited since. No Input or Output is displayed.

  8. For a node that runs inside a For each loop, select an iteration from the Select an execution dropdown to inspect a single run of that node.

    Each iteration is listed by its number, starting with Execution 1. Selecting or hovering over an iteration highlights the nodes and branches that ran during that iteration on the canvas. For nested loops, drill down into an iteration to reach its inner iterations.

  9. For a Subworkflow node, select the name of the called workflow in the Workflow row of the node execution details. The run of the called workflow opens in a new tab.

    The link appears once the called workflow has started. If the called workflow was deleted since the run, the row reads Deleted workflow. The input data of the node displays the called workflow, the value sent to each of its input variables, and the trigger payload it received. The output data displays the exit variables it returned.

    Runs of called workflows

    Canceling the run of a called workflow also stops the run of the calling workflow. Once the run of the called workflow is past the retention period, it can no longer be opened, but the Subworkflow node keeps its input and output data.

Executions can't be resumed from a failed node. Fix the issue, then re-run the workflow from the beginning by selecting Run workflow. While an execution is still running, select it, then select Cancel to stop it early.

docs.title: Display execution logs from a case or alertNext steps
docs.text:
Workflows can be run from the Flow view or from a case or alert page in TheHive. The Automation Center of a case or alert, in its Automations tab, lists the workflow runs launched on that entity. Use it when the workflow was run from the case or alert. Runs started from the Flow view or a trigger aren't tied to a case or alert and appear only in the Flow view logs.

  1. Open a case or an alert.

  2. Go to the Automations tab.

  3. Select the Workflows tab.

    The tab lists the workflow runs launched on the case or alert, with the following columns:

    • Status: Whether the run completed, failed, was canceled, terminated, timed out, or is still in progress
    • Name: The workflow the run belongs to
    • Execution ID: The unique identifier of the run. Select it to open the run in the Flow view in a new tab.
    • Triggered by: Who started the run
    • Start date: When the run started

  • Manage Workflows
  • Manually Run a Workflow

docs.title: TheHive Flow Glossary
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow is the automation engine in TheHive. It runs workflows that respond to events, process data, and execute actions across integrated systems.

Terms are listed alphabetically.

To understand how the concepts relate to each other, see About TheHive Flow.

docs.title: Action node
docs.text: A workflow component that performs generic operations such as sending requests or messages, running Cortex analyzers and responders, or calling an LLM. Action nodes are the output of workflows: they create changes or trigger downstream processes. Available actions include HTTP request, Send email, Analyzer, Responder, and AI.

docs.title: AI action
docs.text: An action node that sends a message to a large language model (LLM) and returns its response. The node uses one of the LLM providers configured in TheHive by an administrator. The response can be constrained to a structured output schema so downstream nodes can consume individual fields.

docs.title: Analyzer action
docs.text: An action node that triggers Cortex analyzers on observables to perform automated analysis and threat intelligence enrichment.

docs.title: CrowdStrike Falcon integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the CrowdStrike Falcon APIs, such as querying devices and vulnerabilities, running response actions on hosts, querying and updating alerts, and looking up threat intelligence indicators. It also manages custom indicators of compromise and detonates file samples in the Falcon sandbox.

docs.title: Elastic Security integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Elasticsearch API, such as searching and indexing documents, running ES|QL queries, and listing Elastic Security detection alerts.

docs.title: Exit variable
docs.text: A named jq expression declared in workflow settings that is evaluated when the workflow completes. Its computed value is stored with the run and returned to the calling workflow when the workflow is called by a Subworkflow node.

docs.title: File reference
docs.text: A small object that stands in for a value stored as a file, such as a large output or binary content. Referencing the variable reads the file content back transparently when it's JSON and small enough. The file metadata is available through the $files namespace.

docs.title: Flow node
docs.text: A workflow component that controls how execution branches, loops over items, pauses, or calls another workflow. Flow nodes include If, For each, Sleep, and Subworkflow.

docs.title: For each flow
docs.text: A flow node that iterates over each item in an array or object, and executes the same sequence of nodes for each entry. Iterations run sequentially by default, or in parallel when the Parallel execution toggle is turned on.

docs.title: Global variable
docs.text: A value shared across all workflows within an organization. Global variables can't be modified within workflows. Global variables can be visible or secret. Secret global variables are intended for sensitive information such as API keys, passwords, or SSL/TLS certificate files. The value of a secret variable is never displayed in the interface and never appears in execution logs.

docs.title: HarfangLab EDR integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the HarfangLab API, such as searching and isolating endpoints, managing alerts, running jobs on agents, searching telemetry, managing indicator of compromise (IOC) rules, and listing Sigma rules.

docs.title: HTTP request action
docs.text: An action node that sends HTTP requests to external APIs and TheHive API.

docs.title: If flow
docs.text: A flow node that evaluates a jq expression and directs execution down two branches based on the boolean result.

docs.title: Input variable
docs.text: A named value passed into the workflow when it starts. It's declared and assigned in the Workflow input section of a Webhook trigger, with a jq expression applied to the incoming request. Input variables for all nodes of the workflow are managed in the workflow settings, for example to rename, describe, or delete them. Its value can also be assigned when the workflow is run from a case or alert page, which assigns the entity identifier to the case_id or alert_id input variable when the workflow declares it. The identifier is also always available in the trigger payload. A Subworkflow node that calls the workflow can also assign its value.

docs.title: Integration node
docs.text: A workflow component that performs operations in TheHive or a third-party product through its API. Each integration node targets one product and exposes its operations as dedicated actions selected within the node. Available integrations include TheHive, Splunk, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Defender (Graph Security API), Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Sentinel, Recorded Future, VirusTotal, CrowdStrike Falcon, Elastic Security, HarfangLab EDR, Jira Cloud, Slack, Microsoft Teams, ServiceNow, OpenCTI, and Wazuh.

docs.title: JavaScript code transformation
docs.text: A transformation node that executes JavaScript scripts within the workflow.

docs.title: Jira Cloud integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Jira Cloud platform REST API, such as creating, editing, transitioning, and searching issues, managing comments, attachments, worklogs, watchers, and votes, and browsing projects and issue metadata.

docs.title: jq expression
docs.text: A query language used to evaluate conditions and manipulate JSON data. It's used in flow nodes to define conditions and collections, and in any node field where an inserted variable reference is wrapped in a jq expression, displayed as a blue reference. The available functions are listed in Jq Functions.

docs.title: Local variable
docs.text: A variable scoped to a single workflow, created during workflow execution with a Set local variable transformation node.

docs.title: Loop output variable
docs.text: A variable declared on a For each flow node to collect results across iterations. Each loop output variable is a named jq expression evaluated after every iteration. The values are aggregated across all iterations and available in the nodes that follow the loop, referenced as $<node_name>.<variable_name>.

docs.title: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API, such as listing, retrieving, and updating alerts, running response actions on devices, and creating indicators.

docs.title: Microsoft Defender (Graph Security API) integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Microsoft Graph security API, such as listing, retrieving, and updating Microsoft Defender XDR alerts and incidents.

docs.title: Microsoft Entra ID integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Microsoft Graph API, such as looking up users, sign-ins, audit logs, devices, and risk detections, and taking account actions such as Disable User or Force Password Reset.

docs.title: Microsoft Sentinel integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Microsoft Sentinel REST API, such as listing, retrieving, and updating incidents, managing incident comments, and listing or writing watchlists.

docs.title: Microsoft Teams integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Microsoft Graph API, such as sending, replying to, updating, and deleting channel messages, and sending chat messages. It also creates chats and channels, adds team and channel members, and lists teams, channels, and messages.

docs.title: Node
docs.text: A building block in a workflow that performs a specific function. Nodes connect sequentially to form workflow logic, with data flowing from one node to the next. Each node receives input from previous steps and produces output for subsequent operations. Node types include trigger, flow, transformation, action, and integration nodes.

docs.title: OpenCTI integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the OpenCTI GraphQL and TAXII 2.1 APIs, such as searching entities, observables, indicators, and relationships, and creating observables, indicators, reports, incidents, relationships, and sightings. It also manages labels, markings, and notes, and requests enrichment from connectors.

docs.title: Output variable
docs.text: A variable scoped to a single workflow. Nodes generate output variables automatically during execution, and all subsequent nodes can reuse them.

docs.title: Python code transformation
docs.text: A transformation node that executes Python scripts within the workflow.

docs.title: Recorded Future integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Recorded Future API, such as enriching and triaging indicators in bulk, looking up domains, IP addresses, hashes, and URLs, and searching analyst notes and threat maps.

docs.title: Responder action
docs.text: An action node that triggers Cortex responders on alerts, cases, observables, tasks, or task logs to perform automated response actions.

docs.title: Scheduler trigger
docs.text: A trigger type within a trigger node that starts the workflow on a recurring schedule. Multiple scheduler blocks can coexist on the same trigger node, each running independently on its own schedule.

docs.title: Send email action
docs.text: An action node that sends emails using TheHive SMTP configuration.

docs.title: ServiceNow integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the ServiceNow Table and Attachment APIs, such as creating and updating incidents and change requests, and searching configuration items, users, and user groups. It also manages record attachments, and reads and writes records in any table.

docs.title: Set local variable transformation
docs.text: A transformation node that creates local variables.

docs.title: Slack integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Slack Web API, such as posting, updating, and deleting messages, managing reactions, reading threads and channel history, and looking up channels and users.

docs.title: Sleep flow
docs.text: A flow node that pauses the execution path for a specified duration before continuing with the next node.

docs.title: Splunk integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Splunk REST API, such as creating and following search jobs, running searches, listing indexes and fired alerts, submitting events, and updating Splunk Enterprise Security findings and investigations.

docs.title: Subworkflow flow
docs.text: A flow node that calls another workflow of the same organization and waits for it to finish. It passes values to the input variables of the called workflow and returns its exit variables as outputs.

docs.title: TheHive integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations in TheHive through TheHive API, such as creating, updating, querying, or deleting cases, alerts, tasks, and observables, managing comments and task logs, or starting a Cortex job.

docs.title: Transformation node
docs.text: A workflow component that processes or manipulates data. It performs custom operations that modify, extract, or format information as it moves through the workflow. Transformation nodes include Set local variable, JavaScript code, and Python code nodes.

docs.title: Trigger node
docs.text: The entry point that initiates workflow execution. Every workflow requires one trigger node, which is automatically created with the workflow. Multiple triggers can be configured within this node and work as OR conditions: any one of them independently starts the workflow. Available trigger types: Webhook and Scheduler.

docs.title: Trigger payload
docs.text: A built-in variable, referenced as $input.payload, automatically available in every run with no declaration or assignment in a Webhook trigger. It carries the data received by the trigger that started the run, such as the JSON body, headers, and query parameters of a webhook request. See Access the Trigger Payload.

docs.title: VirusTotal integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the VirusTotal API, such as scanning URLs and files, and retrieving domain, IP address, file, and analysis reports.

docs.title: Wazuh integration
docs.text: An integration node that performs operations through the Wazuh server API, such as listing, adding, restarting, and deleting agents, and running active responses and file integrity monitoring scans. It also reads security configuration assessment results, rules, CDB lists, and manager logs.

docs.title: Webhook trigger
docs.text: A trigger type within a trigger node that listens for incoming HTTP requests from external systems or TheHive itself. It accepts the GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, and OPTIONS methods unless the accepted methods are restricted. It defines its own authentication method, because the webhook URL is reachable without signing in to TheHive.

docs.title: WorkflowNext steps
docs.text:
An automated process created in TheHive Flow, consisting of interconnected nodes that define automated procedures. Workflows must begin with a trigger node and can include flows, transformations, actions, and integrations.

  • About TheHive Flow
  • Build Your First Workflow
  • Workflow Templates

docs.title: Export or Import a Workflow
docs.text:
6.0 One

Workflows in TheHive Flow exist at the organization level. You can transfer workflows between different TheHive instances or organizations by exporting and importing them. Importing is also how you bring a ready-made workflow template into your organization.

TheHive Flow has no native versioning. To maintain a change history, the recommended strategy is to export workflows and commit them to a Git repository.

docs.title: Export a workflow
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Share a workflow with another organization or TheHive instance.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. In the workflow list, select next to the workflow you want to export.

  3. Select Export.

Your workflow downloads as a YAML file. The file contains the workflow nodes, variables, and settings. It doesn't contain the Webhook and Scheduler triggers of the workflow.

docs.title: Import a workflowNext steps
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Use a workflow from another organization or TheHive instance, or a ready-made workflow template.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select Import workflow.

  3. In the Import workflow drawer, drop a YAML file or select it from your computer. Use the file you obtained from exporting a workflow, or the file you saved from a workflow template.

  4. Optional: In the Name field, enter a new name for the imported workflow.

  5. Select Import.

The imported workflow starts turned off and has no Webhook or Scheduler trigger. Review it, add the triggers it needs, then enable it.

Workflows with a Subworkflow node

A Subworkflow node refers to the workflow it calls by its identifier, which differs in each organization. After importing a workflow that contains one, import the called workflow too if needed, then select it again in each Subworkflow node.

  • Workflow Templates
  • Manage Workflows

docs.title: Jq Functions
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow evaluates jq expressions with gojq, a Go implementation of jq.

The following fields accept jq expressions:

Field What the expression must return The condition of an If flow node A single boolean, true or false The Field to iterate over of a For each flow node An array or an object to iterate over The JQ value of a loop output variable of a For each flow node Any value, collected at each iteration The expression of an input variable in the Workflow input section of a Webhook trigger Any value, assigned to the input variable The exit variables of a workflow Any value, stored with the run Any node field where an inserted variable reference is displayed as a blue jq expression Any value, inserted in the field

In these fields, entering the first characters of a function name displays a list of matching functions with a short description. The JQ button next to $var opens a searchable list of all functions. Selecting a function inserts only its name: the parentheses and arguments must be added by hand, as shown in the Function column of each table.

docs.title: Write a jq expression
docs.text:
An expression receives no input: . alone evaluates to null. Always start from a variable, inserted with the $var button or by entering $ and selecting a suggestion, for example $input.payload.body.host.name | ascii_downcase.

  • | passes the result on its left as the input of the expression on its right.
  • Function arguments are separated by ;, not by ,: sub("a"; "b"). A comma produces several values.
  • In a string, double each backslash: the regular expression \d is written "\\d", and the domain prefix ACME\ is written "ACME\\".

docs.title: How to read the examples
docs.text:
Examples use literal values so the result can be checked. In a workflow, a variable reference replaces the literal, for example $alert.title | ascii_downcase instead of "Phishing" | ascii_downcase.

Functions that produce several outputs, such as range or scan, are wrapped in [ ] in the examples to collect the outputs into an array.

In the function signatures, filter is a jq expression evaluated by the function, such as .severity > 2 in select(.severity > 2). path is a path expression, such as .password in del(.password). The other argument types are plain values.

docs.title: TheHive Flow functions
docs.text:
These functions are specific to TheHive Flow and aren't part of standard jq.

Function Description Example Result uuid Generates a time-ordered UUID version 7 uuid "0192a3b4-5c6d-7e8f-9a0b-1c2d3e4f5a6b" containsany(string) Returns true if the string contains any character from the given set "team" | containsany("aeiou") true trimleft(string) Removes leading characters that belong to the given set "007" | trimleft("0") "7" trimright(string) Removes trailing characters that belong to the given set "end..." | trimright(".") "end" trim(string) Removes leading and trailing characters that belong to the given set. Standard jq trim takes no argument and removes whitespace only "--x--" | trim("-") "x"

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Function Description Example Result length Returns the length of a string, array, or object, or the absolute value of a number "phishing" | length 8 utf8bytelength Returns the number of bytes needed to encode the string in UTF-8 "café" | utf8bytelength 5 keys Returns the sorted keys of an object, or the indices of an array {"title": "Login", "severity": 3} | keys ["severity", "title"] type Returns the type of the input as a string: "null", "boolean", "number", "string", "array", or "object" [1, 2] | type "array" empty Produces no output. In an If condition, the condition evaluates to false [1, empty, 2] [1, 2] not Returns the boolean negation of the input false | not true env Returns the environment variables. TheHive Flow turns this off and returns an empty object env {} transpose Transposes an array of arrays, padding shorter rows with null [[1, 2], [3]] | transpose [[1, 3], [2, null]] builtins Returns the names of all built-in functions with their number of arguments builtins An array of names such as "map/1" modulemeta Returns metadata about a module. Fails in TheHive Flow "m" | modulemeta Error

docs.title: Type selection
docs.text:
Each function returns the input unchanged when it has the expected type, and produces no output otherwise. Combined with map, they filter an array by type.

Function Description Example Result arrays Selects arrays [1, "a", [2]] | map(arrays) [[2]] objects Selects objects [{"a": 1}, "b"] | map(objects) [{"a": 1}] iterables Selects arrays and objects [1, [2], {"a": 3}] | map(iterables) [[2], {"a": 3}] booleans Selects booleans [true, 1, false] | map(booleans) [true, false] numbers Selects numbers [1, "2", 3] | map(numbers) [1, 3] strings Selects strings ["a", 1, null] | map(strings) ["a"] nulls Selects null values [1, null, 2] | map(nulls) [null] values Selects values that aren't null [1, null, "a"] | map(values) [1, "a"] scalars Selects values that aren't arrays or objects [1, "a", [2], {"b": 3}] | map(scalars) [1, "a"] normals Selects normal numbers: finite, non-zero, and not subnormal [0, 1.5, infinite] | map(normals) [1.5] finites Selects numbers that aren't infinite. nan is kept [1, infinite, nan] | map(finites) [1, null]

docs.title: Objects and arrays
docs.text: Function Description Example Result has(any) Returns true if the object has the given key, or the array has the given index {"title": "Login"} | has("title") true in(object) Returns true if the input key exists in the given object "title" | in({"title": "Login"}) true map(filter) Applies the filter to each element of an array [1, 2, 3] | map(. * 2) [2, 4, 6] map_values(filter) Applies the filter to each value of an object, or each element of an array {"a": 1, "b": 2} | map_values(. + 1) {"a": 2, "b": 3} select(filter) Returns the input unchanged if the filter is true, and produces no output otherwise [1, 5, 8] | map(select(. > 4)) [5, 8] del(path) Removes a key from an object, or an element from an array {"user": "alice", "password": "x"} | del(.password) {"user": "alice"} add, add(filter) Adds the elements of an array together: sums numbers, concatenates strings and arrays, merges objects. With a filter, adds the outputs of the filter [1, 2, 3] | add 6 any, any(filter), any(filter; filter) Returns true if any element of the array is true, or satisfies the condition [1, 5] | any(. > 4) true all, all(filter), all(filter; filter) Returns true if all elements of the array are true, or satisfy the condition [1, 5] | all(. > 4) false sort Sorts the elements of an array. Mixed types sort in this order: null, booleans, numbers, strings, arrays, objects [3, 1, 2] | sort [1, 2, 3] sort_by(filter) Sorts the elements of an array by the result of the filter [{"s": 3}, {"s": 1}] | sort_by(.s) [{"s": 1}, {"s": 3}] group_by(filter) Groups the elements of an array by the result of the filter [{"t": "ip"}, {"t": "url"}, {"t": "ip"}] | group_by(.t) [[{"t": "ip"}, {"t": "ip"}], [{"t": "url"}]] unique Returns the sorted elements of an array without duplicates [3, 1, 3] | unique [1, 3] unique_by(filter) Returns one element per distinct result of the filter [{"id": 1, "v": "a"}, {"id": 1, "v": "b"}] | unique_by(.id) [{"id": 1, "v": "a"}] min Returns the smallest element of an array [3, 1, 2] | min 1 max Returns the largest element of an array [3, 1, 2] | max 3 min_by(filter) Returns the element with the smallest result of the filter [{"s": 3}, {"s": 1}] | min_by(.s) {"s": 1} max_by(filter) Returns the element with the largest result of the filter [{"s": 3}, {"s": 1}] | max_by(.s) {"s": 3} reverse Reverses the elements of an array. Fails on a string: use explode | reverse | implode instead [1, 2, 3] | reverse [3, 2, 1] flatten, flatten(number) Flattens nested arrays, fully or down to the given depth [1, [2, [3]]] | flatten(1) [1, 2, [3]] contains(any) Returns true if the input completely contains the argument. For strings, tests for a substring, also inside arrays: ["tor-exit"] | contains(["tor"]) is true "phishing" | contains("ish") true inside(any) Returns true if the input is completely contained in the argument ["a"] | inside(["a", "b"]) true to_entries Converts an object to an array of {key, value} objects {"a": 1} | to_entries [{"key": "a", "value": 1}] from_entries Converts an array of {key, value} objects to an object [{"key": "a", "value": 1}] | from_entries {"a": 1} with_entries(filter) Applies the filter to each {key, value} entry of an object {"a": 1} | with_entries(.value += 1) {"a": 2} pick(path) Keeps only the given paths of the input {"a": 1, "b": {"c": 2, "d": 3}} | pick(.b.c) {"b": {"c": 2}} bsearch(any) Returns the index of the value in a sorted array. If the value is missing, returns -1 - i where i is the position where it would be inserted [1, 3, 5] | bsearch(3) 1

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
A path is an array of keys and indices that locates a value, such as ["a", "b"] for .a.b.

Function Description Example Result path(filter) Returns the path of the value selected by the filter {"a": {"b": 1}} | path(.a.b) ["a", "b"] paths, paths(filter) Returns all paths of the input, or only the paths of values matching the filter {"a": {"b": 1}} | [paths] [["a"], ["a", "b"]] getpath(array) Returns the value at the given path {"a": {"b": 1}} | getpath(["a", "b"]) 1 setpath(array; any) Sets the value at the given path {} | setpath(["a", "b"]; 1) {"a": {"b": 1}} delpaths(array) Deletes the values at the given paths {"a": 1, "b": 2} | delpaths([["a"]]) {"b": 2}

docs.title: Strings
docs.text: Function Description Example Result startswith(string) Returns true if the string starts with the given prefix "INC-42" | startswith("INC-") true endswith(string) Returns true if the string ends with the given suffix "report.pdf" | endswith(".pdf") true ltrimstr(string) Removes the prefix if present "INC-42" | ltrimstr("INC-") "42" rtrimstr(string) Removes the suffix if present "report.pdf" | rtrimstr(".pdf") "report" trimstr(string) Removes the given string from both ends if present "--x--" | trimstr("--") "x" ltrim Removes leading whitespace " a " | ltrim "a " rtrim Removes trailing whitespace " a " | rtrim " a" trim, trim(string) Removes leading and trailing whitespace. With an argument, removes the given characters instead. See TheHive Flow functions " a " | trim "a" split(string), split(string; string) Splits a string on a separator. With two arguments, the first is a regular expression and the second its flags "a,b,c" | split(",") ["a", "b", "c"] join(string) Joins the elements of an array into a string with the given separator ["a", "b"] | join(", ") "a, b" ascii_downcase Converts ASCII letters to lowercase "Phishing" | ascii_downcase "phishing" ascii_upcase Converts ASCII letters to uppercase "Phishing" | ascii_upcase "PHISHING" explode Converts a string to an array of Unicode code points "AB" | explode [65, 66] implode Converts an array of Unicode code points to a string [65, 66] | implode "AB" index(any) Returns the index of the first occurrence of the argument in a string or array "a,b,c" | index(",") 1 rindex(any) Returns the index of the last occurrence of the argument "a,b,c" | rindex(",") 3 indices(any) Returns the indices of all occurrences of the argument "a,b,c" | indices(",") [1, 3] combinations, combinations(number) Returns all combinations of the elements of the input arrays. With a number, combinations of the input array with itself that many times [[1, 2], [3, 4]] | [combinations] [[1, 3], [1, 4], [2, 3], [2, 4]]

docs.title: Regular expressions
docs.text:
Regular expressions use the RE2 syntax. The optional flags argument accepts g for all matches, i for case-insensitive matching, x for extended mode, n to ignore empty matches, and s for single-line mode.

Function Description Example Result test(string), test(string; string) Returns true if the string matches the regular expression "INC-42" | test("^INC-[0-9]+$") true match(string), match(string; string) Returns a match object with offset, length, string, and captures "INC-42" | match("[0-9]+") | .string "42" capture(string), capture(string; string) Returns an object of the named capture groups "INC-42" | capture("(?<id>[0-9]+)") {"id": "42"} scan(string), scan(string; string) Returns all non-overlapping matches "a1b22" | [scan("[0-9]+")] ["1", "22"] splits(string), splits(string; string) Splits the string on a regular expression, producing one output per part "a1b22c" | [splits("[0-9]+")] ["a", "b", "c"] sub(string; string), sub(string; string; string) Replaces the first match with the replacement string "a-b-c" | sub("-"; "_") "a_b-c" gsub(string; string), gsub(string; string; string) Replaces all matches with the replacement string "a-b-c" | gsub("-"; "_") "a_b_c"

docs.title: Conversion and formatting
docs.text:
Function Description Example Result tonumber Converts a string to a number "42" | tonumber 42 tostring Converts the input to a string. Arrays and objects are encoded as JSON 42 | tostring "42" toboolean Converts the strings "true" and "false" to booleans "true" | toboolean true tojson Encodes the input as a JSON string {"a": 1} | tojson "{\"a\":1}" fromjson Parses a JSON string into a value "{\"a\":1}" | fromjson {"a": 1} format(string) Formats the input with the named format: base64, base64d, csv, html, json, sh, text, tsv, uri, or urid. Same as the @base64 shorthand syntax "hi" | format("base64") "aGk="

A format can precede a string: only the \(...) parts are encoded. A typical use is building a pivot URL, for example $input.payload.body.source.ip | @uri "https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/\(.)".

docs.title: Dates and times
docs.text:
Timestamps are Unix timestamps, in seconds. A broken-down time is an array of [year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds, day of week, day of year], with the month, day of week, and day of year starting at 0.

Function Description Example Result now Returns the current Unix timestamp, with decimals now | floor 1790812800 todate Formats a Unix timestamp as an ISO 8601 date string 1700000000 | todate "2023-11-14T22:13:20Z" fromdate Parses an ISO 8601 date string into a Unix timestamp. Fails on fractions of seconds: remove them first with sub("\\.[0-9]+"; "") "2023-11-14T22:13:20Z" | fromdate 1700000000 todateiso8601 Same as todate 1700000000 | todateiso8601 "2023-11-14T22:13:20Z" fromdateiso8601 Same as fromdate "2023-11-14T22:13:20Z" | fromdateiso8601 1700000000 gmtime Converts a Unix timestamp to a broken-down time in UTC 1700000000 | gmtime [2023, 10, 14, 22, 13, 20, 2, 317] localtime Converts a Unix timestamp to a broken-down time in the time zone of the server running TheHive Flow 1700000000 | localtime [2023, 10, 14, 22, 13, 20, 2, 317] on a UTC server mktime Converts a broken-down time to a Unix timestamp [2023, 10, 14, 22, 13, 20, 2, 317] | mktime 1700000000 strftime(string) Formats a Unix timestamp or broken-down time with a format string 1700000000 | strftime("%Y-%m-%d") "2023-11-14" strptime(string) Parses a string into a broken-down time with a format string "2023-11-14" | strptime("%Y-%m-%d") [2023, 10, 14, 0, 0, 0, 2, 317] strflocaltime(string) Formats a Unix timestamp or broken-down time with a format string, in the time zone of the server running TheHive Flow 1700000000 | strflocaltime("%H:%M") "22:13" on a UTC server

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text: Function Description Example Result range(number), range(number; number), range(number; number; number) Generates numbers up to a limit, from a start, with a step [range(1; 4)] [1, 2, 3] while(filter; filter) Repeats an update while the condition is true, producing each value [1 | while(. < 10; . * 2)] [1, 2, 4, 8] until(filter; filter) Repeats an update until the condition is true, producing the final value 1 | until(. > 10; . * 2) 16 repeat(filter) Applies the filter to the input again and again, producing the same result endlessly. Wrap it in limit. To update a value at each step, use while or range [limit(3; 1 | repeat(. * 2))] [2, 2, 2] recurse, recurse(filter), recurse(filter; filter) Produces the input and all its nested values. With a filter, follows the filter instead, optionally while a condition holds {"a": [1]} | [recurse] [{"a": [1]}, [1], 1] walk(filter) Applies the filter to every nested value, bottom up [1, [2]] | walk(if type == "number" then . + 1 else . end) [2, [3]] limit(number; filter) Produces at most the given number of outputs of the filter [limit(2; range(10))] [0, 1] skip(number; filter) Skips the given number of outputs of the filter [skip(2; range(4))] [2, 3] first, first(filter) Returns the first element of an array, or the first output of the filter [3, 1] | first 3 last, last(filter) Returns the last element of an array, or the last output of the filter [3, 1] | last 1 nth(number), nth(number; filter) Returns the element at the given index of an array, or the output at that position of the filter [3, 1, 2] | nth(1) 1 isempty(filter) Returns true if the filter produces no output [] | isempty(.[]) true

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text: Function Description Example Result error, error(string) Fails the expression, with the input or the argument as the error message. Wrap the expression in try and catch to get a fallback value instead: try ("abc" | tonumber) catch "not a number" {"a": 1} | .b // error("Missing b") Error Missing b halt Stops the expression without an error. Values already produced are kept, and the following ones are dropped. Inside [ ], the array is never produced, so the example isn't wrapped. An If condition using it evaluates to false 1, 2, halt, 3 1 and 2 halt_error, halt_error(number) Fails the expression with the input as the error message. Stops like halt when the input is null. The exit code argument is ignored "Unexpected status" | halt_error Error Unexpected status

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
A stream represents a value as a sequence of [path, value] pairs.

Function Description Example Result tostream Converts the input to a stream {"a": [1]} | [tostream] [[["a", 0], 1], [["a", 0]], [["a"]]] fromstream(filter) Rebuilds a value from a stream fromstream({"a": [1]} | tostream) {"a": [1]} truncate_stream(filter) Removes the given number of leading path levels from a stream [1 | truncate_stream([[0], 1], [[1, 0], 2], [[1, 0]], [[1]])] [[[0], 2], [[0]]]

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text: Pitfall What happens What to do Comparing a string to a number "73" > 70 and "5" > 70 both return true: any string is greater than any number Convert first: $<node_name>.body.risk_score | tonumber > 70 Separating arguments with , sub("a", "b") doesn't pass two arguments: the comma produces two values Separate arguments with ;: sub("a"; "b") A condition that returns several values $<node_name>.body.observables[] | .dataType == "ip" returns one boolean per observable, and the If node fails with too many jq values Reduce the result to a single boolean with any, all, or length > 0 A condition that returns nothing An empty result, from a select that keeps nothing or from halt, evaluates to false Make the case explicit with isempty when needed A condition that doesn't return a boolean A number or a string makes the If node fail with did not yield a boolean End the condition with a comparison Starting from . . evaluates to null: .alert.id returns null, and split(",") fails Start from a variable Fractions of seconds in a date "2026-09-29T08:12:31.482Z" | fromdate fails Use sub("\\.[0-9]+"; "") | fromdate Timestamps in milliseconds TheHive, Elastic, and many APIs return milliseconds: todate then returns a date in the year 58709 Divide by 1000 Months in a broken-down time Months range from 0 to 11: September is 8 Add 1 for display, or use strftime localtime and strflocaltime They use the time zone of the server running TheHive Flow, not the time zone of the analyst Prefer gmtime and strftime, and state UTC in the text contains on an array of strings ["tor-exit"] | contains(["tor"]) returns true, because strings match as substrings Use any(.[]; . == "tor") for a strict match Single backslashes in strings "ACME\j" is invalid Double backslashes: "ACME\\j", and in a regular expression "\\d" or "\\." Endless generators repeat or range(1e12) stop after 100,000 results, and the expression fails Wrap generators in limit(<number>; <stream>) Secret variables in a For each node The workflow validation rejects $secret in the Field to iterate over, because the iterated list is stored as is Use secret variables in the fields of action and integration nodes

docs.title: Manage Global Variables
docs.text:
6.0 One

Use global variables to share fixed values across all workflows within an organization in TheHive Flow. These values are centrally managed and can't be modified within workflows.

Local variables

If you need variables whose values are set during execution, use local variables. They're scoped to a single workflow and created with a Set local variable transformation node.

docs.title: Create a global variable
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeVariables

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select the Global variables tab.

  3. Select .

  4. In the Create a variable drawer, enter the following information:

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Name *

    A unique name for your global variable within the organization.

    - Secret

    Turn on this toggle to hide confidential information such as API keys, passwords, or SSL/TLS certificate files. The value of a secret variable is never displayed in the interface and never appears in execution logs or API responses. Leave it off for visible values such as API URLs or team identifiers.

    - Value *

    The global variable type and its value. The available types are Boolean, JSON, List, Number, and String.

    - Description

    A description of the global variable.

  5. Select Save.

Once created, a global variable can be referenced in any node field that supports variables. Insert the reference with the $var button, or enter $ in the field and start entering the variable name to filter the suggestions. In both cases, select one of the suggestions to insert the reference. You can't enter it in full manually. Inserted references are displayed in the following form:

  • $global.<variable_name>: For a visible variable
  • $secret.<variable_name>: For a secret variable

docs.title: Modify a global variable
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeVariables

Variables used in workflows

While a variable is used in a workflow, you can modify its name, value, and description, but not its type or its secret setting. Renaming a variable automatically updates its references in the workflows that use it. The Usage count column in the Global variables tab shows how many times a variable is used.

  1. In the Global variables tab, select the name of the global variable you want to modify.

  2. In the Edit a variable drawer, update the fields.

    If you turn off the Secret toggle, enter the value again. The existing value stays hidden and isn't carried over to the visible variable.

  3. Select Save.

docs.title: Delete a global variableNext steps
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/deleteVariables

Variables used in workflows

A global variable that's used in a workflow can't be deleted. Remove its references from all workflows first. The Usage count column in the Global variables tab shows how many times a variable is used.

  1. In the Global variables tab, select next to the global variable you want to delete.

  2. Select Delete.

  3. Select OK.

  • Manage Workflows
  • Manage Input and Exit Variables

docs.title: Manage Input and Exit Variables
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Workflow input and exit variables define the interface of a workflow, so it can exchange data with external systems, or with another workflow that calls it through a Subworkflow node.

Input variables can be declared and assigned directly in the Workflow input section when configuring a Webhook trigger, using a jq expression applied to the incoming request. When the workflow is run from a case or alert page, input variables can receive the case or alert identifier. When the workflow is called by a Subworkflow node, input variables receive the values entered in that node. Input variables can also be declared in the workflow settings. Use the settings for a workflow without a Webhook trigger, and to manage input variables for all nodes of the workflow, for example to rename, describe, or delete them. Reference input variables in nodes with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting the variable from the suggestions. An inserted reference is displayed as $input.<variable_name>. The value each input variable got for a run is displayed in its run summary.

Exit variables are named jq expressions evaluated when the workflow completes. Their values are stored with the run and displayed in its run summary. When the workflow is called by a Subworkflow node, the nodes that follow it in the calling workflow read the exit variables as outputs of that node.

Testing workflows with input variables

Input variables can't be passed when running a workflow manually from the workflow editor. If your workflow relies on input data to run, add a Set local variable node at the beginning with hardcoded test values. A manual run from a case or alert page passes a single input, the entity identifier, assigned to the case_id or alert_id input variable when the workflow declares it.

docs.title: Create an input or exit variable
docs.text:
1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Select , then Settings.

  4. Add the variable:

    • For an input variable, go to the Input variables section, select , enter a Variable name, select a Type, and enter an optional Description. The name must be unique in the workflow. The available types are String, Number, Boolean, Array, JSON, and Raw. String is the default. Use Raw for a file uploaded with a webhook request. The name payload is reserved for the trigger payload and can't be used.
    • For an exit variable, go to the Output variables section, select , and enter an Output name and a JQ value. In the JQ value field, reference a variable with the $var button, or by entering $ and selecting the variable from the suggestions.

    TheHive Flow evaluates the exit variable expression when the workflow completes, so it can reference any variable of the run, including the outputs of the last nodes. An exit variable can't reference a secret global variable. The functions available in expressions are listed in Jq Functions.

    Accessing a field from a variable

    To access a field, enter .<field_name> directly after the variable.

    Exit variable examples

    • $<node_name>.body._id: Returns the identifier of the case or alert created by a TheHive integration node.
    • $<node_name>.body | map(.data): Returns the values of the observables listed by a TheHive integration node as an array, for example with the Post Query action.
    • $<node_name>.body | map(select(.ioc)) | length: Returns the number of listed observables flagged as indicators of compromise (IOCs).
    • {caseId: $<node_name>.body._id, status: (if $<node_name>.code == 201 then "created" else "failed" end)}: Returns an object combining several outputs.

An input variable has no value until it's assigned. Assign it in the Workflow input section of a Webhook trigger, through a run from a case or alert page, or in the Subworkflow inputs section of a Subworkflow node that calls the workflow.

docs.title: Delete an input or exit variableNext steps
docs.text:
1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow from the list.

  3. Select , then Settings.

  4. In the Input variables or Output variables section, select next to the variable you want to delete.

    An input variable that's referenced by a node or assigned a value in a Webhook trigger can't be deleted. Remove those uses first.

Workflows called by a Subworkflow node

Deleting or renaming an input variable of a workflow that other workflows call through a Subworkflow node doesn't update those calling workflows. A calling workflow that assigned a value to that input variable can't run until its node is updated. Deleting or renaming an exit variable breaks the references to it in the calling workflows.

docs.title: Manage Workflows
docs.text:
6.0 One

Workflows in TheHive Flow consist of interconnected nodes that define automated processes. They begin with a trigger and can include flow, transformation, action, and integration nodes. Workflows are scoped to the organization and shared among all members with sufficient permissions. There's no personal or user-isolated workspace.

Relationship to existing automation features

TheHive Flow workflows cover most of the use cases handled by existing automation features in TheHive, including notifications, alert feeders, functions, and Cortex responders. These features remain available and usable on their own. TheHive Flow adds multi-step logic, conditional branching, scheduled execution, and a visual workflow editor, all natively within TheHive, without requiring code or an external tool.

Reusing workflows

You can import workflows from other TheHive instances or organizations.

docs.title: Create a workflow
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Create workflows in TheHive Flow to automate operations when specific events occur.

  1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select .

  3. In the Workflow information drawer, enter the following information:

    Fields marked with * are mandatory.

    - Name *

    The name of your workflow.

    - Description

    A description of your workflow.

    - Tags

    Free text tags to categorize and filter workflows.

    - Timeout

    The maximum allowed execution time for the entire workflow. Defaults to 1 hour if left blank. The minimum allowed value is 30 seconds.

    You can also configure different timeout values at the node level. In that case, the shortest timeout value applies.

    The timeout also prevails over the duration of a Sleep flow node: if the duration exceeds the workflow timeout, the execution times out before the pause completes.

  4. Select Save.

    TheHive creates a workflow with a default trigger node. The trigger node is the entry point that initiates workflow execution.

  5. Optional: To declare the workflow's input and exit variables, select , then Settings, and fill in the Input variables and Output variables sections.

    You can also declare and assign input variables directly when configuring a Webhook trigger. A run from a case or alert page assigns the case or alert identifier to an input variable named case_id or alert_id when the workflow declares it. The identifier is also always available in the trigger payload.

  6. Optional: Create global variables to store fixed values shared across workflows. See Manage Global Variables for detailed instructions.

    Local variables

    If you need variables whose values are set during execution, use local variables. They're scoped to a single workflow and created with a Set local variable transformation node.

  7. Select Add a trigger to configure one or more triggers in the trigger node.

    For configuration instructions, see Add a Trigger.

    Manual trigger from the workflow editor

    The trigger node always lists a Manual entry, alongside any triggers you configure. It requires no configuration and can't be removed: you can manually run a workflow from the workflow editor even without configuring any triggers.

  8. Add nodes to build your workflow by dragging the previous node connector to an empty area of the canvas.

  9. Select the node you want to add:

    • Flow nodes to control workflow branching and loops
    • Transformation nodes to process and manipulate data
    • Action nodes to perform generic operations such as sending requests or messages, running Cortex analyzers and responders, or calling an LLM
    • Integration nodes to perform operations in TheHive or third-party products through their APIs

    For configuration instructions, see Configure a Flow Node, Configure a Transformation Node, Configure an Action Node, or Configure an Integration Node.

Once created, the workflow is automatically saved.

docs.title: Duplicate a workflow
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Duplicate a workflow to reuse its structure, or to keep a copy before making significant changes, because workflows have no versioning.

  1. In the workflow list, select next to the workflow you want to duplicate.

  2. Select Duplicate.

The copy takes the name of the original workflow followed by - Copy. To rename it, select next to the copy, then Settings. The copy starts turned off and has no Webhook or Scheduler trigger: add the triggers it needs, then enable it.

docs.title: Duplicate a node
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

No versioning

There's no workflow versioning. Any modification is applied immediately to the active workflow. Duplicate a workflow before making significant changes. To keep a history, export your workflows and version them in a Git repository.

  1. In a workflow, select on the node you want to duplicate.

  2. Select Duplicate.

docs.title: Delete a node
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Trigger node can't be deleted

The trigger node is mandatory and can't be deleted from a workflow. However, you can delete individual triggers inside the trigger node.

Deleting a node invalidates references to its outputs

Later nodes can reference the deleted node's output or local variables. After the deletion, these references become invalid and the affected nodes report errors. Until you update or remove the invalid references, a workflow can't be enabled, and an already enabled workflow rejects every run attempt, whether triggered or manual.

No versioning

There's no workflow versioning. Any modification is applied immediately to the active workflow. Duplicate a workflow before making significant changes. To keep a history, export your workflows and version them in a Git repository.

  1. In a workflow, select on the node you want to delete.

  2. Select Delete.

docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Deleting a branch can invalidate references to outputs

When the branch is the only path to a node whose output variables are referenced downstream, the confirmation shows a warning. After the deletion, these references become invalid and the affected nodes report errors. Until you update or remove these references, a workflow can't be enabled, and an already enabled workflow rejects every run attempt, whether triggered or manual.

No versioning

There's no workflow versioning. Any modification is applied immediately to the active workflow. Duplicate a workflow before making significant changes. To keep a history, export your workflows and version them in a Git repository.

  1. In a workflow, hover over the branch between two nodes to reveal its actions.

  2. Select .

  3. Select Delete.

docs.title: Enable a workflow
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Enable a workflow to run it automatically when triggered. You can also run an enabled workflow manually from the workflow editor or from a case or alert page.

Resolve errors before enabling

You can't enable a workflow that contains errors. Errors are marked in the workflow with . Resolve all errors before enabling the workflow.

In the workflow editor, select Enable workflow.

docs.title: Turn off a workflow
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Turn off a workflow to edit it without affecting production operations. A workflow that's turned off never runs. Its triggers are ignored and manual runs are unavailable. A Subworkflow node that calls it fails, so turning it off also affects the workflows that call it.

In the workflow editor, select Disable workflow.

docs.title: Delete a workflowNext steps
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/deleteWorkflows

Permanent action

Deleting a workflow is permanent and can't be undone. To pause a workflow temporarily, turn it off instead.

Workflows that call the deleted workflow through a Subworkflow node can't run until another workflow is selected in that node.

  1. In the workflow list, select next to the workflow you want to delete.

  2. Select Delete.

  3. Select OK.

docs.title: Manually Run a Workflow
docs.text:
6.0 manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows One

Execute your workflow on demand, regardless of its trigger configuration: from the workflow editor while building it, or from a case or alert page in TheHive.

Prerequisite

You must enable a workflow, and resolve any errors marked with , before you can run it manually.

Testing workflows with input variables

Input variables can't be passed when running a workflow manually from the workflow editor. If your workflow relies on input data to run, add a Set local variable node at the beginning with hardcoded test values. A manual run from a case or alert page passes a single input, the entity identifier, assigned to the case_id or alert_id input variable when the workflow declares it.

docs.title: Run a workflow from the workflow editor
docs.text:
1. Go to the Flow view from the sidebar menu.

  2. Select a workflow.

  3. In the workflow editor, select Run workflow.

docs.title: Run a workflow from a case or alertNext steps
docs.text:
manageOrchestrator/readWorkflows manageOrchestrator/writeWorkflows

Run a workflow on a specific case or alert from its Automation Center, in the Automations tab.

  1. Open a case or an alert.

  2. Go to the Automations tab.

  3. Select the Workflows tab.

    The tab lists the workflow runs already launched on the case or alert.

  4. Select Run workflows.

  5. Select one or more workflows, then select Launch action(s).

Each selected workflow runs once. TheHive passes the identifier of the case or alert to the run as a variable named case_id or alert_id. The identifier is available in the nodes as $input.payload.case_id or $input.payload.alert_id, through the trigger payload. To reference it as $input.case_id or $input.alert_id instead, declare an input variable with that exact name.

docs.title: Workflow Templates
docs.text:
6.0 One

TheHive Flow provides ready-made workflow templates that cover common security automation scenarios. Each template is available as YAML code in its own section. Save the code as a .yaml file, import it into your organization, then adapt some of its elements to your environment.

docs.title: Customization common to all templates
docs.text:
Templates contain placeholders instead of real connection details: https://thehive.example.com for the URL of TheHive and <THEHIVE_API_KEY> for its API key. Templates that call third-party products use placeholders for their credentials too, such as <SLACK_BOT_TOKEN> or <JIRA_API_TOKEN>. A workflow can't run until you replace them.

Create the global variables before importing a template, so they're ready to select while you adapt the workflow:

  1. Create a global variable holding the URL of your TheHive instance.

  2. Create a secret global variable holding the API key used to authenticate against TheHive.

  3. Create the global variables listed in the section of the template, if any, for the third-party products it calls.

After import, replace the placeholders with your variables in the Base URL and Bearer token fields of every TheHive integration node.

A template file doesn't contain triggers. A template that starts from a Webhook or Scheduler trigger needs it added after import, as described in its section.

docs.title: Alert triage
docs.text:
The Alert triage template automates the first triage of alerts coming from a third-party detection product, in this template an Elastic Security EDR.

Each alert the product sends to the Webhook trigger becomes a normalized alert in TheHive, with its severity, observables, and MITRE ATT&CK techniques carried over. The workflow then checks the reputation of the IP address and hash observables against Recorded Future.

When threat intelligence confirms an indicator of compromise (IOC), the workflow raises the alert severity to Critical, escalates the alert to a case, and lists the malicious indicators in a case comment. Alerts without a confirmed IOC stay in the alert queue for manual review.

Before importing this template, prepare the following elements:

  • Recorded Future API key: Create a secret global variable holding your Recorded Future API key.
  • Custom fields: The normalization script fills a sourcefields custom field on the alert. Create this custom field in TheHive with sourcefields as its technical name and the String type. TheHive rejects the alert creation when this custom field doesn't exist. To skip this step, remove the customFields section from the Normalize Alert script after import.

After importing this template, adjust the following elements:

  • TheHive connection: Set the base URL and API key in every TheHive node, as described in Customization common to all templates.
  • Recorded Future API key: Select your secret global variable instead of the <RECORDED_FUTURE_API_KEY> placeholder in the API Token field of both Recorded Future integration nodes, Recorded Future IP check and Recorded Future Hash check. Replace these nodes with your own intelligence provider if you don't use Recorded Future.
  • Trigger: Add a Webhook trigger to the workflow. In its Workflow input section, assign $request.body to the ElasticAlert input variable, then configure the detection product to send its alerts to the trigger URL. To test the workflow without Elastic Security, send it the sample alert at the end of this section.
  • Normalization script: The Normalize Alert Python node maps Elastic Security fields, such as kibana.alert.severity and host.ip, to TheHive alert fields. Rewrite this mapping if your alerts come from another product. The script reads most fields directly and fails when an alert lacks one of them, for example registry.path on an alert that doesn't involve the registry. It adds a hash observable only when the alert carries process.hash.sha256.
  • Data type conditions: The If dataType IP and If dataType Hash conditions route observables to enrichment. Adapt them if you enrich other data types.
  • Escalation threshold: The If Recorded Report Malicious condition escalates at a risk score of 65 or higher, and the TheHive add Comment Case node lists the indicators reaching the same score. Change this value in both nodes to match your triage policy.

docs.title: Command line analysis
docs.text:
The Command line analysis template reveals what the PowerShell command lines attached to an alert do and surfaces the IOCs they contain. It has no trigger: run it manually from an alert in TheHive.

Malicious commands are often obfuscated with a Base64-encoded -EncodedCommand argument, or one of its abbreviations such as -Enc or -ec: the workflow decodes them and documents the decoded command on the alert, both as a comment and as a new command-line observable. It then adds the IP addresses, URLs, domains, and hashes it finds as observables, extracted from the decoded command or from the raw command line when no encoding is present.

Before importing this template, create a command-line observable type in TheHive. Without it, alerts can't carry the observables this workflow reads and creates.

After importing this template, adjust the following elements:

  • TheHive connection: Set the base URL and API key in every TheHive node, as described in Customization common to all templates.
  • Command lines to analyze: The Set Command Line Array node selects the command-line observables of the alert from the Get Alert Observables node output. Change its filter if your command lines use another observable type.
  • Extraction patterns: The If Base64 Encoded condition detects the -EncodedCommand argument and its abbreviations, in any case and with a - or / prefix. The Python code nodes extract IOCs with regular expressions. They discard domain matches that are file names, such as payload.ps1, or PowerShell and .NET type names, such as Net.WebClient. Extend these patterns if your commands use other encodings or if you want to extract other data types.

  3ff19619-cb57-4545-9f90-b61f3c159f6e:
    id: 3ff19619-cb57-4545-9f90-b61f3c159f6e
    name: Extract IOCs Decoded Command
    type: action
    on_success: 7a6dff56-9d50-4ecb-a8cd-9e59673da929
    command:
      command: strangebee.code.execute.python@v3_11
      version: v1.0.0
      type: strangebee
      parameters:
        script: >-
          import re


          cmd =
          flow.get('$steps["0d87781c-739f-40e6-8e84-add53fa70554"].b64_decode')
          or ""


          patterns = {
              "ip":     r'\b(?:(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\d|[01]?\d\d?)\.){3}(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\d|[01]?\d\d?)\b',
              "url":    r'https?://[^\s"\'<>]+',
              "domain": r'\b(?:[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}\b',
              "hash":   r'\b[a-fA-F0-9]{64}\b|\b[a-fA-F0-9]{40}\b|\b[a-fA-F0-9]{32}\b',
          }


          # A "domain" match ending with one of these extensions is a file name

          FILE_EXTS = {
              '.exe', '.dll', '.ps1', '.psm1', '.psd1', '.bat', '.cmd', '.sys', '.vbs', '.vbe',
              '.js', '.jse', '.wsf', '.hta', '.msi', '.scr', '.cpl', '.ocx', '.drv', '.lnk',
              '.bin', '.dat', '.tmp', '.log', '.txt', '.csv', '.ini', '.cfg', '.xml', '.json',
              '.zip', '.rar', '.7z', '.gz', '.tar', '.cab', '.iso', '.img', '.jar', '.py',
              '.sh', '.php', '.doc', '.docx', '.docm', '.xls', '.xlsx', '.xlsm', '.pdf',
              '.rtf', '.png', '.jpg',
          }


          # Hosts of extracted URLs are always kept as domains, whatever their
          case

          url_hosts = {re.match(r'https?://([^/:?#]+)', u).group(1) for u in
          re.findall(patterns["url"], cmd)}


          def is_domain(match):
              if match in url_hosts:
                  return True
              labels = match.split(".")
              # Mixed-case label = .NET / PowerShell type (Net.WebClient, System.IO.File)
              if any(l != l.lower() and l != l.upper() for l in labels):
                  return False
              return "." + labels[-1].lower() not in FILE_EXTS


          seen = set()

          iocs = []

          for dtype, pattern in patterns.items():
              for match in re.findall(pattern, cmd):
                  if dtype == "domain" and not is_domain(match):
                      continue
                  key = f"{dtype}:{match}"
                  if key not in seen:
                      seen.add(key)
                      iocs.append({"dataType": dtype, "data": match})

          flow.set("iocs", iocs)

docs.title: GetCVECircl
docs.text:
The GetCVECircl template turns the CVEs published by CIRCL for a given vendor and product into alerts in TheHive.

The workflow queries the CIRCL search API for the configured vendor and product and keeps the entries that are complete CVE records. It creates one alert per CVE with the type CVE, the source CIRCL, and the CVE identifier as source reference. Each alert carries a structured description covering the technical description, the affected product and versions, the vulnerability type, recommended actions, and references.

TheHive rejects an alert matching the type, source, and source reference of an existing one, so a new run fails on the CVEs already imported rather than duplicating them. Run it manually from the workflow editor, or add a Scheduler trigger to fetch new CVEs at a regular interval.

The Build Your First Workflow tutorial builds a simplified version of this workflow step by step. Import this template to get the result directly, or follow the tutorial to learn the underlying concepts along the way.

After importing this template, adjust the following elements:

  • TheHive connection: Set the base URL and API key in every TheHive node, as described in Customization common to all templates.
  • Vendor and product: The Set vendor + product node ships with apple and macos. Set the two variables to the vendor and product you monitor, spelled as the CIRCL API expects them.
  • Alert description: The Set Alert Title & Description node reads the first entry of each list in the CVE record, such as the first affected product and the first reference. Adapt the description template if you need other fields.
  • Server verification: The Get CVE Circl node ships with Certificate Authorities set to Disabled, so it doesn't verify the identity of the CIRCL server. Set it to Default unless a proxy on your network intercepts TLS traffic.

docs.title: Slack alert manager
docs.text:
The Slack alert manager template lets your team triage new TheHive alerts directly from Slack: an emoji reaction acknowledges the alert, raises its severity, or closes it as a false positive.

A Webhook trigger wired to a TheHive notification starts the workflow when an alert is created. The workflow posts a message announcing the alert title and severity in a Slack channel, then watches the message for about 3 minutes. Emoji reactions drive actions on the alert in TheHive:

Reaction Action in TheHive :hand: Adds a comment acknowledging the alert with the name of the Slack user who reacted :exclamation: Sets the alert severity to Critical :x: Sets the alert status to FalsePositive

The workflow also copies new Slack thread replies to the alert as comments.

Before importing this template, create a secret global variable holding your Slack bot token. The token needs the chat:write, reactions:read, channels:history, and users:read scopes, or groups:history instead of channels:history for a private channel. Invite the bot to the channel the workflow posts in.

After importing this template, adjust the following elements:

  • TheHive connection: Set the base URL and API key in every TheHive node, as described in Customization common to all templates.
  • Slack credentials: Select your secret global variable instead of the <SLACK_BOT_TOKEN> placeholder in the Bearer token field of every Slack node. In the Slack Send Message node, replace the <SLACK_CHANNEL_ID> placeholder with the identifier of the channel to post in.
  • Trigger: Add a Webhook trigger to the workflow. In its Workflow input section, assign $request.body to the TheHiveAlert input variable. Then create the notification in TheHive with the AlertCreated trigger and a Webhook notifier pointing to the trigger URL.
  • Email notification: The Send Email - Critical Alert node ships with N/A placeholders and no branch to the rest of the workflow. To notify by email when an alert turns critical, set the sender and recipient addresses and add a branch to the node from the Update Alert - Severity Critical node. Otherwise, remove it.
  • Alert status: The :x: reaction sets the FalsePositive status. Change it if your organization uses other alert statuses.
  • Watch duration: The For Each (While) loop runs nine iterations with a 20-second pause. Reactions and replies added afterward are ignored. Increase these values to watch reactions for longer, within the 1-hour timeout of the workflow.

docs.title: Suspicious email campaign
docs.text:
The Suspicious email campaign template processes the emails your users report and detects phishing campaigns: it enriches each reported email alert and groups the alerts belonging to the same campaign into a single case.

Users forward suspicious emails to a mailbox monitored by the email intake connector, which creates one alert per email with the .eml file attached. A Scheduler trigger runs the workflow at a regular interval, for example every 15 minutes.

Each run retrieves the new alerts created by the connector and parses each email with the EmlParser Cortex analyzer. It updates the alert with the sender, subject, and a preview of the email, and adds the suspicious sender and domain as observables.

The workflow then searches for an open case with the same email subject and sender. If one exists, the workflow merges the alert into the most recent one. Otherwise, it escalates the alert to a new case carrying a campaign identifier. In both cases, the workflow adds a page with the email headers to the case.

Before importing this template, prepare TheHive and Cortex:

  • Custom fields: Create the custom fields that the workflow fills, with the String type and the following technical names. For alerts, these are sender, recipient, reporter, and reporteddate. For cases, it's campaign. TheHive rejects the update requests when these custom fields don't exist.
  • Email intake: Keep the default email-intake tag on the alerts created by the email intake connector. The Get Unprocessed Email-Intake Alerts node selects alerts by this tag and the New status. The Find EML Attachment Observable node reads the .eml file observable the connector adds to each alert. The workflow expects forwarded emails: on an email that wasn't forwarded, the extracted sender and date can be wrong.
  • Cortex analyzer: Enable the EmlParser analyzer on a Cortex server connected to TheHive. The email preview requires the email_visualisation option of the analyzer, off by default. Turn it on in the analyzer configuration in Cortex. Without it, the analyzer returns no rendering of the email and the Upload Email Screenshot as Attachment node fails.

After importing this template, adjust the following elements:

  • TheHive connection: Set the base URL and API key in every TheHive node, as described in Customization common to all templates. The Add Email Headers Page to Case (Merged) and Add Email Headers Page to Case (New) nodes are HTTP request nodes calling TheHive API directly. In both, replace https://thehive.example.com at the start of the URL field with your global variable, and <THEHIVE_API_KEY> with your secret global variable in the Authentication section.
  • Cortex analyzer: In the Run EmlParser Analyzer node, select your Cortex server and the EmlParser analyzer. The template ships with no Cortex server and an <EMLPARSER_ANALYZER_ID> placeholder.
  • Trigger: Add a Scheduler trigger with an interval matching your email volume, typically every 15 to 30 minutes.
